answer: Husky is an npm package that manages Git hooks through package.json. Because .git/hooks is not committed to the repository, raw hooks do not propagate to teammates. Husky solves this by installing hooks from package.json into .git/hooks when running npm install — every team member gets the same hooks automatically.

question: What is the commit-msg hook and how is it used with Conventional Commits?
answer: The commit-msg hook runs after you type a commit message but before the commit is saved. It receives the path to the file containing the message. question: Explain how you would set up a pre-commit hook with Husky and lint-staged to lint only staged files.
answer:
The goal is linting only the files actually staged for this commit, not the whole project, so the hook stays fast even on a large codebase.

After installing husky and lint-staged and running npx husky init, add a lint-staged block to package.json:

{
  "lint-staged": {
    "*.{ts,js}": ["eslint --fix", "prettier --write"],
    "*.{css,html}": ["prettier --write"]
  }
}

Then point .husky/pre-commit at npx lint-staged. From then on, every git commit runs ESLint and Prettier only against the staged files: unfixable lint errors abort the commit with the error shown, and any auto-formatting changes need to be re-staged before committing again.

This is a standard setup on frontend teams because it enforces quality without slowing commits down as the codebase grows.
hint: Husky pre-commit → lint-staged → ESLint + Prettier on staged files only → abort on errors.

question: What is Node.js?
answer: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine that lets you run JavaScript outside the browser — on servers, CLIs, and desktop apps. It uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model, making it efficient for data-intensive real-time applications.

question: Two requests hit your server at the same time — one reads a huge file, the other just returns a quick JSON response. The quick one finishes first even though it arrived second. What does "non-blocking I/O" mean in Node.js?

question: Your server handles thousands of concurrent connections on a single thread without ever spawning a new one per request. What is the event loop in Node.js?

question: What is the global object in Node.js?

question: Your team is choosing a backend for a real-time chat API expected to handle 50,000 simultaneous connections, mostly idle waiting for messages. Why is Node.js a strong fit here, and where would that same strength become a liability?
answer:
Most of those 50,000 connections spend almost all of their time waiting on I/O — waiting for the next message, not doing computation — and Node.js's single-threaded event loop can hold thousands of idle connections open cheaply because it is never blocked while waiting.

That same strength turns into a liability the moment real CPU work shows up in the request path — image processing, video encoding, or heavy synchronous parsing. That kind of work occupies the one thread the event loop runs on, freezing every other connection until it finishes.

For CPU-heavy work, the fix is to offload it to worker_threads or a separate service, rather than running it inline on the main thread.
hint: Great for I/O-bound APIs and real-time; poor for CPU-heavy tasks that block the event loop.

In the original code, only the very first readFile('a.txt', ...) callback checks if (err) return cb(err); before continuing. async function merge(cb) {

    const a = await fs.promises.readFile('a.txt');
    const b = await fs.promises.readFile('b.txt');
    const c = await fs.promises.readFile('c.txt');
    const d = await fs.promises.readFile('d.txt');
    await fs.promises.writeFile('out.txt', a + b + c + d);
    cb(null);
  } catch (err) {
    cb(err);
  }
}

A single try/catch now wraps every await in the chain, so an error from any one of the four reads — or the write — is caught in exactly one place instead of depending on four separate manual checks that are easy to forget. answer:
The built-in http module does not parse the request body automatically. The req object is a readable stream, so the body data arrives as a sequence of chunks over time rather than as a value that's already available when the handler runs.

To read the body, the chunks need to be collected as they arrive and combined once the stream ends:

req.on('end', () => {
  const data = JSON.parse(body); // JSON: JavaScript Object Notation
  res.end('ok');
});

question: Describe a real use case for Node.js streams and why they are better than loading data into memory.
answer:
A server endpoint exporting a large database result set as a CSV file is a good example. Without streams, every row would need to be queried into an array and the entire CSV string built in memory before sending anything — using as much memory as the whole result set, and making the client wait for the full build before a single byte arrives.

With streams, a query stream is piped through a transform that converts each row to a CSV line, and piped straight into the response:

dbStream.pipe(csvTransform).pipe(res);

Memory now stays flat regardless of result set size, the client starts receiving data immediately, and if they disconnect partway through, the stream simply stops instead of continuing to build something nobody is reading. The same pattern applies to file reads, video transcoding, or any case where the data is larger than available memory, or where time-to-first-byte matters.
hint: Stream large data (CSV export, video, file download) to keep memory constant and start fast.

question: A Node.js API that normally handles hundreds of requests per second suddenly stalls completely whenever one particular endpoint is hit — that one request finishes, but everything else queued up behind it during that time. What's the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
answer:
The affected endpoint is almost certainly doing central-processing-unit (CPU)-bound work — such as image processing, heavy JSON parsing, or synchronous cryptography — directly on the event loop thread.

Input/output (I/O)-bound work, like a database query or an outbound HTTP call, does not block anything else, because the single thread is free to handle other requests while it waits for a response. CPU-bound work has nothing to wait on: it keeps that one thread busy computing, so every other request queues up behind it until the work finishes.

The fix is to move that work off the event loop entirely, for example:

  • Run it in a worker_threads thread
  • Fork a separate process for it with child_process.fork()
  • Delegate it to a separate service

Any of these keeps the main thread free to keep serving every other request while the CPU-heavy work happens elsewhere.
hint: I/O-bound = event loop handles it fine. CPU-bound = blocks loop — use worker_threads or fork.

question: You find an AWS access key hardcoded directly in a controller file, and that file just got pushed to a public GitHub repository. Why is this worse than it sounds, and how should that key have been handled instead?
answer:
Once a key is pushed, it exists in the Git history forever — even deleting it from the latest commit does not remove it from history, and automated bots actively scan public repositories for exactly this pattern. The key should be treated as compromised the instant it is pushed, not quietly removed and forgotten.

Secrets like this belong in environment variables instead of source code:

  • Locally, in a gitignored .env file loaded with the dotenv package.
  • In production, the platform's own secret store — for example AWS (Amazon Web Services) Secrets Manager or Kubernetes Secrets — read via process.env at startup.

This separation is also what lets the same build run in development, staging, and production with different behavior just by changing environment variables, and lets a compromised secret be rotated without touching a single line of code.
hint: Env vars separate config from code — secrets in code get committed to git and leak.

question: Describe an effective testing strategy for a Node.js Express API with a database.
answer:
A layered approach covers different risks at different speeds:

  • Unit tests exercise individual functions — validators, transformers, pure logic — in isolation, with dependencies mocked and no database involved.
  • Integration tests run service and repository code against a real test database, such as Postgres running in Docker, to verify the actual SQL and business rules work together, not just that the mocks were called correctly.
  • Application programming interface (API) tests, using a tool such as supertest, start the whole application against a test database and hit real endpoints, asserting on the actual HTTP response and resulting database state — the closest thing to how a real client experiences it.

Across all three layers, the tests need to be deterministic, with no state leaking between tests, and focused on behavior rather than implementation details that would break on every refactor.
hint: Unit (mocked) → integration (real DB) → API (Supertest) — each layer tests a different concern.

question: How do you detect and fix a memory leak in a Node.js application?

question: Describe a strategy to scale a Node.js API from one server to handle 10x traffic.
answer:
The first move is measuring, not scaling blindly: a load testing tool such as k6 or autocannon, combined with application performance monitoring data, shows exactly where time is being spent before anything is changed — scaling the wrong layer wastes effort and can even make things worse.

If the bottleneck is genuinely compute, running the app in cluster mode — via PM2 or Node.js's own cluster module — uses every CPU core on the box instead of just one, often the cheapest first win.

Beyond that, horizontal scaling (running multiple instances behind a load balancer) requires the app to be stateless first, which usually means moving sessions out of memory and into something like Redis so any instance can serve any request.

If the database turns out to be the real bottleneck, connection pooling, read replicas, and proper indexing typically matter more than adding application servers, and offloading slow background work to a queue keeps it from tying up request-handling capacity at all.

The mistake to avoid is scaling infrastructure before confirming where the real bottleneck actually is.
hint: Cluster → stateless + Redis sessions → horizontal + load balancer → DB pool + cache → queue.

question: Describe how to build a complete dark mode implementation in a Tailwind project, including persistence.
answer: Set darkMode: 'class' in tailwind.config.js so dark mode is toggled by a class rather than only following the OS setting. question: Your team's brand color is scattered as raw hex codes across 40 components, and a rebrand just changed the primary color. Updating it means finding every occurrence by hand. What should have been set up in tailwind.config.js to avoid this?
answer: A design token system — extending Tailwind's theme with semantic names instead of using raw colors directly in components. Instead of a hex value scattered everywhere, theme.extend.colors defines something like primary: { DEFAULT: '#3B82F6', dark: '#2563EB' }, and every component uses bg-primary instead of the hex code. Changing the brand color then means editing one line in the config, and every component that referenced primary picks it up automatically. question: How do you control transition duration and easing in Tailwind?
answer: duration-{n} sets the transition duration: duration-150 = 150ms, duration-300 = 300ms, duration-500 = 500ms. ease-{type} sets the easing: ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out (default), ease-linear. Example: transition-colors duration-300 ease-out. Combine with delay-{n} to add a delay.

question: What are the built-in animate-* utilities in Tailwind and what do they do?
answer: Tailwind includes four built-in animations: animate-spin (continuous 360° rotation — loading spinners), animate-ping (scale + fade out like a sonar pulse — live indicators), animate-pulse (fade in/out — skeleton loading screens), animate-bounce (bounce up and down — scroll cues). answer: Define the keyframes and the animation in tailwind.config.js: theme: { extend: { keyframes: { wiggle: { '0%, 100%': { transform: 'rotate(-3deg)' }, '50%': { transform: 'rotate(3deg)' } } }, animation: { wiggle: 'wiggle 1s ease-in-out infinite' } } }. Then use animate-wiggle in HTML.

question: Why should you always add motion-reduce:animate-none to animated elements?
answer: prefers-reduced-motion is an OS-level accessibility setting for people with vestibular disorders or motion sensitivity, for whom animation can cause nausea or dizziness. motion-reduce:animate-none turns the animation off when that setting is on (motion-reduce:transition-none does the same for transitions). WCAG 2.1 (SC 2.2.2) also asks for a way to pause, stop, or hide moving content.

question: Describe how to build a smooth accordion component using only Tailwind transitions.
answer: The core problem is that CSS transitions can't animate to height: auto — you can only transition between two concrete values, and auto isn't one. The common workaround is animating max-height instead: the collapsed panel sits at max-h-0 overflow-hidden transition-all duration-300, and toggling to something like max-h-96 lets it expand smoothly, since max-height does support transitions. The trade-off is the easing looks slightly off, because the animation is really running through a range of unused max-height values, not the panel's actual content height — a JS-measured scrollHeight set as the max-height dynamically fixes that at the cost of a bit of JavaScript. Either way, pairing it with aria-expanded on the trigger and motion-reduce:transition-none keeps it accessible and respectful of users who've asked for reduced motion.
hint: max-h-0 → max-h-96 with overflow-hidden transition-all — toggle with JS, add motion-reduce.

question: What does the @tailwindcss/forms plugin provide?

question: What does the @tailwindcss/typography plugin provide and how is it used?

question: What is a Tailwind plugin and how do you write a simple one?
answer: A Tailwind plugin is a function that receives helper methods to add new utilities, components, or base styles programmatically. Add to tailwind.config.js: plugins: [ plugin(function({ addUtilities }) { addUtilities({ '.text-shadow': { textShadow: '2px 2px 4px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.3)' } }) }) ]. question: What is DaisyUI and how does it relate to Tailwind CSS?
answer: DaisyUI is a Tailwind CSS plugin that adds semantic component class names (btn, card, badge, navbar, modal) on top of Tailwind utilities. Instead of bg-blue-600 text-white px-4 py-2 rounded font-bold, you write btn btn-primary. It includes built-in themes (dark, light, cupcake, cyberpunk). It's a component library that uses Tailwind under the hood without requiring JavaScript for interactions.

question: Describe how you would choose between DaisyUI, Headless UI, and raw Tailwind for a project.
answer: It comes down to how much design freedom you need versus how fast you need to ship. Raw Tailwind gives full control over every pixel with no imposed aesthetic, right when the product needs a genuinely distinctive brand and the team has the design bandwidth for it, at the cost of building everything by hand. Headless UI gives fully accessible, unstyled interactive components — dialogs, listboxes, comboboxes — with keyboard navigation and ARIA handled for you, so you only need to supply the visual styling; it's the right fit when a component needs to be genuinely accessible and you don't want to reinvent that logic. DaisyUI gives pre-styled component classes and themes for the fastest path to something polished, at the cost of losing some of the explicitness utility classes normally give you — a good fit for internal tools or admin dashboards where shipping speed matters more than a distinctive look. In practice, many teams mix these: Headless UI for complex interactive pieces, raw Tailwind for layout and custom components, and DaisyUI reserved for lower-stakes internal tooling.

question: How does Tailwind remove unused CSS in production?
answer: Tailwind scans the files listed in the content array of tailwind.config.js and removes any utility class that doesn't appear in those files. The content array uses glob patterns: content: ['./src/**/*.{html,js,ts,tsx,vue}']. In Tailwind v3+ with JIT mode always on, only classes that appear in content files are ever generated — no separate purge step needed.

options.option: Tailwind automatically detects and removes unused CSS during npm run build
content: [] glob patterns tell Tailwind which files to scan — JIT purges unused
options.comment: If a class doesn't appear as a complete string in scanned files, it won't be in the output.

question: Why must you use complete class names in Tailwind rather than building them dynamically?
answer: Tailwind's scanner looks for complete class name strings — it doesn't execute JavaScript. If you write 'bg-' + color, the scanner sees the string 'bg-' + color and won't generate bg-red-500 or bg-blue-600. Always write complete names: const classes = { red: 'bg-red-500', blue: 'bg-blue-600' }. A safelist in tailwind.config.js can also force classes to be included even if not found in content.

question: Why is a Tailwind project's production CSS file usually small?
answer: Tailwind scans your template files and only generates the utility classes you actually use. A production file is often just a few KB gzipped (5–20KB is a common ballpark), compared with several MB if every possible class were generated.

question: What is the safelist option in tailwind.config.js used for?
answer: safelist forces specified classes to be included in the production CSS even if they don't appear in your content files. Use it for: classes generated dynamically from a database or API, classes used in a CMS-rendered HTML block, or classes in libraries loaded at runtime. Example: safelist: ['bg-red-500', 'text-blue-600', { pattern: /^(bg|text)-brand-/, variants: ['hover', 'dark'] }].

question: Your team's production CSS bundle for a Vite + React app comes out to 400KB, and someone points out the Tailwind content config is set to './src/**/*' instead of specific file extensions. Why would that one line cause such a bloated build?
answer: Tailwind's JIT engine scans whatever files match the content glob for class names it needs to generate — set it too broadly, like './src/**/*' with no extension filter, and it ends up scanning JSON files, test files, and anything else sitting in src, which can pull in class-name-looking strings that were never meant to be real utility classes and bloats what gets generated. Scoping it precisely, like './src/**/*.{ts,tsx}', keeps the scan limited to actual component files. The same discipline applies to safelist — adding broad patterns there just re-includes classes the purge step was specifically trying to remove, undermining the whole point of JIT scanning in the first place. Done correctly, the final CSS output for a typical app is usually well under 15KB gzipped.
hint: content array + JIT + cssMinify in Vite + specific file extensions = lean production CSS.

question: What is a pull request on GitHub?

question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?

question: What is a merge conflict and how does it happen?
answer: A merge conflict happens when two people edit the same lines in the same file on different branches. Git cannot decide which version to keep, so it marks the conflict and asks you to resolve it manually.

question: What does CI stand for in DevOps?

question: What does 'shift left' mean in DevOps?

question: What is the key cultural difference between traditional IT and DevOps?

question: What is the 'you build it, you run it' principle in DevOps?

question: What is idempotency in IaC?
answer: Idempotency means running the same IaC code multiple times always produces the same result without causing duplicate or broken resources. If the resource already exists and matches the config, Terraform does nothing. Safe to re-run.
hint: Run it 10 times, get the same result — no duplicates, no side effects.

options.option: The ability to run infrastructure in multiple cloud regions simultaneously
Running the same code multiple times always produces the same safe result
options.comment: Idempotency is why IaC is safer than scripts — scripts often fail or duplicate on re-run.

options.option: A security feature that prevents unauthorized changes to infrastructure
The process of testing infrastructure code before it runs in production

question: What is a Terraform state file?
answer: Terraform keeps a state file (terraform.tfstate) that records what infrastructure it has created. This is how Terraform knows what exists and what needs to change on the next apply. Store it remotely (S3, Terraform Cloud) when working in a team — never commit it to Git.

question: What is the difference between Terraform and Ansible?
answer: Terraform provisions infrastructure — creates servers, databases, networks. Ansible configures what's already running — installs software, manages files, runs commands on existing servers. They complement each other: Terraform to build, Ansible to configure.

question: What is a Terraform provider?
answer: A provider is a plugin that lets Terraform talk to a specific API. The AWS provider knows how to create EC2 instances and S3 buckets. The GitHub provider can manage repos and teams. You declare which providers you need and Terraform downloads them on terraform init.

question: What is configuration management in DevOps?
answer: Configuration management is the practice of keeping all servers and environments consistently configured using code. Instead of manually tweaking each server, you define the desired state in code and a tool (Ansible, Puppet, Chef) enforces it automatically.
hint: Define the desired server state in code — the tool enforces it on every server consistently.

question: What is configuration drift and why is it dangerous?
answer: Configuration drift happens when servers that should be identical slowly become different due to manual changes, one-off patches, or ad-hoc fixes. Over time, bugs appear that are impossible to reproduce — 'it works on server A but not server B'. Configuration management tools detect and fix drift automatically.
hint: Servers that should be identical slowly diverge — causes unreproducible bugs.

question: What is an Ansible playbook?
answer: A playbook is an Ansible file (written in YAML) that describes a series of tasks to run on servers. Example tasks: install Nginx, copy a config file, start a service, create a user. Playbooks can target specific groups of servers defined in an inventory.

question: What is desired state configuration?
answer: Desired state configuration means you declare what state you want a system to be in — 'Nginx should be installed and running' — and the tool checks the current state and only makes changes if needed. If Nginx is already running, nothing happens. This is the foundation of idempotent configuration management.

question: What is Vault (by HashiCorp) used for in DevOps?
answer: Vault is a secrets management tool. It securely stores and controls access to sensitive values like API keys, database passwords, and TLS certificates. Applications request secrets from Vault at runtime — secrets never live in config files or environment variables in plain text.

question: What is the difference between mutable and immutable infrastructure?
answer: Mutable infrastructure means you update existing servers in place — patch, reconfigure, upgrade. Immutable infrastructure means you never modify running servers. Instead, you build a new server image with the changes and replace the old one. Immutable is more predictable — what you tested is exactly what runs in production.

question: What is an Ansible inventory?
answer: An inventory is a file (or dynamic source) that lists all the servers Ansible manages, grouped by role. Example: [web] server1.example.com, [db] db1.example.com. Playbooks target a group — ansible-playbook deploy.yml --limit web runs only on web servers.

question: Why should you store configuration as code in version control?
answer: Storing configuration in Git gives you: a history of every change (who changed what and when), the ability to roll back to a previous working state, peer review via pull requests before a config change goes live, and the ability to spin up identical environments from scratch at any time.

question: What are the three pillars of observability?
answer: The three pillars are: Metrics (numbers over time — CPU, error rate, request latency), Logs (timestamped text records of what happened), and Traces (end-to-end journey of a single request through multiple services). Together they tell you what is broken, when it broke, and why.
hint: Metrics = numbers; Logs = events; Traces = request journey. Together they explain any failure.

question: What is Prometheus used for in DevOps?
answer: Prometheus is an open-source monitoring system that collects metrics by scraping HTTP endpoints on your services at regular intervals. It stores time-series data and supports powerful queries with PromQL. Usually paired with Grafana for visualization and Alertmanager for alerting.

question: What is Grafana and how does it relate to Prometheus?
answer: Grafana is an open-source visualization tool. It connects to data sources like Prometheus, InfluxDB, or Elasticsearch and renders dashboards with charts, graphs, and alerts. Prometheus stores the data; Grafana makes it readable. A typical setup: Prometheus scrapes → stores data → Grafana queries and displays.

question: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
answer: Monitoring tells you when something is wrong (known failures, predefined alerts). Observability lets you understand WHY it's wrong — even for failures you've never seen before. A system is observable when you can answer any question about its internal state by examining its outputs (metrics, logs, traces) without deploying new code.

Monitoring covers servers; observability covers only application-level events

question: What is an SLI (Service Level Indicator)?
answer: An SLI is a specific metric that measures the health of a service from the user's perspective. Common SLIs: availability (% of requests that succeed), latency (% of requests under 200ms), error rate (% of requests returning 5xx errors). SLIs are the numbers you measure against your SLO target.

options.option: A legal contract that defines uptime guarantees between provider and customer
A measured metric (e.g. request success rate) that tracks service health

question: What is the difference between SLI, SLO, and SLA?
answer: SLI (Indicator) = what you measure (e.g. 99.7% of requests succeeded this month). SLO (Objective) = the internal target you aim for (e.g. 99.9% success rate). SLA (Agreement) = the contractual promise to customers, often with financial penalties for breach (e.g. 99.5% uptime or you get a refund).

question: What is an error budget in the context of SLOs?
answer: An error budget is the amount of allowed downtime or errors before you breach your SLO. If your SLO is 99.9% availability, your error budget is 0.1% — about 43 minutes per month. When the budget is nearly spent, the team slows down risky releases. When it's full, you can move fast. It balances reliability with innovation.

question: What are the four golden signals of monitoring?
answer: The four golden signals (from Google's SRE book): Latency (how long requests take), Traffic (how many requests per second), Errors (rate of failed requests), and Saturation (how 'full' the system is — CPU, memory, queue depth). Monitor these four and you can detect most production problems.

question: What is a health check endpoint and why is it important?
answer: A health check endpoint (typically GET /health or /ping) returns a 200 OK when the service is working correctly. Load balancers and orchestrators like Kubernetes use it to automatically remove unhealthy instances from traffic rotation. Without it, broken instances silently receive requests and return errors.

question: What is an incident in the context of DevOps and SRE?
answer: An incident is any unplanned event that disrupts a service or degrades its reliability below the SLO target — an outage, a spike in error rates, a security breach, or severe performance degradation. Incidents are declared, managed, and resolved through a structured response process.
hint: Any unplanned disruption that breaks your SLO — outage, error spike, security breach.

options.option: A planned maintenance window that takes the service offline temporarily
An unplanned event that disrupts service or breaches the SLO target
options.comment: The lower the severity threshold for declaring an incident, the faster you respond.

options.option: A failed deployment that is caught by CI tests before reaching production

question: What are MTTD and MTTR, and why do they matter?
answer: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) measures how long from a failure starting until the team knows about it. MTTR (Mean Time to Resolve) measures how long from detection to full recovery. Lower MTTD means better alerting. Lower MTTR means better runbooks, tooling, and on-call practices. Both directly impact user experience during incidents.
hint: MTTD = time to know it's broken. MTTR = time to fix it. Both should be as low as possible.

options.option: Mean Time to Deploy and Mean Time to Release — CI/CD pipeline metrics
MTTD = time until detection; MTTR = time until full recovery
options.comment: Target: MTTD in minutes (good alerting), MTTR in under an hour (good runbooks + ownership).

options.option: Mean Time to Test and Mean Time to Review — software quality metrics
Metrics that measure how many deployments are made per day and week

question: What is a blameless post-mortem?
answer: A blameless post-mortem is a written analysis of an incident that focuses on what happened and why — not who is at fault. The goal is to find systemic causes and prevent recurrence. Blame creates fear; blameless culture creates transparency. People report incidents honestly when they know they won't be punished.
hint: What + why, not who. Finds systemic causes, creates a culture where incidents are reported honestly.

options.option: A meeting where all team members defend their actions during the incident
Analysis focused on systemic causes, not individual fault — enables honesty
options.comment: A good post-mortem produces action items that make the system safer, not scapegoats.

options.option: An automated report generated by monitoring tools after each outage
A meeting that only senior engineers attend to protect junior developers

question: What is a runbook in incident response?
answer: A runbook is a documented step-by-step guide for responding to a specific type of incident — 'if the database connection pool is exhausted, do X, Y, Z'. Good runbooks let any on-call engineer resolve known issues at 3am without needing to call an expert. They reduce MTTR significantly.
hint: Step-by-step guide for a known failure type — lets any on-call engineer fix it without an expert.

options.option: A script that automatically detects and fixes production incidents without human input
Step-by-step guide for a known incident type — reduces MTTR for on-call
options.comment: Great runbooks also include how to verify the fix and when to escalate if steps don't work.

options.option: A schedule that defines which engineer is on-call each week of the year
A log of every incident that occurred during a calendar year for auditing

question: What is an on-call rotation and what makes it sustainable?
answer: An on-call rotation shares the responsibility of responding to production incidents across a team. One engineer is primary on-call at a time, rotated weekly or bi-weekly. Sustainable on-call requires: good runbooks, alert fatigue management (noisy alerts must be fixed), a secondary backup, and post-incident recovery time to compensate for sleep disruption.
hint: Shared weekend/night duty, rotated. Sustainable with runbooks, low noise, and recovery time.

options.option: A policy where a single senior engineer handles all production incidents forever
Shared on-call duty rotated across the team — sustainable with low alert noise
options.comment: Alert fatigue is real: if on-call is paged 20 times per night, the runbook isn't the problem.

options.option: A customer support rotation where agents take turns answering live chat
A schedule where each team deploys on a different day to avoid conflicts

question: What is chaos engineering and what problem does it solve?
answer: Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures into a system — kill a server, slow a network, crash a dependency — to verify that the system handles failure gracefully and that the team's incident response works. Netflix's Chaos Monkey is the famous example. It exposes hidden weaknesses before real failures do.
hint: Deliberately break things in a controlled way to find hidden weaknesses before real failures do.

options.option: Writing messy, unstructured code to test if automated linting catches all issues
Injecting controlled failures to find system weaknesses before real ones hit
options.comment: Start small: kill one pod in staging. Graduate to production only after strong observability.

options.option: Randomly assigning tasks to developers to test team adaptability under pressure
A load testing technique that sends 10x normal traffic to find bottlenecks

question: What is the incident command structure and who is the incident commander?
answer: During a major incident, one person acts as Incident Commander (IC) — they coordinate the response, delegate tasks, and make decisions. Others focus on technical investigation and communication. The IC does NOT do technical work — they keep everyone aligned, track time, and communicate status to stakeholders. Clear roles prevent 'too many cooks' chaos.
hint: IC coordinates and communicates — doesn't fix the issue. Prevents everyone debugging at once.

options.option: The most senior engineer who diagnoses and fixes the root cause personally
The coordinator who delegates, aligns the team, and handles communication
options.comment: Large incidents also have a Communication Lead (updates status page) and Scribe (records timeline).

options.option: An automated bot that pages the right team based on alert routing rules
The engineer who wrote the failing code and must fix it before others help

question: A production database outage lasted 40 minutes last week — detected by a customer complaint, not internal alerting, and the root cause was an unindexed migration that locked a hot table. You're asked to write the post-mortem. What should it actually contain, and why does the wording matter?
answer:
A useful post-mortem covers five things:

  • Summary and impact: a short description of what happened and who it affected.
  • Timeline: when it started, when it was detected, what was investigated, and when it was resolved.
  • Root cause: the real technical cause, here the unindexed migration locking a hot table.
  • Contributing factors: what made it worse, such as detection relying on a customer complaint instead of an alert.
  • What went right: for example, how quickly the team rolled back once the cause was found.

It should end with specific, owned, dated action items, such as "add a migration lock check to the deploy process by a real date", not a vague aspiration like "add better alerting".

The wording matters because it decides whether people fix the system or protect themselves. "The deploy process didn't catch this" invites a process fix, while "someone forgot to check" makes people defensive and more likely to hide problems next time. A blameless post-mortem gets to the truth faster.
hint: Summary → timeline → root cause → contributing factors → what went well → owned action items.

question: What are DORA metrics?
answer: DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) metrics measure software delivery performance with four numbers: Deployment Frequency (how often you deploy), Lead Time for Changes (idea to production), Change Failure Rate (% of deploys that cause incidents), and MTTR (time to restore after failure). Elite teams deploy multiple times per day with an MTTR under an hour.

Metrics that measure cloud infrastructure costs and resource utilization

question: What is lead time for changes in DevOps?
answer: Lead time for changes measures how long it takes from a developer committing code to that code running in production. Elite teams achieve under one hour. Long lead times often indicate slow reviews, too many manual steps, or large batches of change — all risks that accumulate before reaching users.

question: What is a value stream in DevOps and why map it?
answer: A value stream is the end-to-end sequence of steps to deliver value to a customer — from idea to deployed feature. Value stream mapping visualizes each step, the time it takes, and the wait time between steps. It exposes bottlenecks: 'code review waits 2 days, deploy needs manual approval for 3 hours'. Eliminating waste (wait time) reduces lead time.

question: What is a feedback loop in DevOps and why should it be short?
answer: A feedback loop is how quickly developers learn whether their change worked — did the tests pass, did the build succeed, is the feature working in production. Short loops (minutes, not hours) mean mistakes are caught and corrected while the code is fresh in the developer's mind. Long loops waste time and compound errors.

question: What is technical debt and how does it affect DevOps practices?
answer: Technical debt is the cost of shortcuts taken to ship faster — poorly structured code, missing tests, outdated dependencies, manual processes. Like financial debt, it accrues interest: the longer it sits, the slower future development becomes. High technical debt slows CI/CD, makes refactoring risky, and increases change failure rate. DevOps teams budget time each sprint to pay it down.
hint: Shortcuts that slow future work — high debt makes CI/CD slow and deploys risky.

options.option: The actual money owed to cloud providers for overused infrastructure resources

Legacy systems that cannot be migrated to modern cloud infrastructure

question: What does 'deploy small, deploy often' mean and why is it a core DevOps principle?
answer: Deploying small, frequent changes reduces risk in every dimension: less code to review, easier to pinpoint what broke, faster rollback if something goes wrong. Large infrequent releases are risky — months of changes in one deploy, impossible to isolate bugs, rollback means losing everything. Small deploys move fast with low risk.
hint: Small batch = easy to review, easy to rollback, easy to find what broke. Big batch = all the risk.

options.option: A strategy where each deployment contains only one line of code changed

options.option: Deploying to multiple cloud regions simultaneously to reduce per-region load
Running the deployment pipeline more than once per day for redundancy

question: A team's DORA metrics show deployment frequency at once a week, lead time at 4 days, an 8% change failure rate, and a 45-minute MTTR. Which of these points to the actual bottleneck, and what would you change first?
answer:
The bottleneck is the combination of low deployment frequency and long lead time. The change failure rate (8%) and mean time to recovery, or MTTR (45 minutes), are both reasonably healthy. So the problem is everything that happens between code being finished and it reaching production.

Digging into where those 4 days go usually turns up something like:

  • code sitting in review for two days
  • a manual quality assurance (QA) pass taking another day
  • a once-a-week release meeting gating the deploy

The highest-leverage fixes are a review service-level agreement (SLA) so pull requests don't sit idle, replacing the manual QA gate with automated tests in continuous integration (CI), and dropping the weekly release meeting so any passing build can ship. That's continuous delivery instead of batched releases.

The change failure rate may tick up for a while as deploys get more frequent. That's normal, and canary deployments and better test coverage are there to catch it before it becomes a real outage.
hint: Measure all four → find where time is lost → remove the gate → measure again. Data drives decisions.

question: What is a "metric" in an observability context?
answer: A metric is a numeric measurement of system behavior sampled over time (e.g. request count, latency, CPU usage).

question: A <script> tag with your JS file is placed in the <head> before any HTML content in <body>, and the console shows "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'addEventListener')" for a button that's clearly in the HTML. What's happening, and how do you fix it without touching the HTML?
answer:
When a <script> tag sits in the <head> before any markup, the browser executes it before it has parsed the button element into the DOM (Document Object Model). At that point document.querySelector returns null, because no matching element exists yet, and calling addEventListener on null throws.

<script src="app.js" defer></script>

We can fix this without touching the HTML in two ways: adding the defer attribute to the script tag, or moving the script to just before </body>. Both delay execution until the DOM has been fully parsed, so the button exists by the time our code runs.
hint: Where does the script tag sit relative to the button in the HTML?

question: Your teammate says 'JavaScript is a scripting language, so it can't do real backend work.' What's wrong with that reasoning, and what does the same JavaScript engine actually power outside the browser?
answer:
The runtime, not the language, determines where code can execute. The same JavaScript language that runs in a browser also runs inside Node.js on a server, with full filesystem, network, and database access — completely outside any browser sandbox.

Calling JavaScript "just a scripting language" describes how the code is interpreted, not what it is capable of doing. Node.js powers real production backend APIs, command-line tools, and servers at scale, so the reasoning that scripting languages cannot do backend work does not hold up.
hint: Think about what actually determines where code can run — the language, or something else?

NaN is a special value that lives within JavaScript's number type — it represents the result of an invalid or undefined numeric operation, such as 0 / 0 or parseInt('abc'), rather than the absence of a number type altogether.

typeof NaN;              // "number"
typeof (0 / 0);          // "number"
typeof parseInt('abc');  // "number"

Since NaN is still stored and behaves like a number under the hood, typeof correctly classifies it as "number" — it is a number that simply does not represent any valid numeric value.
hint: NaN is a value of a type, not the absence of one

question: You save a JavaScript file, but your browser keeps showing the old version even after refreshing. A teammate says 'hard refresh with Ctrl+Shift+R.' Why does a normal refresh not pick up the change?
answer:
Browsers cache static files like JavaScript to avoid re-downloading them on every page load. A normal refresh often reuses that cached copy if the server has not explicitly told the browser the file changed.

A hard refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R) forces the browser to bypass the cache entirely and re-fetch every file fresh from the server, which is why it picks up the edit when a normal refresh does not.
hint: Think about what a browser tries to avoid re-downloading on every page load.

question: Your HTML has <script src="app.js"></script> right before </body>, but when you open the page, nothing in app.js seems to run and the console shows a 404 for app.js. The file definitely exists in your project folder. What's the most likely mistake?
answer:
The src path is almost certainly wrong relative to where the HTML file is being served from. A 404 means the browser is looking for app.js somewhere it is not — usually because the file actually lives in a subfolder like /js/app.js or /src/app.js, and the script tag needs that full path spelled out rather than just the filename.

Checking the Network tab in DevTools for the exact URL (Uniform Resource Locator) being requested is the fastest way to confirm where the browser is actually looking versus where the file really lives.
hint: Check the Network tab to see exactly what URL the browser actually requested.

question: Why would a developer set up ESLint and Prettier on a brand-new JavaScript project before writing any real code, instead of adding them later once the project is bigger?
answer:
Adding a linter and formatter early means every line of code follows the same rules from the start, instead of having to retroactively reformat and fix an entire existing codebase later, which is a much bigger and riskier change.

It also catches real bugs early — an unused variable or a missing await gets flagged the moment it is written, rather than after it has already caused a confusing issue in production.
hint: Think about how much harder it is to apply new rules retroactively across an already-large codebase.

console.log(1 + '1'); // "11"
console.log(1 + 1);   // 2

console.log(1 + 1) prints 2 because both operands are numbers, so + performs actual addition. The behavior of + depends entirely on the types of its operands, which is why mixing a number and a string with it is a common source of unexpected bugs.

let age = 25;
// birthday...
age = 26; // allowed, no error

Since age genuinely needs to be reassigned here, it should have been declared with let instead, which allows reassignment. const is the right choice specifically for values that are never meant to be reassigned — seeing const signals at a glance that the variable will always refer to the same value.
hint: const is about the binding, not necessarily about the value never changing.

question: You write if (userInput = 'admin') { grantAccess(); } intending to check whether userInput equals 'admin', but access gets granted no matter what the user types. What's the bug, and how do you fix it?
answer:
A single = is assignment, not comparison. The line if (userInput = 'admin') actually sets userInput to the string 'admin' and then evaluates the truthiness of that assignment — which is always truthy since it is a non-empty string, so the if always passes.

if (userInput === 'admin') {
  grantAccess();
}

The fix is using === to actually compare values instead of assigning one. This is exactly the kind of bug a linter catches automatically, which is one reason teams enable that rule by default.
hint: Count the equals signs in that if condition.

question: You write a function that should return 'weekday' or 'weekend' based on a day number 0-6, using a switch statement, but forget a break after the first case, and both case 0 and case 1 end up returning 'weekend'. What's happening, and why does switch behave this way by design?
answer:
Without a break, JavaScript's switch statement "falls through" to the next case and keeps executing from there, instead of stopping after the matching case — so case 0 runs, has no break, and execution just continues into case 1's code too.

switch (day) {
  case 0:
  case 1:
    return 'weekend';
  default:
    return 'weekday';
}

This fall-through behavior is intentional in the language, useful in cases where multiple case labels are meant to share the same code, but it is a common bug when a break is simply forgotten.
hint: Check whether the matching case has anything telling execution to stop before the next case begins.

}

Default parameters only kick in when an argument is missing entirely or explicitly passed as undefined — both count as "not provided." null is a real, deliberate value in JavaScript, distinct from "nothing was passed," so the default does not override it, and null gets used as-is.

question: Your codebase has the same 15-line validation logic copy-pasted into six different form handlers, and a bug fix now needs to be applied to all six copies individually. What should have been done from the start, and what does that change now?
answer:
That logic should have been pulled into its own reusable function the first time it was duplicated — a single validateForm(data) function that each of the six handlers calls, instead of six independent copies.

Fixing the bug now means rewriting that shared function once, and every caller automatically gets the fix, instead of hunting down and manually patching six separate places, some of which will inevitably get missed or drift out of sync over time.
hint: Think about how many places you'd have to touch to fix one bug.

question: A function is being called with the wrong value somewhere in a chain of calls, but you don't know where. What's a faster way to find out than adding console.log before every function call, and how does it work?
answer:
Setting a breakpoint in DevTools' Sources panel pauses execution exactly at that line. From there, the code can be stepped through line by line, inspecting every variable's actual value at each point — instead of guessing where to place console.log calls ahead of time and re-running the whole thing after each guess.

It is especially useful when the bug is intermittent or deep inside a call chain, since the actual call stack and state can be watched changing in real time rather than reconstructed from scattered log output.
hint: Think about a tool that lets you pause and inspect live state instead of predicting where to log.

question: You add console.log(user) to debug an object, and it prints fine — but by the time you click to expand it in the console, the values shown are different from what they were when the log actually ran. What's going on?
answer:
The console often logs a live reference to the object, not a frozen snapshot of its state at that exact moment. If the object gets mutated somewhere else in the code after the log statement runs but before it is expanded in the console, what is shown is its current state, not what it looked like when it was logged.

console.log(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(user)));

Using that pattern, or reading specific values into a template string immediately, captures the actual state at that point in time instead of a live reference.
hint: Consider whether what's printed is a frozen snapshot, or a live pointer to the object.

question: A script throws an error and the console shows a stack trace, but a teammate says they always read stack traces from the bottom up first, not the top. Why might that actually be a useful habit?
answer:
The top of a stack trace is where the error was actually thrown, which is useful, but the bottom often shows where the whole chain of calls started — which can reveal whether the broken code path was even supposed to run in this situation at all.

Reading both directions matters: top-down to find the exact failing line, and bottom-up to understand the broader context of how execution got there. That bottom-up view is often the more useful question when the error itself is generic, like "undefined is not a function".
hint: Consider which end of the trace tells you where execution started versus where it broke.

function addItem(list, item) {

Returning a new array like this leaves the original untouched and gives back a fresh array with the item added.

question: You need to check whether a specific product id exists in a large array of thousands of product objects, and it's called on every keystroke in a search box. A teammate suggests converting the array to a Map keyed by id first. Why would that actually make a real difference here?
answer:
Searching an array with .find() or .some() has to check items one by one in the worst case, which gets slower as the array grows — doing that on every keystroke against thousands of items adds up fast.

A Map looks up a key directly rather than scanning, so checking existence stays fast regardless of how large the collection gets.

The one-time cost of building the map upfront, for example with new Map(products.map(p => [p.id, p])), pays for itself the moment we are doing repeated lookups against the same data, which is exactly this situation.
hint: Compare flipping through a phone book page by page versus jumping straight to a name.

question: document.getElementById('title').textContent = 'Hello'; You expect this to render bold text, but the page literally shows the text Hello on screen. What went wrong, and what should you use instead?
answer:
textContent treats whatever is assigned to it as plain text, not HTML (HyperText Markup Language) — it does not parse tags, it just displays them literally as characters on the page. innerHTML is what actually parses a string as HTML and renders the tags as real elements.

title.textContent = '<b>Hello</b>'; // shows the literal text <b>Hello</b>
title.innerHTML = '<b>Hello</b>';   // renders as bold Hello

The trade-off is that innerHTML will execute any markup it is given, including from untrusted sources, so it should only be used with content we trust. textContent is actually the safer default when we are just inserting plain text.
hint: textContent and innerHTML handle the string you assign to them very differently.

question: A page has 500 list items, and you need to add a click handler to each one. Instead of attaching 500 individual event listeners, a teammate suggests attaching one listener to the parent <ul> and checking event.target inside it. Why does that work, and why might it be better?
answer:
Events in the DOM (Document Object Model) "bubble" up from the element that was actually clicked, through its ancestors, all the way to the document — so a click on any <li> also triggers on its parent <ul>, and event.target tells us exactly which <li> was really clicked.

Attaching one listener to the parent instead of 500 to each child uses far less memory and setup time, and it automatically works for any new <li> added to the list later, since there is nothing new to attach a listener to.
hint: Events don't stay put — they travel upward through the DOM tree.

So if there is genuinely no error at all, the more likely explanation is that the selector matched a different, wrong element, or something else in the flow silently swallowed an error before this ran.

The first thing to check is console.log(heading) right after the query, to see exactly what was actually selected.

question: A search input calls fetchResults(input.value) on every keyup event, hitting the server on every single keystroke and overwhelming it under real typing speed. What technique fixes this, and how does it work?
answer:
Debouncing fixes this. Instead of calling fetchResults immediately on every keystroke, we wait a short delay, such as 300ms, after the user stops typing before actually firing the request, canceling and restarting that delay every time a new keystroke comes in.

let timer;
input.addEventListener('keyup', () => {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  timer = setTimeout(() => fetchResults(input.value), 300);
});

So if someone types five characters quickly, only one request fires, right after they pause, rather than five separate requests for every character along the way.
hint: Think about waiting for a pause in typing rather than reacting to every single keystroke.

A form's default behavior is to actually submit and reload the page the instant the button is clicked, regardless of what other JavaScript is running in the handler at the same time.

Calling preventDefault() on the event stops that default browser behavior, giving the validation code control over whether the form actually submits at all.

question: A dropdown menu is supposed to close when you click anywhere outside of it, so you attach a click listener to the whole document that closes the dropdown. But now clicking the button that opens the dropdown also immediately closes it again. What's happening, and how do you fix it?
answer:
The click that opens the dropdown also bubbles up to the document, where the "click outside" listener is attached — so that same click both opens the dropdown and immediately triggers the close logic.

document.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  if (toggleBtn.contains(e.target) || dropdown.contains(e.target)) return;
  dropdown.classList.add('hidden');
});

The fix is checking inside the document listener whether the click's target was the toggle button or inside the dropdown itself, using .contains(), and skipping the close in that case. Alternatively, calling event.stopPropagation() on the toggle button's own click handler means that click never reaches the document listener at all.
hint: That same click doesn't stay on the button — think about where else it travels.

answer:
fetch is asynchronous — it returns a Promise immediately, before the network request has actually completed, so data is a pending Promise object at the moment console.log runs, not the resolved user data. The value inside only becomes available once the Promise resolves, which happens later.

async function getUser() {
  const res = await fetch('/api/user');
  return res.json();
}
getUser().then(data => console.log(data));

Fixing this means either awaiting inside an async function and returning the resolved value, or handling the result inside a .then() callback. console.log(getUser()) can never print the real data directly, because the function returns before the data exists.
hint: Look at what fetch() itself returns immediately, before the network call finishes.

question:
fetch('/api/user')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data.name))
  .catch(err => console.error('Failed:', err));

A request to an API that's currently down doesn't trigger .catch() at all — it goes into .then() and crashes reading data.name from what turns out to be an HTML error page. Why doesn't .catch() fire for a failed request here?
answer:
fetch only rejects on true network failures, like no connection at all. It does not reject just because the server responded with an error status like 404 or 500 — a 404 is still a "successful" response as far as fetch is concerned, so .then() runs anyway, and res.json() tries to parse whatever body came back, whether or not it is actually valid JSON (JavaScript Object Notation).

fetch('/api/user')
  .then(res => {
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    return res.json();
  })
  .then(data => console.log(data.name))
  .catch(err => console.error('Failed:', err));

The fix is checking res.ok inside the first .then() and manually throwing an error if the response was not actually successful, so a bad status code gets routed into .catch() too.
hint: Check what fetch() actually rejects on, versus what it treats as a normal successful response.

question: Your app fetches a list of 200 products from an API, and a teammate wants to also fetch each product's reviews, but writing it as 200 sequential await fetch() calls in a loop makes the page take 20+ seconds to load. What's the fix?
answer:
Sequential awaiting means each request waits for the previous one to fully finish before starting the next, so 200 requests run one after another instead of overlapping — that is what stretches it out to 20 seconds.

const reviews = await Promise.all(
  products.map(p => fetch(`/api/reviews/${p.id}`).then(r => r.json()))
);

Firing them all at once with Promise.all(), mapping each product to its own fetch call and then awaiting the whole array of promises together, lets the browser run many requests concurrently instead of one at a time. This is dramatically faster as long as the API (Application Programming Interface) and browser can actually handle that many parallel requests.
hint: Awaiting inside a loop makes each request wait for the previous one — is there a way to launch them all together?

question: A site stores a user's auth token with localStorage.setItem('token', token) so they stay logged in. A security reviewer flags this as risky compared to using an httpOnly cookie instead. What's the actual risk with localStorage here?
answer:
Anything stored in localStorage is readable by any JavaScript running on that page, including a malicious script injected through an XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) vulnerability located anywhere else on the site.

If an attacker manages to get even a few lines of JavaScript executing on the page, they can call localStorage.getItem('token') and steal the session outright. An httpOnly cookie is deliberately inaccessible to JavaScript entirely, so even if an attacker achieves script execution on the page, they still cannot read the token directly out of it.
hint: Think about who else can read localStorage besides your own trusted code.

answer:
localStorage can only store strings. Passing an actual object to setItem implicitly calls .toString() on it, and the default toString() for a plain object just produces the literal string '[object Object]', discarding the real data entirely.

localStorage.setItem('user', JSON.stringify(user));
const user = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('user'));

The fix is to serialize the object before storing it with JSON.stringify(user), and to parse it back out with JSON.parse() when reading it later.
hint: localStorage can only hold strings — think about what happens when you hand it something that isn't one.

question: A shopping cart page uses sessionStorage to hold cart items so they survive a page refresh, but a user opens the same site in a second browser tab and their cart there is empty, even though they added items in the first tab. Is this a bug?
answer:
This is not a bug — it is sessionStorage working exactly as designed. It is scoped per browser tab rather than shared across the whole browser the way localStorage is, so a second tab genuinely starts with its own empty session storage even when it is on the very same site.

If the cart needs to be shared across tabs, localStorage, which persists per-origin across all tabs, or a server-backed cart would be the right tool instead. The choice between the two storage mechanisms should be deliberate, based on whether cross-tab sharing is actually a requirement for the feature.
hint: Think about whether sessionStorage is shared browser-wide or scoped to just one tab.
