This prints 'Sam 30'.

Destructuring with a default value works the same way default function parameters do: if the property is missing from the object entirely, or is explicitly undefined, the default kicks in. age is not present on the source object at all, so it falls back to 30.

Only an actual value, even something falsy like age: 0, would override the default.
hint: Destructuring defaults follow the same rule as default function parameters — when exactly does a default kick in?

answer:
The spread order is backwards. Later spreads override earlier ones for matching keys, so spreading ...defaults after ...userSettings means every default value overwrites whatever the user actually set, including fontSize — exactly backwards from the intent.

const merged = { ...defaults, ...userSettings };

The fix is spreading the defaults first, then letting the user's actual choices override them.
hint: Pay attention to the order the two objects are spread in — for overlapping keys, order decides the winner.

question: A teammate rewrites several function declarations as arrow functions inside a class, and now this inside those methods refers to something unexpected when the method is passed as a callback, like button.addEventListener('click', this.handleClick). What's different about arrow functions here?
answer:
Arrow functions do not have their own this — they capture this from whatever scope they were defined in, permanently, and never rebind it no matter how they are later called.

A regular function method's this is determined by how it is called, which is exactly why passing this.handleClick as a raw callback loses its this binding to the class instance.

class Widget {
  handleClick = () => {
    this.doSomething(); // this stays bound to the instance
  };
}
button.addEventListener('click', widget.handleClick);

With an arrow function defined as a class field, this stays locked to the instance no matter where the function gets called from later, which is actually why arrow functions are often deliberately used for callback-style class methods.
hint: Recall what determines this inside a regular function versus what determines it inside an arrow function.

answer:
A default export does not carry a name inside the module system at all. It is imported without curly braces, and whoever imports it is free to call it whatever they like.

// Button.js
export default function Button() {}

// correct import:
import Button from './Button.js';

// wrong — looks for a NAMED export called Button:
import { Button } from './Button.js';

Curly braces, as in import { Button }, are reserved for named exports specifically. Trying to destructure-import a default export that way simply fails to find anything called Button among the module's named exports, because there isn't one — the import comes through as undefined or fails outright depending on the module system.
hint: Check whether Button.js used export default or a named export.

answer:
This is a circular dependency: a.js needs something from b.js, and b.js needs something from a.js in return. Whichever module happens to start executing first ends up receiving a still-incomplete version of the other one, because that other module has not finished running its own top-level code yet to actually populate the exported value.

Which file ends up with the incomplete value depends on load order, which is why the symptom can look random from one run to the next. The real fix is not to work around the cycle but to remove it: the piece of code both files depend on should be extracted into its own separate module that neither file needs to import from the other for.
hint: Think about which file's top-level code hasn't finished running yet.

question: A large app bundles all its JavaScript into one 2MB file that loads on every single page, even pages that only use a small fraction of that code. A teammate suggests using dynamic import() for rarely-used features. How does that actually help here?
answer:
A static import at the top of a file always gets bundled into the main output, since the bundler has to include everything reachable from the entry point up front, whether or not it ends up being used on a given page.

button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const { openEditor } = await import('./feature.js');
  openEditor();
});

A dynamic import('./feature.js') instead loads that module as a separate chunk on demand, only when the line actually runs, so a feature used by 5% of visitors no longer has to be downloaded by the other 95%. This is what powers code-splitting: the initial bundle contains only what is needed immediately, and everything else loads lazily as it is actually needed.
hint: Static imports always ship in the main bundle — dynamic ones don't have to.

answer:
The try/catch itself works fine, and config really does become {} — the crash is happening one line later, in config.settings.theme.

{} has no settings property, so config.settings is undefined, and reading .theme off of undefined throws a completely separate TypeError.

Catching the parse error does not protect code further downstream that assumes a full, specific object shape exists. That code needs its own defensive check, like config.settings?.theme, rather than relying on the earlier try/catch to have covered it.
hint: The try/catch only guards the JSON.parse call — what happens on the next line?

answer:
The await is on the wrong line. fetch() itself is not awaited, so res is actually a pending Promise, not a real Response object, and calling .json() on a Promise does not do what is intended.

async function loadData() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/data'); // await belongs here
    const data = await res.json();
    return data;
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err);
  }
}

The fix is awaiting the fetch call itself, not just the .json() call after it, so both steps are genuinely inside the code the try/catch is monitoring.
hint: Check exactly which expression the await keyword is attached to

question: A payment processing function wraps its entire body in a single try/catch and logs 'payment failed' for any error, whether it's a network timeout, an invalid card number, or a bug in the code itself. A teammate says this makes debugging real issues much harder. Why?
answer:
One generic catch-all treats every failure the same way, so a legitimate "card declined" response gets logged identically to an actual network outage or a genuine bug in the code. There is no way to tell from the logs which one actually happened, or to show the user a message that matches what really went wrong.

Inspecting the error's type or message inside the catch block lets the code respond differently to each case: retry a timeout, show a clear message for a declined card, and alert the team loudly for an unexpected bug, rather than treating all three the same.
hint: Think about what information gets lost when every failure gets the same log message

question: You clone a project, run npm install, and it installs fine — but a teammate on a different machine gets a slightly different set of dependency versions and hits a bug you don't see. Both of you have the same package.json. What's the likely cause, and what file prevents this?
answer:
The likely cause is that package.json specifies version ranges, such as ^4.2.0, rather than exact pinned versions. Because of this, npm install can legitimately resolve to different actual versions on different machines, or even on the same machine at different times, if a compatible newer version was published in between.

The package-lock.json file is what prevents this. It pins the exact resolved version of every dependency in the tree, not just the top-level ones. As long as it is committed to the repository and both machines actually install from it, everyone ends up with an identical dependency tree instead of merely a compatible one.

package.json says what's allowed; package-lock.json says what's actually installed.
hint: package.json usually specifies version ranges, not exact pinned versions.

question: Running npm install in a project throws a wall of dependency conflict errors that didn't happen last week, even though nobody changed package.json. What's a likely cause, and what helps confirm it?
answer:
A likely cause is that a dependency, or a dependency of a dependency, published a new version in between that turns out to be incompatible with something else in the tree. Since package.json version ranges let npm resolve to whatever matching version currently exists on the registry, an npm install run today can pull in something different than it did last week, even though package.json itself never changed.

Comparing the current package-lock.json against the last known-good version in Git history helps confirm this. If the lockfile shows a dependency's resolved version changed even though nobody edited package.json, that is a strong signal an upstream package moved underneath the project.
hint: Nothing in package.json changed, but something upstream might have.

question: A teammate suggests running npm audit fix --force to quickly resolve a list of security vulnerabilities npm reported. Why might that be riskier than it sounds?
answer:
--force allows npm to install major version upgrades of dependencies in order to resolve the reported vulnerabilities, even though a major version bump can include breaking API changes that have nothing to do with security. It can silently upgrade a package in a way that changes its behavior or breaks the code, not just patch the vulnerable code path.

A safer approach is reviewing what plain npm audit fix (without --force) would change first, since that only applies non-breaking patch and minor updates. Any remaining vulnerabilities that require a major bump can then be handled manually, checking each package's changelog before accepting the upgrade.
hint: --force can cross a boundary that plain npm audit fix stays safely behind.

question: A page is missing <!DOCTYPE html> at the very top, and a form on that page renders with slightly different spacing and box sizing depending on which browser opens it. What does the doctype actually control, and why does leaving it out cause this specific kind of inconsistency?
answer:
The doctype's job isn't to describe the document's version so much as to tell the browser which rendering mode to use. With <!DOCTYPE html> present as the very first line, the browser renders in "standards mode," applying the modern HTML and CSS spec consistently across browsers.

Without it, some browsers fall back to "quirks mode," which deliberately emulates the inconsistent, non-standard rendering behavior of very old browsers for backward compatibility. Box sizing, form control dimensions, and other layout details genuinely differ between the two modes, which is exactly why the same form can look subtly different depending on the browser once the doctype is missing.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>...</head>
<body>...</body>
</html>

The fix is simply to put <!DOCTYPE html> as the literal first line of the file, before anything else, including whitespace or comments.
hint: Think about what "quirks mode" versus "standards mode" changes in a browser's rendering engine.

question: A teammate asks why HTML needs a doctype and separate CSS and JavaScript files at all, when they could just style everything with inline style= attributes and skip the doctype entirely, since the page 'looks fine' either way in their testing. What's the actual risk they're not seeing?
answer:
Their page might look fine in their one browser during testing, but different browsers can interpret unstructured or non-standard markup inconsistently, especially in quirks mode without a doctype — the risk shows up later, on a browser or device they didn't test, not immediately in front of them.

Separating structure, presentation, and behavior also isn't just a style preference — it makes the page maintainable as it grows, since changing the look later means editing one stylesheet instead of hunting through inline style attributes scattered across every element.

question: Someone writes Warning — the bold and italic tags are closed in the wrong order — and asks why the page still looks fine instead of throwing an error. What is the browser actually doing behind the scenes to make that work?
answer:
Browsers don't reject malformed HTML the way a compiler rejects broken code. Instead, every browser runs an HTML parsing algorithm with built-in error-recovery rules that silently repair common mistakes like incorrectly nested or unclosed tags.

For overlapping tags like the example above, the parser effectively reconstructs a valid tree behind the scenes, as if it had been written correctly in the first place:

<b><i>Warning</i></b>

It closes <i> early where needed and re-opens it after, so the final Document Object Model (DOM) ends up well-formed even though the source markup wasn't.

This forgiveness is convenient, but it comes with a real cost: different browsers can, in edge cases, repair the same broken markup slightly differently, producing inconsistent results. Writing correctly nested, valid markup from the start — and checking it with a validator — avoids depending on error-recovery behavior that isn't actually guaranteed to be identical everywhere.
hint: The browser has to build a single, well-formed DOM tree no matter what the source markup looks like — how does it decide what that tree should be?

question:
Welcome to Our Store

Browse our latest products below.

The browser tab shows nothing and search engines can't tell what the page is about, even though the body has visible content. What's the structural mistake, and where should the fix go?
answer:
The page is almost certainly missing a <title> element inside <head> — visible content lives in <body>, but the tab title and what search engines primarily use to understand the page's topic both come from <title> in <head>, which is invisible on the page itself.

Adding <title>Page Name</title> inside <head> fixes both the blank tab and gives search engines a real signal about the page's content.

question: A stylesheet is linked with <link rel="stylesheet"> at the very bottom of <body> instead of inside <head>, and users briefly see plain, unstyled content flash before the styling kicks in. Why does placement inside <head> actually matter here, beyond just "that's where it belongs"?
answer:
The browser parses HTML top to bottom and starts rendering content as it goes, applying whatever CSS it has already loaded at that point. If a stylesheet link sits at the bottom of <body>, the browser has already painted most or all of the page's content by the time it discovers and loads that stylesheet.

That produces exactly the symptom described: a visible flash of unstyled content, followed by a jarring re-render once the CSS finally applies. Placing it inside <head> means the browser discovers and starts loading it before any body content is painted, so styles are ready by the time there's anything to render:

<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
hint: Think about the order the parser encounters things, and what's already been painted by the time it reaches the bottom of the page.

question: A team keeps every <script> tag at the bottom of <body>, right before the closing tag, instead of putting them in <head> for tidier organization. What's the actual trade-off they're making by doing that?
answer:
By default, a <script> tag is render-blocking and parser-blocking: when the browser's HTML parser reaches one, it has to stop, fetch the script if it's external, execute it fully, and only then continue parsing the rest of the document.

If scripts sit in <head>, that pause happens before any of the page's visible content has even been parsed, which can noticeably delay when the user sees anything at all. Placing scripts at the end of <body> lets the browser parse and paint all the visible content first, and only pause for scripts once there's already something on screen.

The trade-off is mostly organizational — some developers prefer having all document metadata, including scripts, together in <head> — but the defer attribute on a <head>-placed <script> achieves the same non-blocking benefit without moving it to the bottom, since deferred scripts run only after parsing finishes anyway.
hint: Consider what a script tag forces the parser to do the moment it's encountered, by default.

question: A teammate wraps a warning in Warning: to make it stand out, and an accessibility review flags it. What's actually going on between and here, beyond how the text looks?
answer:
<b> and <strong> often look identical, both rendering bold by default, but they mean different things under the hood. <strong> tells assistive technology that the content genuinely matters, so a screen reader can announce it with added emphasis, while <b> is a purely visual style with no semantic weight attached.

Since this is a real warning that a user needs to notice, we should use <strong> instead so the importance carries through for screen reader users too, not just for people who can see the bold styling.
hint: Think about what a screen reader actually announces differently.

question: Someone writes three sentences on separate lines inside a single <div> in their HTML file, expecting each to appear on its own line on the page, but they all render as one continuous line instead. What's happening here?
answer:
Browsers collapse whitespace in HTML source code by default, and that includes line breaks typed in the editor. A newline in the file is just whitespace to the renderer, not an instruction to start a new visual line.

To actually get separate lines, we need real HTML structure, such as wrapping each sentence in its own <p> element, or inserting a <br> where a break is genuinely wanted.
hint: Whitespace in the source and whitespace on the rendered page aren't the same thing.

question: If <strong> is the semantically "correct" choice for bold-looking text, is there ever a genuine case where <b> is actually the right tag to reach for?
answer:
Yes. <b> fits when text should stand out visually but carries no real importance in meaning, like a keyword in a product name or the lead-in words of an article styled bold purely as a convention.

The test we can apply is whether losing the bold styling would also lose something meaningful about the content. If the answer is no, <b> is appropriate; if losing the styling would also lose a signal of real importance, that's when <strong> is the better fit.

question:
A page includes this link:

<a href="https://trusted-partner.example.com" target="_blank">
  Partner Resources
</a>

A security audit flags this link as a vulnerability even though it goes to a trusted-looking URL. What's the actual risk, and what attribute closes it?
answer:
A page opened with target="_blank" can, in older browsers or without protection, access window.opener and redirect the original tab to a phishing page. The new tab effectively gets partial control over the tab that opened it, even if the link points somewhere legitimate today.

Adding rel="noopener noreferrer" severs that connection, so the new tab has no reference back to the page that opened it.

<a href="https://trusted-partner.example.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">
  Partner Resources
</a>

question: A whole card component is wrapped in a <div> with a JavaScript click handler acting like a link, instead of using a real <a>. Someone testing with a keyboard alone says they can't reach it at all. What's actually missing?
answer:
A plain <div>, even with a click handler attached, is not focusable and has no built-in keyboard behavior. A keyboard-only user tabs through a page using the browser's native focus order, which only includes naturally interactive elements like links, buttons, and form controls by default — a <div> is invisible to that Tab order entirely.

A real link is focusable automatically, appears in Tab order, and activates on Enter, all without any extra work:

<a href="/product/42">View product</a>

Reproducing that on a <div> would require manually adding tabindex="0", a keydown handler for Enter and Space, and an appropriate ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) role — effectively rebuilding, by hand and imperfectly, behavior the native element already provides.
hint: Think about what makes an element reachable by pressing Tab in the first place.

question:
A codebase uses this pattern in a bunch of places instead of a real href or a <button>:

<a href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="deleteItem()">Delete</a>

Beyond losing normal link behavior, what actually goes wrong here?
answer:
The bigger problem is semantic, not just functional. An <a> tag is announced by screen readers as a link, and users generally expect links to navigate somewhere, not to perform a destructive action like deleting something. Using a link element for a button-like action misleads assistive technology users about what activating it will actually do.

On top of that, href="javascript:void(0)" means there's still no real destination, so all the same browser-native link behaviors break: no meaningful middle-click or right-click "open in new tab", no URL preview on hover, and no crawlability.

The correct fix is to use an actual button for an action like delete, since buttons are the semantically correct element for triggering behavior, and reserve real links for genuine navigation to a real URL:

<button type="button" onclick="deleteItem()">Delete</button>
hint: Ask what a screen reader announces this element as, and whether that description matches what actually happens when it's activated.

question: Say someone builds a pricing table with a bunch of styled <div>s instead of an actual <table>, and it looks pixel-perfect. What actually breaks for a user relying on a screen reader?
answer:
Visually the div version can look identical, but a screen reader has nothing structural to latch onto — just a stack of divs, no notion of which cell belongs to which row or column. A real <table> exposes that relationship natively, especially when the header cells use <th scope="col">, so assistive tech can announce something like 'Price, column Basic Plan' as the user moves through the data.

Rebuilding that same relationship on divs is possible with ARIA roles like role="table", role="row", and role="cell", but it's extra work to reproduce something the native <table> element already does correctly.
hint: Think about what information a real <table> gives assistive tech that a styled div can't.

question: When would we reach for an <ol> over a <ul>, and does it actually matter if the visual bullets look the same either way?
answer:
The visual marker is just CSS, so it can look identical either way, but the choice between <ol> and <ul> is really about whether the sequence itself carries meaning. Step-by-step instructions, a ranked list of results, or anything where swapping two items would change the meaning belongs in an <ol>. A list of navigation links, tags, or features where the order is just presentational belongs in a <ul>.

This matters beyond styling because screen readers announce ordered lists differently, often reading out the position like 'item 2 of 5', which is genuinely useful when the number matters and just noise when it doesn't.
hint: Consider what a screen reader announces differently between the two.

question: We need one table header to visually sit above two sub-columns, like 'Q1 Sales' spanning both a 'Units' and 'Revenue' column underneath it. How would we actually build that inside <thead>?
answer:
We can build two header rows inside <thead>: a top row where the 'Q1 Sales' <th> uses colspan="2" to stretch across both sub-columns, and a second row underneath with the individual 'Units' and 'Revenue' headers.

<thead>
  <tr>
    <th colspan="2">Q1 Sales</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th>Units</th>
    <th>Revenue</th>
  </tr>
</thead>

For this to stay accessible, the sub-column headers should also carry scope="col", and in more complex cases the data cells can reference specific header ids with the headers attribute so assistive tech knows exactly which of the two header rows a value belongs to.
hint: Two header rows, and one attribute that stretches a cell across columns.

question: Lighthouse flags an <img> for missing an alt attribute, but the image is purely decorative and doesn't add any real information. Why isn't just adding something like alt="image" the right fix?
answer:
For a genuinely decorative image, the correct fix is an explicitly empty attribute, alt="", which tells screen readers to skip the image entirely instead of announcing something unhelpful like "image" or a filename.

Leaving the alt attribute off completely is actually worse than an empty one, since some screen readers fall back to reading out the whole file path or filename, which is far more disruptive than a properly empty alt that signals there's nothing here worth announcing.

question:
<div class="hero">
  <img src="hero-3000x2000.jpg" alt="Featured product">
</div>

<!-- hero-3000x2000.jpg is a 3000x2000px photo,
     but the page's CSS displays it at only 400x300px -->

This hero image takes 4 seconds to load on mobile because the full-size photo downloads regardless of how small it's actually shown. What HTML feature addresses this without needing a CDN or image-editing pipeline?
answer:
The srcset and sizes attributes let the browser choose from several image files based on the actual display size and the device's pixel density, instead of always downloading the same huge original.

<img src="hero-800.jpg"
     srcset="hero-400.jpg 400w, hero-800.jpg 800w, hero-1600.jpg 1600w"
     sizes="(max-width: 600px) 400px, 800px"
     alt="Featured product">

With a handful of resized versions described in srcset, a phone downloads a file sized for its screen, not the multi-megabyte image a 4K monitor would need. It's a pure HTML fix with no build pipeline or CDN (content delivery network) required, though those help at scale.

question: A <video> with autoplay set works fine in testing on desktop Chrome, but on several mobile browsers it just sits there paused with no error at all. What's the most likely reason?
answer:
Most mobile browsers block autoplay for videos that have audio enabled, specifically to stop sound from suddenly playing the moment a page loads on someone's phone. This is a deliberate browser policy rather than a bug in the markup.

Adding the muted attribute alongside autoplay is what typically restores the autoplay behavior, since a silent autoplaying video is treated as far less disruptive than one with sound, and most browsers only allow autoplay when muted is present too.

question: A search input just shows a magnifying glass icon with no visible text label, and the developer added aria-label="Search" directly on the input. Is that an acceptable way to label it, or does it need something else?
answer:
An aria-label is a perfectly valid way to give an input an accessible name when there's genuinely no room for a visible label, and it does get announced by screen readers just like a real <label> would. So technically, yes, that input is labeled.

The trade-off is that aria-label text isn't visible on screen, which means sighted users relying on voice control software, or anyone visually scanning the page, get nothing to look at. A common middle ground is a real <label> that's visually hidden with a CSS class rather than removed from the DOM, since that stays available to more assistive technologies than an ARIA attribute alone and doesn't rely on a single tool interpreting it correctly.
hint: Weigh what aria-label gives you against what a visually-hidden real label would give you instead.

question: Does everything that's true about associating a <label> with a text input also apply the same way to a <select> dropdown or a <textarea>?
answer:
Yes — both the wrapping approach and the for/id pairing work identically for <select> and <textarea> as they do for a regular text input, since all of these are form controls that support being labeled the same way.

<label for="country">Country</label>
<select id="country">
  <option>India</option>
</select>

Clicking the label text in either case moves focus into the control, and for a <select> specifically, it can even open the dropdown in some browsers. The one thing worth remembering is that a label only ever associates with one control, so a group of several checkboxes or radios each still needs its own label, or a shared <fieldset>/<legend> around the whole group.
hint: Think about which form controls the labeling rules actually cover.

question: Inside the same <form>, what actually changes if a <button> has type="button" instead of the default type="submit"?
answer:
A plain <button> inside a <form> defaults to type="submit", so clicking it submits the form the normal way and triggers native validation on any required or pattern fields first. Setting type="button" strips that default behavior entirely — clicking it does nothing on its own, it only does something if JavaScript attaches a click handler to it.

This distinction trips people up most often when a form has more than one button, like a 'Submit' and a 'Save draft' side by side — if the second one is left as the default submit type without a handler stopping it, clicking it submits the whole form unintentionally instead of running whatever custom logic was intended.
hint: Consider what the default button type does the moment it's clicked, with no JavaScript involved at all.

question: What actually happens under the hood when a screen reader user jumps between page regions on a semantically-marked-up page instead of an all-div one?
answer:
Elements like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, and <footer> each carry an implicit ARIA landmark role — roughly banner, navigation, main, complementary, and contentinfo. Screen readers build a landmarks list from these roles automatically.

That list is what powers shortcuts like "jump to main content" or "list all regions," letting a user skip straight to the part of the page they actually want instead of listening through everything from the top.

  • A <div id="main"> has no such role, so it never appears in that landmarks list
  • A visually identical layout built from real elements gives the exact same navigation shortcuts for free
Semantic elements aren't just cleaner markup — they're the actual data source assistive tech uses to build its navigation shortcuts.
hint: Think about ARIA landmark roles and what generates a screen reader's regions list.

question: You're marking up a one-page site with blocks like About, Services, and Contact, plus a blog listing where each post is its own item. How do you decide which parts get <section> and which get <article>?
answer:
The test is whether a piece of content would still make sense pulled completely out of the page and placed somewhere else on its own — a syndicated feed, a different site, a search result. If yes, it's an <article>.

A single blog post passes that test: it has its own title, author, and body, and reads fine in isolation. About, Services, and Contact don't — they're thematic groupings of a single page's content, not standalone units, so <section> fits them better.

<section id="services">
  <h2>Services</h2>
  ...
</section>

<section id="blog">
  <h2>Latest Posts</h2>
  <article>...</article>
  <article>...</article>
</section>

Notice the blog listing itself is a <section> (a thematic group), while each post inside it is an <article> (self-contained).
hint: Ask whether the content would still make sense if it were syndicated or moved to another page entirely.

question: A documentation site skips real heading tags entirely — every heading is a <div class="h1-style"> or <div class="h2-style"> styled with CSS to look the right size. Visually it looks identical to a properly structured page. What breaks for a screen reader user, and what should change?
answer:
Screen readers build a page outline from actual heading elements, <h1> through <h6>, and many users navigate by jumping heading-to-heading rather than reading linearly, similar to skimming a table of contents. A styled <div> carries none of that structural information, no matter how large or bold the CSS makes it look.

To that user, a page like this has no outline at all — every heading-looking block announces as plain, unremarkable text, and heading-navigation shortcuts return nothing.

The fix is to use real heading elements for anything that functions as a heading, reserving CSS purely for how they look:

<h1>Getting Started</h1>
<h2>Installation</h2>
<h2>Configuration</h2>
  <h3>Environment Variables</h3>

Visual size and real semantic level are two separate concerns — a heading's font size should come from CSS, but its meaning has to come from the actual tag.
hint: Consider how a screen reader builds its heading-based outline of a page.

question: Since type="email" already validates email format for us, is there ever a good reason to also add a pattern attribute on top of it?
answer:
The built-in type="email" check is intentionally permissive — it mostly just confirms there's an @ with something reasonable on either side, following the HTML spec's own definition of a valid email, which is looser than what most people picture as a 'real' email format.

Adding a pattern on top makes sense when a specific business rule needs enforcing beyond that baseline, like restricting signups to a particular company domain with a pattern matching that domain. It's still not a substitute for verifying the address actually exists or belongs to the person, which realistically only happens by sending a confirmation email and having them click a link in it.
hint: Think about how loose the built-in email format check actually is.

question: If a form's submission is handled entirely through a JavaScript click handler on the submit button rather than listening for the form's submit event, does the browser still run HTML's built-in validation like required and minlength?
answer:
Not automatically, no. Native constraint validation, the kind that required, minlength, and pattern rely on, is tied to the form's actual submit event firing, so if a click handler just reads field values and sends them off directly, that event never fires and none of those checks run on their own.

To get that validation back without changing the interception approach, the code can call form.reportValidity() manually before sending the request — it runs the same built-in checks and shows the browser's native error bubbles, returning false if anything fails so the manual submit logic can bail out early.
hint: There's a method that manually triggers the same checks the browser would normally run automatically.

question: For a field that should stay numbers-only as the user types, not just at submit time, is there any built-in HTML attribute that filters keystrokes live, or does that always need JavaScript?
answer:
No plain HTML attribute filters individual keystrokes as they happen for a text-type input — pattern and required only get checked when the form is submitted, not on every keypress. The closest built-in option is switching the input to type="number", since browsers do restrict what characters can be typed into that specific input type at the keystroke level.

If the field genuinely needs to stay type="text", for something like a formatted code with dashes, real-time filtering needs a JavaScript input event listener that strips or rejects disallowed characters as they're typed, since there's no purely declarative HTML way to do that.
hint: Consider whether any attribute you'd put directly on the input runs on every keypress versus only at submission.

question:
We're embedding a third-party chat widget with a bare iframe and nothing else, like this:

<iframe src="https://widget.example.com"></iframe>

A security review flags it even though the vendor is reputable today. What's the actual concern, and what attribute would we reach for?
answer:
A plain iframe with no restrictions can run scripts, submit forms, open popups, and request various browser permissions by default. If that vendor's domain is ever compromised, sold, or repurposed later, we've effectively handed it a lot of capability with no guardrails in place.

The sandbox attribute lets us lock that down. Adding sandbox="allow-scripts", for example, permits scripts to run but blocks everything else that isn't explicitly listed, so even a misbehaving or compromised embed is contained to a much smaller blast radius.
hint: Think about what a plain iframe is allowed to do by default, and which attribute narrows that down.

question: A product page embeds a Google Maps <iframe> near the bottom, well below the fold, and a Core Web Vitals audit still blames it for a chunk of the page's load time even though almost nobody scrolls that far. Why is a frame nobody sees still costing anything, and what's the fix?
answer:
An <iframe> starts fetching and rendering its content as soon as the browser parses the tag, regardless of whether that part of the page is currently visible. The map's scripts and tiles end up competing for bandwidth and main-thread time with the content someone actually sees first.

Adding loading="lazy" to the iframe defers that work until the frame is about to scroll into the viewport, so a map nobody reaches on most visits stops taxing the initial load at all.
hint: The fix is the same attribute used to defer offscreen images.

question: Our parent page tries to read iframe.contentWindow.document to pull some text out of an embedded page hosted on a different domain, and the browser throws a security error instead. Why does that fail, and is there a proper way to get data across?
answer:
This is the browser's same-origin policy at work. A page on one origin is not allowed to directly read or modify the DOM of a page from a different origin, even when that page is embedded intentionally inside an <iframe> on the same screen, otherwise any site could snoop on or tamper with content it merely embeds.

The supported way around that boundary is the postMessage API. Both the parent and the iframe can send each other structured messages explicitly, with each side choosing exactly what it exposes rather than one having free access to the other's internals.
hint: Direct DOM access across origins is blocked on purpose, but there's a messaging API built for exactly this.

question: A custom on/off toggle switch is built as a <div> styled to look like a switch, with a JavaScript click handler to flip its state. A keyboard-only user says they can't interact with it at all. What's actually missing beyond making it focusable?
answer:
A plain <div> isn't part of the Tab order and isn't operable from the keyboard by default, so the very first problem is that it can't be reached at all. Adding tabindex="0" fixes that reachability, but reachability alone doesn't make it usable.

Assistive technology still has no idea what kind of control this is or what state it's in, because a styled <div> carries no semantic information. A real fix needs several pieces together:

  • role="switch" so assistive tech announces it as an on/off control, not just "clickable"
  • aria-checked="true" or "false", kept in sync with the actual state
  • A keyboard handler so pressing Space or Enter toggles it, since a <div> only fires click events from a mouse by default
<div role="switch" tabindex="0" aria-checked="false">
  Notifications
</div>

This is exactly why a native <input type="checkbox"> styled to look like a switch is usually the simpler path — all of this comes built in for free.
hint: Reachability and operability are two separate problems — tabindex only solves one of them.

question: A mobile nav's hamburger menu button is written as just <button><svg>...</svg></button>, with no visible text. A screen reader announces it only as 'button,' with no clue what it opens. What's the fix, and why doesn't a visual tooltip solve it?
answer:
The button has an icon but no accessible name, so a screen reader has nothing to announce besides its role. Adding aria-label="Open menu" gives it one directly:

<button aria-label="Open menu">
  <svg>...</svg>
</button>

Now it announces as "Open menu, button" instead of just "button." A visually hidden text span placed inside the button works just as well and has the advantage of also being findable by in-page text search:

<button>
  <svg aria-hidden="true">...</svg>
  <span class="sr-only">Open menu</span>
</button>

A hover tooltip alone doesn't help here because screen reader users are frequently navigating by keyboard or by touch, not hovering a mouse over the icon — so a tooltip that only appears on hover is invisible to precisely the audience that needs the missing label most.
hint: Think about who actually triggers a hover tooltip, and who doesn't.

question: A modal dialog is implemented so that when it opens, focus stays exactly where it was on the page behind it, and pressing Tab moves through elements on the page behind the modal, not through the modal's own buttons. Why is this a real accessibility problem, and what should happen instead when the modal opens?
answer:
A mouse user can click into the modal wherever focus happens to be, but keyboard and screen reader users rely entirely on focus to know where they are. If focus stays on the background page, they may not know a modal opened at all, and tabbing through hidden background content is disorienting. It can even let them activate things they can't see.

When a modal opens, it should:

  1. move focus into the modal, usually to its first focusable element or its heading
  2. trap Tab inside the modal while it's open
  3. return focus to where it was before the modal opened, once it closes

The native <dialog> element opened with showModal() handles much of this automatically.

question: Our page has a solid <title> and good content, but when someone shares the link on LinkedIn, the preview card shows a random logo and a generic one-line description instead of anything specific to the page. What's actually missing?
answer:
Social platforms don't build their share preview from the regular <title> and page content, they look for Open Graph tags like <meta property="og:title">, <meta property="og:description">, and <meta property="og:image"> inside <head>.

Without them, the platform falls back to guessing from whatever image and text it can scrape off the page, which is exactly why the card looks generic. Adding those tags gives us direct control over exactly what title, description, and image show up whenever the link is shared.
hint: Social preview cards read a specific family of meta tags, not the visible page content.

question: Every product page on our store has <meta name="description" content="Buy quality products online">, technically present and correctly formatted on all of them. A content review still flags it as a problem, why?
answer:
The tag being present and syntactically valid doesn't make it useful. Search engines often use this description as the snippet shown under the page's title in results, and the same generic sentence repeated across hundreds of product pages tells a searcher nothing about what's actually on any one of them.

It also wastes an opportunity: a description written specifically for that product, its name, its key feature, its price, tends to earn a better click-through rate than a placeholder that could belong to any page on the site.
hint: The tag is valid HTML, the problem is what's inside it, and that it's identical everywhere.

question: Our single-page app swaps out the visible content as the user navigates between views with the router, but the <title> tag never changes, it's stuck on whatever the first route rendered. Why does that actually cause problems, beyond just looking a little off?
answer:
People rely on the browser tab title and on browser history entries to tell pages apart, especially with several tabs open or a long back-button history. If the title never changes, every view in the app looks identical in the tab bar and in history, which makes it genuinely harder to find the right tab or go back to the right screen.

It hurts search visibility too, search engines and anyone sharing a link use the title as the primary label for that specific view, so a static title makes every route in the app look like the same page to a crawler. The fix is to update document.title programmatically whenever the app's internal navigation changes what's showing, so the title tracks the current view rather than the first one loaded.
hint: Think about what people, and crawlers, actually use the tab title for when a page never technically reloads.

question: What is a WeakRef in JavaScript?

question: What does the debounce technique do?
answer: Debounce resets a timer on each event. The function only runs after a quiet period of N ms with no new events. Ideal for search-as-you-type: fire only after the user stops typing.

question: Why should memoization only be applied to pure functions?

question: What is the most common cause of a memory leak with DOM event listeners?

question: What is a "detached DOM node" memory leak?
answer: If you store a reference to a DOM element in a variable and then remove the element from the page, the element cannot be collected. It remains in memory as a "detached" node, potentially holding a large subtree.

question: How does JavaScript decide when to garbage collect an object?
answer: Modern engines use reachability analysis (mark-and-sweep). If no path from the global root can reach an object, it is collected. Setting a variable to null removes one reference — GC happens when all references are gone.

question: A developer caches API results in a plain object that grows indefinitely. What is the problem?

question: Why use a WeakMap for private instance data instead of a regular Map?
answer: A regular Map keeps a strong reference to its keys. If you use instances as keys, they stay alive as long as the Map exists. WeakMap holds keys weakly — when the instance is collected, its private data disappears too.

question: A teammate writes a loop that attaches click handlers to 5 buttons, expecting each to log its own index (0–4). Instead, every button logs 5. The loop uses var. They ask: "The callbacks are created inside the loop — why don't they each capture their own i?" What is the real explanation?
answer:
The variable i declared with var is hoisted to the enclosing function (or global) scope, so there is only one i binding shared by the whole loop. All five callback closures reference that same binding rather than five separate copies.

for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  button[i].addEventListener('click', () => console.log(i));
}
// every button logs 5

By the time any button is actually clicked, the loop has already finished running and i has reached its final value of 5. Switching the declaration to let creates a fresh binding for each iteration, so every closure captures its own copy and logs its own index instead.
hint: var is function-scoped — all five closures share the same i binding.

question: You need a counter module that exposes increment, decrement, and reset, but the count variable must be inaccessible from outside. A teammate says "just use a global variable — it's simpler." Why is the closure-based approach the correct one, and what problem does the global cause?
answer:
A closure-based counter wraps count inside an outer function's scope, so only the methods returned from that function can read or change it. No other code can reach in and modify count directly, whether by accident or on purpose.

function createCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    decrement: () => --count,
    reset: () => (count = 0),
  };
}

A global variable, by contrast, is reachable from any script running on the page. A third-party library, a typo in an unrelated file, or even a line typed into the browser DevTools console could all corrupt it. The closure gives us true encapsulation without needing a class at all.
hint: Closures create private state; globals can be mutated by any code.

question: A React developer has a useEffect that sets up a setInterval. Inside the callback, they read a `count` state variable, but it always shows 0 even after the state has updated. They are confused because count looks fine in the render. What is happening and how do you fix it?
answer:
The setInterval callback is created once, when the effect first runs on mount, and it closes over whatever count was at that moment, which is 0. When the component re-renders after a state update, the interval callback keeps referencing that original binding rather than the new one, so it always logs 0 even though the rendered UI shows the current value.

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    setCount(c => c + 1); // functional updater, no stale read
  }, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);

The fix is to use the functional updater form of setState, setCount(c => c + 1), so the callback never needs to read count directly at all. Alternatively, we could include count in the effect's dependency array so a new interval, and a fresh closure, is created every time it changes.
hint: The interval callback closes over the initial count value — this is a stale closure.

question: You are reviewing a codebase written before ES Modules existed. You find a pattern where every feature is wrapped in a function that immediately executes and returns an object. A new developer asks why the original authors didn't just write plain objects. What was the closure-based IIFE solving?
answer:
Before import/export existed, every variable declared at the top level of a script was global, which was a serious problem once a page loaded many scripts side by side. The IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) solved this by creating its own function scope.

const myModule = (function () {
  let privateState = 0;
  function helper() { /* hidden */ }
  return {
    doSomething() { return ++privateState; },
  };
})();

Helper functions and internal state declared inside the IIFE stay hidden from every other script on the page; only the object it returns is exposed. This was the standard way to get encapsulation and avoid naming collisions before ES Modules brought true file-level scope.
hint: IIFEs created private scope before the module system existed.

question: A function successfully reads a variable from an outer scope, but a teammate insists it shouldn't work because "the variable is in a different function." They believe scope means the variable only exists within the braces it was declared in. How do you correct their mental model?
answer:
JavaScript uses lexical scope, which means a function's accessible variables are determined by where the function is written in the code, not where it happens to be called from. An inner function has access to its own local scope plus every scope that encloses it, all the way up to the global scope, and this chain of enclosing scopes is called the scope chain.

So a function reading a variable from an outer function is not a special case or a bug; it is exactly how scoping is meant to work. If a variable is not found locally, JavaScript walks up through each enclosing scope until it either finds a matching name or reaches the global scope, at which point it throws a ReferenceError.

Scope in JavaScript is about where code is written, not where it is executed from.
hint: Scope chain: inner functions have access to all enclosing scopes, not just their own.

question: A developer argues that JavaScript classes are fundamentally different from prototypes and that using classes is "proper OOP." Another disagrees and says classes are just syntax sugar. Who is right, and what does the code actually do under the hood?
answer:
The second developer is correct: ES6 class syntax is sugar over the same prototype-based inheritance JavaScript always had. A class declaration compiles down to a constructor function whose methods are placed on its prototype property.

class Dog {
  bark() { return 'woof'; }
}
// roughly equivalent to:
function Dog() {}
Dog.prototype.bark = function () { return 'woof'; };

instanceof, Object.getPrototypeOf, and the rest of the prototype chain all behave identically whether the code was written as a class or a plain constructor function. What classes add is stricter rules, since they must be called with new and always run in strict mode, plus cleaner inheritance syntax via extends and super, but the underlying mechanism is unchanged.
hint: Classes compile to prototype-based code — same internal mechanism, cleaner syntax.

question: A developer creates a subclass and gets a ReferenceError: "Must call super constructor in derived class before accessing this or returning from derived constructor." They only added a new property — they did not change the constructor logic. What rule did they violate?
answer:
In a derived class, one that uses extends, the parent class is responsible for actually creating the this object; the subclass constructor does not create it on its own. JavaScript enforces this by requiring super() to run before this can be accessed.

class Animal {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name) {
    super(name);   // must come first
    this.legs = 4; // now safe to use `this`
  }
}

Omitting super() entirely, or referencing this before calling it, throws the ReferenceError. It does not matter that only one new property was being added: super(), with whatever arguments the parent constructor needs, still has to run before this is touched.
hint: super() must be called before any use of this in a derived class constructor.

question: You add a method to an object's prototype after several instances have already been created. A teammate is surprised that all existing instances immediately have access to the new method. How do you explain why this works?
answer:
Instances do not take a snapshot of the prototype at the moment they are created. Instead, each one holds a live [[Prototype]] link back to the constructor's prototype object.

function Dog() {}
const rex = new Dog();
Dog.prototype.bark = () => 'woof';
rex.bark(); // 'woof' — works even though rex existed first

When a method is called on an instance, JavaScript first looks for it on the instance itself, and if it is not found there, follows the [[Prototype]] link to the prototype object. Because every instance shares that same prototype object, adding a method to it becomes visible to all of them immediately, and there is nothing on the instances themselves that needs updating.
hint: Instances do not copy methods — they look them up on the prototype at call time.

question: A teammate uses instanceof to check the type of data coming from an API and sometimes gets unexpected false results. They are sure the data is the right type. What is a common reason instanceof can give surprising results, and what is a more reliable alternative?
answer:
instanceof works by walking the prototype chain and checking whether the constructor's prototype object appears anywhere in it. It can give a false negative when the object comes from a different JavaScript realm, such as an iframe, a Web Worker, or a separately bundled copy of the same library, because in that case the constructor is a different object in memory even though it looks identical.

A more reliable check in that situation is Object.prototype.toString.call(value), which returns a standard tag such as "[object Array]" regardless of which realm the value came from. Checking for specific properties and methods the value is expected to have, sometimes called duck typing, is another practical alternative.
hint: instanceof walks the prototype chain — it can fail across different realms or versions.

question: A developer loops over an object's properties with for...in and is surprised to see inherited methods from the prototype showing up. They expected only the properties they explicitly set. How do you explain what for...in iterates, and how do you fix the loop?
answer:
for...in iterates every enumerable property on the object and everything along its entire prototype chain, not just the properties set directly on the object. If a prototype method happens to be enumerable, which can happen with older patterns or manual prototype assignment, it shows up in the loop too.

for (const key in obj) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) {
    console.log(key, obj[key]);
  }
}

The standard fix is to guard the loop body with Object.hasOwn(obj, key) or obj.hasOwnProperty(key). The more modern alternative is to avoid for...in altogether and use Object.keys(obj), which returns only the object's own enumerable string keys, or Object.entries(obj) for key-value pairs.
hint: for...in includes inherited enumerable properties — use hasOwnProperty or Object.keys().

question: A class method works correctly when called on the instance, but throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'setState')" when passed as a callback to addEventListener. The code is identical — only the call site changed. Explain what happened to this.
answer:
When a method is called as obj.method(), JavaScript sets this to obj, which is implicit binding. But once the method is extracted and passed around as a standalone function reference, like element.addEventListener("click", this.handleClick), the browser ends up calling it as a plain function with no receiver at all.

class Widget {
  handleClick() { this.setState(); } // `this` is undefined here
}
el.addEventListener('click', widget.handleClick);

Because classes run in strict mode automatically, this defaults to undefined in that case rather than falling back to the global object, which is why accessing this.setState throws. The fix is to bind the method in the constructor (this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this)), define it as an arrow function class field, or wrap the call in an arrow function: addEventListener("click", () => this.handleClick()).
hint: Passing a method as a callback detaches it from the object — this becomes undefined in strict mode.

question: A developer defines a method on an object using an arrow function and is surprised that this inside it does not refer to the object. They thought arrow functions "inherit" this. What is the correct explanation?
answer:
Arrow functions do not have their own this. They inherit it from the surrounding lexical scope at the point where they are defined, not from whatever object they end up attached to.

const obj = {
  name: 'Widget',
  greet: () => console.log(this.name), // `this` is NOT obj
};

When an arrow function is used as a method inside an object literal, its surrounding scope at definition time is the module or global scope, not the object, so this does not refer to the object at all. Methods that need this to refer to the instance should be written as regular functions instead. Arrow functions are better suited to callbacks written inside a method, where we actually want the outer this to be preserved.
hint: Arrow functions capture this from where they are defined, not the object they are assigned to.

question: A developer uses .call(), .apply(), and .bind() interchangeably, saying they all do the same thing. A teammate disagrees. Clarify how each one differs and when you would choose one over the other.
answer:
All three change what this refers to inside a function, but they behave differently.

  • .call(thisArg, arg1, arg2) invokes the function immediately, passing arguments individually.
  • .apply(thisArg, [arg1, arg2]) also invokes immediately, but takes the arguments as an array, which is useful when they are already collected in one.
  • .bind(thisArg) does not invoke the function at all; it returns a new function with this permanently bound, ready to be called later or stored somewhere.

call and apply are typically reached for when borrowing a method for a one-off call, while bind is the right choice when a method is being passed around as a callback that needs a stable this.
hint: call/apply invoke immediately; bind returns a new function with this pre-set.

question: A junior developer calls a constructor function without the new keyword and is confused that instead of creating an object, some properties got added to the global object. Explain why this happened and how new changes the behaviour.
answer:
Without new, calling a constructor function is just a regular function call. In non-strict mode, this defaults to the global object, so an assignment like this.name = "Alice" ends up attaching a property to window or global instead of a new object.

function Person(name) { this.name = name; }
Person('Alice');                // pollutes the global object
const p = new Person('Alice');  // creates a real instance

With new, JavaScript creates a fresh empty object, sets its [[Prototype]] to the constructor's prototype, calls the function with this bound to that new object, and returns it. The new keyword is what actually gives a constructor function its object-creation behaviour, without it the function just executes its body against whatever this happens to default to. Strict mode, and class syntax by extension, guards against this accidental global pollution by leaving this as undefined when no proper binding exists.
hint: Without new, this in a constructor is the global object (or undefined in strict mode).

question: Code has both a .bind() call and a method call on an object at the same time. A developer is unsure which binding wins. Walk through the four binding rules and their priority order.
answer:
JavaScript resolves this using four rules, applied in priority order from lowest to highest.

  1. Default binding (lowest): a standalone function call leaves this as the global object, or undefined in strict mode.
  2. Implicit binding: calling a function as obj.method() sets this to obj.
  3. Explicit binding: .call(), .apply(), or .bind() override whatever implicit binding would otherwise apply.
  4. new binding (highest): when a function is invoked with new, this is the newly created object, and not even bind can override this.

So if a function that was already bound with .bind() is later called with new, the bound this is ignored and this becomes the freshly created instance instead.
hint: Priority: new > explicit (bind/call/apply) > implicit (method call) > default.

question: A developer writes a regex to extract content between the first pair of HTML tags. The pattern /<.*>/ matches the entire string from the opening tag to the last closing tag instead of stopping at the first one. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
answer:
The .* quantifier is greedy by default, meaning it expands to match as many characters as possible while still letting the overall pattern succeed. So /<.*>/ matches starting at the first < but keeps extending all the way to the very last > in the string, swallowing everything in between.

const html = '<p>hi</p><span>bye</span>';
html.match(/<.*>/)[0];   // whole string, greedy
html.match(/<.*?>/)[0];  // '<p>', lazy

Making the quantifier lazy with .*? tells the engine to match as few characters as possible, so it stops at the very first > it encounters. /<.*?>/ captures just the first tag. For HTML parsing beyond a simple case like this, a real parser such as DOMParser or a library like cheerio is more reliable than a regex.
hint: The default quantifier is greedy — add ? to make it lazy: /<.*?>/

question: A developer uses regex.test() in an if statement and it works the first call. The second call on the same string returns false even though the string has not changed. The regex has the global flag. Why?
answer:
When a regex has the global (g) flag, it keeps a stateful lastIndex property that records where the previous match ended. The next call to .test() or .exec() resumes searching from that position instead of starting over at 0.

const re = /foo/g;
re.test('foo bar'); // true, lastIndex now 3
re.test('foo bar'); // false, resumes searching after index 3

After a successful match, lastIndex advances past it; after a failed match, it resets back to 0. That is why alternating calls on the same string alternate between true and false. This can be avoided by resetting regex.lastIndex = 0 between calls, creating a fresh regex each time, or simply dropping the g flag when only a boolean result is needed.
hint: A regex with the g flag has stateful lastIndex — test() advances it on each match.

question: A developer needs to extract the year, month, and day from dates formatted as "2024-07-15". They use str.match(/\d+/g) and get an array of three strings. A teammate suggests using capture groups instead. What advantage do capture groups offer here?
answer:
str.match(/\d+/g) does return ["2024","07","15"], but the result depends entirely on position, so if the date format ever changes, every piece of code reading that array has to be updated too.

const re = /(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})-(?<day>\d{2})/;
const { groups } = '2024-07-15'.match(re);
groups.year;  // '2024'
groups.month; // '07'

Named capture groups put each value on match().groups under a semantic name, .year, .month, and .day, instead of a numeric index. The code reading the result becomes self-documenting, and it stays correct even if extra capture groups are added earlier in the pattern.
hint: Named capture groups give semantic labels to each part via match().groups.

question: A form validates email with a simple regex and accepts "user@" as a valid email. A teammate wants to tighten it but says regexes are the wrong tool for email validation entirely. Who is right?
answer:
Both developers have a valid point here. A simple pattern like /^\S+@\S+\.\S+$/ is reasonable for immediate feedback in a form, since it catches obviously malformed input without pulling in unnecessary complexity.

At the same time, the full RFC 5322 email specification is famously complex, and a fully compliant regex is enormous, and even then it cannot verify that the address actually exists or can receive mail. A practical approach combines a lightweight client-side regex for fast UI feedback with a confirmation email that verifies the address actually works.

Client-side validation is for user experience, not security — the server should always re-validate independently, since it can be bypassed entirely.
hint: Basic regex catches obvious mistakes; full RFC 5322 email validation belongs to the server.

question: A developer needs to sanitize user input by replacing all occurrences of multiple consecutive spaces with a single space. They write str.replace(" ", " ") and it only replaces the first occurrence. How do you fix this and what does the corrected version look like?
answer:
String.prototype.replace only replaces the first occurrence when the first argument is a plain string rather than a regex. That is why str.replace(" ", " ") collapses only the first pair of spaces it finds.

str.replace(/ +/g, ' ');
// or, for a literal fixed-length match:
str.replaceAll('  ', ' ');

To replace every occurrence, a regex with the global (g) flag is needed: str.replace(/ +/g, " "), where / +/ matches one or more consecutive spaces and g makes sure every match is replaced, not just the first. The modern str.replaceAll() works well for literal strings without a regex, but since it only matches exact text, collapsing a variable number of spaces still calls for the regex approach.
hint: String.replace without a regex only replaces the first match — use /pattern/g to replace all.

question: A user reports that a web app freezes for several seconds when they click "Process". Looking at the code, you find a synchronous loop that processes 100,000 records. setTimeout callbacks and UI updates are not firing during this time. Explain what is blocking the browser and propose two solutions.
answer:
The synchronous loop occupies the call stack for the entire time it runs. The event loop can only process queued callbacks — timers, events, microtasks — when the call stack is empty, so everything else stays frozen until the loop finishes.

function processAll(records) {
  for (let i = 0; i < records.length; i++) {
    processRecord(records[i]);
  }
}

Two approaches address this. Breaking the work into chunks and using setTimeout to yield control between chunks lets the browser repaint and process events between each batch:

function processInChunks(records, size = 500) {
  let i = 0;
  function next() {
    const end = Math.min(i + size, records.length);
    for (; i < end; i++) processRecord(records[i]);
    if (i < records.length) setTimeout(next, 0);
  }
  next();
}

The other option is moving the processing to a Web Worker, a separate thread that runs JavaScript in parallel without touching the main thread, which keeps the UI responsive throughout since the main thread is never blocked.
hint: Synchronous code blocks the call stack — the event loop cannot pull any callbacks while it runs.

question: A developer writes code with both setTimeout(fn, 0) and Promise.resolve().then(fn). They expect them to run in the order they were written since both have no delay. But the Promise callback always runs before the setTimeout even when setTimeout comes first. Why?
answer:
setTimeout(fn, 0) schedules fn as a macrotask in the task queue. Promise.resolve().then(fn) schedules fn as a microtask in the microtask queue. These are two different queues with different priority.

console.log('start');
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'));
console.log('end');
// Logs: start, end, promise, timeout

The event loop has a rule: after each task, including the initial script execution, it completely drains the microtask queue before pulling the next macrotask. So regardless of the order in which the two callbacks were registered, all pending microtasks run before the next setTimeout callback fires.
hint: Promise .then callbacks are microtasks — microtasks drain before any macrotask fires.

question: A developer wraps a slow API call with async/await and expects the rest of the page to remain responsive. Another developer says "it's still blocking because it waits." Who is right, and what does await actually do to the thread?
answer:
The second developer is wrong about the mechanism. await suspends only the async function it appears in — it does not block the call stack or the rest of the page.

async function loadData() {
  const res = await fetch('/api/data'); // engine pauses here
  return res.json();
}
loadData();
console.log('this still runs immediately');

The JavaScript engine pauses the async function at the await and returns control to the event loop, which is free to run other callbacks, handle UI events, and process timers while the awaited promise is pending. When the promise resolves, the rest of the async function is scheduled as a microtask.

Blocking would mean no other code runs at all — async/await is the opposite of that.
hint: await suspends only the async function — the main thread is free; it is not blocking.

question: A component sets up a setInterval to poll an API every 5 seconds. The developer forgets to clear it when the component is removed. Months later, a user reports increasing network requests over time. Connect the missing cleanup to the event loop and memory behaviour.
answer:
setInterval schedules a callback in the task queue repeatedly until clearInterval is called. Without a matching clearInterval in the component's cleanup or unmount logic, the interval keeps running even after the component no longer exists in the DOM — making one API call every 5 seconds forever, plus one more for every additional time the component mounts without cleaning up.

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(poll, 5000);
  return () => clearInterval(id); // missing this is the bug
}, []);

The callback closure also keeps all captured variables alive, including any component state references, which prevents garbage collection of that state. The fix is to call clearInterval(id) in the cleanup function every time an interval is created.
hint: An uncleaned interval keeps firing and its closure keeps its references alive indefinitely.

question: A developer writes a recursive function that schedules itself using Promise.resolve().then(recurse) and notices the browser tab freezes completely — no scroll, no clicks, nothing. But the same approach with setTimeout(recurse, 0) would work fine. Explain why the Promise version freezes the tab.
answer:
After each macrotask, the engine drains the entire microtask queue before moving on to anything else. If a microtask schedules another microtask, which schedules another, infinitely, the queue never empties.

function recurse() {
  Promise.resolve().then(recurse); // never yields to the macrotask queue
}
recurse();

The event loop gets stuck in the microtask drain loop and can never pull the next macrotask, which is what handles scroll events, repaints, and timer callbacks. The tab becomes completely unresponsive.

function recurse() {
  setTimeout(recurse, 0); // yields back to the event loop each time
}
recurse();

setTimeout(recurse, 0) schedules a macrotask instead, so the engine processes one call, drains the empty microtask queue, renders a frame, then processes the next timer — the tab stays alive and responsive.
hint: Infinite microtask recursion starves the macrotask queue — no UI or events can fire.

question: A developer has a class that wraps a collection of items. They want to use it with for...of, spread syntax, and destructuring without exposing the internal array directly. What do they need to implement and why does it work with all three?
answer:
for...of, the spread syntax (...), and destructuring all rely on the iterable protocol: they call [Symbol.iterator]() on the target and then repeatedly call .next() on the returned iterator until done is true.

class Collection {
  #items = [];
  add(item) { this.#items.push(item); return this; }
  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    return this.#items[Symbol.iterator]();
  }
}

const c = new Collection().add(1).add(2).add(3);
for (const item of c) console.log(item);
console.log([...c]);
const [first] = c;

By adding [Symbol.iterator]() to the class, returning an appropriate iterator object (or writing it as a generator function), the class becomes iterable and automatically works with all three syntax forms without ever exposing the underlying array.
hint: Implement [Symbol.iterator]() to make the class iterable — all three syntax forms use this protocol.

question: A developer spreads an infinite generator into an array — [...gen()] — and the tab freezes. They thought generators were lazy. Explain why this happened and how to correctly take only the first N values.
answer:
Generators are lazy — they only compute a value when asked for one. But the spread operator asks for every value at once: it calls .next() in a loop until it sees done: true. An infinite generator never returns done: true, so the spread loop runs forever and freezes the tab.

function* naturals() {
  let n = 1;
  while (true) yield n++;
}

// [...naturals()] would hang forever

function take(iterable, n) {
  const result = [];
  for (const value of iterable) {
    if (result.length >= n) break;
    result.push(value);
  }
  return result;
}

take(naturals(), 5); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

The safe way to take only N values is a manual for...of loop with a counter and a break statement, as shown above, or an equivalent take(n, iterable) helper. Many utility libraries also provide a take() function for this exact purpose.
hint: Spread consumes the entire iterator — infinite generators need a manual loop with a break.

question: An API returns results page by page. A developer needs to process all results without loading everything into memory at once. A teammate suggests fetching all pages first with Promise.all, then processing. Explain why an async generator is the better approach.
answer:
Promise.all fetches every page in parallel and holds all of the results in memory before any processing even begins. For a large dataset that could mean hundreds of megabytes resident at once.

async function* fetchAllPages(url) {
  let next = url;
  while (next) {
    const res = await fetch(next);
    const page = await res.json();
    yield page.items;
    next = page.nextUrl;
  }
}

for await (const items of fetchAllPages('/api/results')) {
  processItems(items);
}

An async generator (async function*) fetches one page, yields it, and only fetches the next page when the consumer asks for another value via for await...of. Memory stays roughly constant, since only one page is held at a time.

If processing stops early, for example because a matching record was already found, any further pages are simply never fetched — something Promise.all cannot do, since it has already committed to fetching everything upfront.
hint: Async generators pull one page at a time on demand — no memory spike and early-exit is possible.

question: A developer needs to write a generator that yields the values from several other generators in sequence. They write a loop calling .next() manually on each sub-generator. A teammate points out there is a built-in syntax for this. What is it and why is it cleaner?
answer:
yield* delegates all yielded values from an expression to the outer generator's caller, transparently.

function* inner() {
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
  return 'inner done';
}

function* outer() {
  const result = yield* inner();
  console.log(result); // 'inner done'
  yield 3;
}

[...outer()]; // [1, 2, 3]

Instead of manually looping with gen.next() and re-yielding each value, yield* inner() streams all of inner's values inline. It also correctly captures the sub-generator's return value, shown above as the result of the yield* expression, which a hand-written loop would normally miss.

It is shorter, more readable, and it also correctly forwards edge cases like generator.throw() and generator.return() into the delegated generator.
hint: yield* delegates to another iterable — no manual .next() loop needed.

question: A developer wants to create a range(start, end, step) utility that can be used in for...of loops like Python's range(). They are unsure whether to use a generator function or a class with Symbol.iterator. What are the trade-offs?
answer:
A generator function such as function* range(start, end, step) is the quickest approach — it is a single function that produces values lazily and is immediately usable in a for...of loop. The downside is that each call to range() creates a new, non-reusable iterator; once it has been consumed, calling .next() again just returns done: true.

function* range(start, end, step = 1) {
  for (let i = start; i < end; i += step) yield i;
}

for (const n of range(0, 10, 2)) console.log(n);

A class implementing [Symbol.iterator]() is reusable instead: the same range object can be iterated multiple times, because each new for...of loop asks it for a fresh iterator.

For a utility used once per loop, a generator is sufficient. If the range object needs to be stored somewhere and iterated more than once, the class approach is the better fit.
hint: Generator function is simpler for one-off sequences; class allows reuse and multiple iterators.
