A postmortem process that names no root cause, assigns no owner to the resulting action items, and never checks whether they were completed isn't blameless, it's just directionless, and teams sometimes hide behind the word "blameless" specifically to avoid that harder work.
hint: Blameless means not punishing the person for the mistake, not skipping ownership of the system fix that follows from it.

question: How do you run a postmortem meeting well, not just write the document?
answer:
A postmortem meeting works best with a clear facilitator who isn't the person most directly involved in the incident, since someone close to the failure is naturally inclined to defend their own decisions rather than lead an open exploration of what happened. Building and circulating a rough timeline before the meeting, rather than reconstructing it live in front of everyone, tends to make much better use of the group's time, since the meeting can then focus on discussing why things happened and what to do about it rather than on establishing basic facts.

It also helps to explicitly separate the discussion into distinct phases: what happened (the facts), why it happened (contributing factors, ideally more than one), and what's being done about it (the action items), because groups that skip straight to solutions often fix the most visible symptom while missing a deeper contributing cause. The meeting isn't really finished until every action item has a specific owner and a rough timeline attached to it - an action item with no owner reliably becomes a line in the document that never happens.
hint: Have a neutral facilitator, pre-build the timeline before the meeting, separate facts/causes/actions, and end with an owner on every action item.

question: How would you get a team to actually act on retro action items instead of forgetting them?
answer:
The most common failure mode is that action items get written down in a document that's never looked at again until the next retro, so the first fix is usually mechanical: action items need to live somewhere the team already looks daily, like the same board or backlog used for regular work, rather than in a separate retro archive. Giving each one a named owner and, ideally, a rough size estimate at the time it's created makes a real difference too, since an unowned item phrased as a general improvement is much easier to quietly let slide than one with a specific person and a specific date attached.

It also helps to open every retro by reviewing what happened to the previous batch of action items before generating new ones, since that visible follow-through is what signals to the team that the process has teeth. Teams that keep proposing new action items every cycle without ever revisiting old ones tend to quietly stop taking the exercise seriously, because the pattern teaches them that nothing said in the room actually changes anything afterward.
hint: Put action items where the team already tracks work, give each a named owner, and open every retro by reviewing what happened to the last batch.

question: How would you pitch investing in developer experience to a non-technical exec?
answer:
The pitch lands better when it's translated into the language an executive already uses to make decisions - cost, risk, and speed to market - rather than technical detail about tooling or pipelines. Slow build times, flaky tests, and painful local setup all have a direct dollar cost in engineer time that can usually be estimated: if a team of thirty engineers loses even thirty minutes a day to a slow build, that's a meaningful chunk of fully-loaded salary cost being spent waiting rather than shipping, and that number tends to get attention in a way that a complaint about slow builds doesn't.

The other angle worth using is competitive speed: every hour lost to friction is an hour not spent on the features or fixes that actually move the business forward, and in a market where competitors ship faster, that gap compounds. It's worth pairing the ask with a concrete, time-boxed pilot rather than an open-ended investment - proposing to fix one specific, measurable pain point and reporting back the before-and-after numbers tends to build far more executive trust than a broad promise to improve developer experience in general.
hint: Translate developer pain into dollar cost and lost shipping speed, and back the ask with a small measurable pilot rather than an open-ended request.

question: How would you design a "golden path" for common tasks without mandating it?
answer:
The hard part of a golden path without a mandate is less the tooling and more the marketing of it, since a path that isn't required only succeeds if it's genuinely the easiest option available - if it's slower or more restrictive than doing things the old ad-hoc way, engineers will simply avoid it while nodding along in meetings. That means the path needs to actually work well for real teams' use cases from the start, which usually means co-designing it with a couple of willing early-adopter teams rather than building it in isolation and presenting it as finished.

Early, visible wins matter more than documentation here: a team that adopts the path and can point to concretely faster onboarding, fewer production incidents, or noticeably less on-call pain becomes a far more convincing advocate than any internal announcement. It also helps to make the golden path the option that's actively maintained and supported - quick to get help on, quick to get new capabilities added to - while leaving the alternative unsupported rather than banned; most engineers gravitate toward the option that gets fixed fastest when something goes wrong, without ever needing to be told to.

A golden path people are forced onto is a policy; a golden path people choose is genuinely golden.
hint: Win over a couple of real teams first with genuine ease and visible results, then let organic word of mouth and better support drive adoption rather than a mandate.

question: How do you measure ROI on automation work with no obvious dollar figure?
answer:
Even without a direct dollar figure, most automation work can be translated into time saved multiplied by frequency, and time can be converted into a rough cost using fully-loaded engineer salary - if automating a manual deployment step saves twenty minutes and it happens ten times a week, that's a concrete, defensible number even though no invoice anywhere says "automation savings." It's worth being honest that this is an estimate and stating the assumptions behind it, rather than presenting a suspiciously precise number that invites more scrutiny than it can survive.

Beyond direct time savings, some of the real value shows up as avoided cost rather than saved cost - fewer production incidents caused by manual error, faster onboarding because a new hire doesn't have to learn a fragile manual process, or reduced key-person risk because the knowledge is now encoded in automation instead of living in one person's head. These are harder to put a single number on, but they're worth naming explicitly alongside the time-saved calculation, since a decision-maker weighing the investment usually wants the fuller picture, not just the cleanest number.
hint: Convert time saved into a rough cost estimate using engineer time, and name the avoided-incident and reduced-key-person-risk value alongside it even if those aren't as easily quantified.

question: How do you stop things from sliding back after an improvement effort's initial win wears off?
answer:
Regression after an initial improvement is common because the conditions that created the improvement - focused attention, a specific project, maybe a few extra weeks of investment - usually go away right after the visible win, while the underlying pressures that caused the original problem, like deadlines, understaffing, or the path of least resistance, don't go anywhere. The most durable fix is usually baking the improvement into something that enforces itself rather than relying on ongoing discipline: a linting rule or CI check instead of a style guide people are supposed to remember, an automated dependency-update bot instead of a quarterly reminder to update packages.

Where the improvement can't be fully automated, it helps to assign explicit, ongoing ownership rather than treating it as a one-time project with a defined end date - someone needs to actually watch the relevant metric on a recurring basis and treat a regression as something to investigate, not just observe. It's also worth building a lightweight, periodic check-in into an existing recurring meeting rather than creating a new one, since a dedicated check-in on whether the improvement stuck is itself the kind of overhead that tends to get the first cut when things get busy again.
hint: Automate the improvement into a check or tool wherever possible, assign ongoing ownership rather than treating it as a finished project, and review it inside an existing recurring meeting.

question: How would you scale a successful improvement from one team to the whole org?
answer:
The instinct to mandate the same solution everywhere immediately is usually the wrong first move, because what worked for one team often depended on specifics of its stack, its size, or its existing tooling that don't hold everywhere else. A better first step is understanding why it worked for that team - separating the reusable underlying idea from the team-specific implementation details - since the thing worth scaling is usually the principle, not necessarily the exact script or configuration.

From there, it tends to work better to pilot the idea with one or two more teams with genuinely different contexts, such as a different stack, a different size, or a different maturity level, before declaring it ready for the whole org, since that surfaces the edge cases that the first team's success hid. Rolling it out with dedicated support - office hours, a point person, migration help - rather than a one-time announcement makes a real difference to adoption speed too, and it helps to expect and budget time for the rollout itself, since scaling almost always takes noticeably longer than the original pilot did.
hint: Extract the reusable principle from the original success, validate it with a couple of differently-shaped teams first, then roll it out with real support rather than just an announcement.

question: How do you tell a team that's actually improving from one that's just gaming its metrics?
answer:
The clearest tell is usually whether the improvement generalizes to things the metric wasn't directly measuring. A team that's genuinely getting better at, say, incident response will also show improvement in related but unmeasured signals - customer complaints trending down, engineers reporting the on-call experience has actually gotten less stressful - while a team gaming time to restore service might just be reclassifying incidents as lower severity or restarting a service to mask a problem instead of fixing it, which leaves everything around the metric unchanged or worse.

It's also worth looking at whether the underlying work that should produce the improvement is actually visible: real deployment frequency gains usually come with visible investment in pipeline automation and smaller pull requests, while a gamed number often has no such supporting evidence anywhere in the team's actual work. Talking directly to the team and to people adjacent to it, such as a support team or an on-call peer team, tends to reveal gaming much faster than staring at the dashboard alone, since the people closest to the work usually already know if a number stopped meaning what it used to mean.

A metric that's been optimized without the underlying reality changing has stopped being a signal and started being a target.
hint: Check whether related, unmeasured signals improved too and whether there's real supporting work behind the number, rather than trusting the metric in isolation.

question: What does being "on-call" actually involve day to day?
answer:
Being on-call mostly means carrying the responsibility to notice and respond to production alerts during a defined shift, not necessarily being buried in incidents. On most days the job looks like normal work with a phone or pager nearby, and the on-call engineer checks dashboards periodically, acknowledges automated alerts within an agreed response window, and triages anything that fires to figure out whether it needs immediate action or can wait until business hours.

When something does need attention, the on-call person is expected to start investigating quickly, decide whether to escalate to others, and communicate status even before the issue is fully understood. A good on-call setup also includes clear handoff notes at the end of a shift, a runbook or playbook for common alerts, and a way to escalate to a second engineer or a manager when things get overwhelming, so the responsibility never rests on one person with no backup.
hint: On-call is mostly steady monitoring punctuated by occasional real incidents, not constant firefighting.

question: Why do teams write postmortems at all?
answer:
Postmortems exist because incidents are expensive lessons, and without a deliberate process to capture what happened, teams tend to fix only the immediate symptom and forget the underlying conditions until a similar failure happens again. Writing one down forces a team to slow down after the pressure of an incident has passed and actually trace the chain of events, rather than relying on memory that fades within days.

Beyond the individual fix, postmortems build an organizational memory that new engineers can learn from, and they create a track record that helps justify investment in reliability work that might otherwise be deprioritized in favor of new features. Teams that skip this step often end up repeating the same class of failure every few months because nobody ever connected the dots across separate incidents.
hint: Postmortems turn a costly failure into organizational learning instead of a forgotten fire drill.

question: How would you explain an incident to people who aren't engineers?
answer:
When explaining an incident to a non-technical audience, it helps to lead with impact rather than mechanism: what the customer or business experienced, how many people were affected, and for how long, before getting into any technical detail at all. Phrases like "the checkout page was returning errors for about 12 minutes" land far better than describing a database connection pool exhaustion, even if that is the real underlying cause.

It also helps to separate three things clearly: what went wrong, what we did about it, and what we are doing to make sure it does not happen again. Analogies can help when the underlying concept is unfamiliar, for example comparing an overloaded server to a cashier who cannot serve more customers than the queue allows, but the analogy should support the explanation rather than replace the honest facts about impact and timeline.
hint: Lead with customer impact and timeline, not the technical mechanism.

question: Root cause isn't obvious and there's pressure for an ETA — what do you do?
answer:
When the root cause is not obvious and someone is asking for an ETA (Estimated Time of Arrival/completion), the instinct to give a reassuring guess should be resisted, because a missed ETA damages trust more than an honest "we don't know yet" does. A better approach is to separate mitigation from diagnosis: impact can often be reduced through a rollback, a feature flag, or a traffic shift well before the actual root cause is understood, and that buys time without making promises that cannot be kept.

For communicating status, it works well to give a time-boxed update instead of a fake ETA, such as "another update will go out in 20 minutes regardless of what is found," which keeps stakeholders informed without forcing a guess. Under pressure, it also helps to bring in a second pair of eyes or split the investigation into parallel tracks, since a single person staring at logs under time pressure is more likely to miss something than a small group working different hypotheses at once.
hint: Separate mitigating impact from finding root cause, and give time-boxed updates instead of guessed ETAs.

question: How do you decide when an incident is "resolved" vs. just "mitigated"?
answer:
An incident is "mitigated" once customer-facing impact has stopped or been reduced to an acceptable level, but the underlying cause may still be present in the system, just no longer triggering visible symptoms; a rollback or a traffic reroute is a classic example of mitigation. An incident is only "resolved" once the actual root cause has been addressed or a permanent fix is in place, and the team is confident the same trigger will not cause the problem again.

Treating mitigation as resolution is a common mistake, because it closes the incident in name only while the underlying risk quietly waits to resurface, often at a worse time. A useful discipline is to keep an incident open, or at least track a linked follow-up item, until the root cause has an owner and a fix, even if the customer-facing severity has already dropped to zero.
hint: Mitigated means impact stopped; resolved means the root cause itself is fixed.

question: How would you set up on-call for a team of 6 so nobody burns out?
answer:
With six people, a sustainable rotation usually means each person is on primary on-call roughly one week out of six, which is enough spacing to recover between shifts, plus a secondary or backup rotation so the primary is never the only line of defense. It also helps to rotate the "first responder" and "escalation" roles separately, so the same person is not both waking up for every alert and also the one everyone escalates to when things get hard.

Burnout tends to come less from the number of shifts and more from alert volume and unclear boundaries, so it is worth actively tuning alert thresholds to cut noisy, non-actionable pages, and setting an explicit policy that a rough night gets compensated with time off or a lighter following week. Rotating the schedule transparently, publishing it well in advance, and allowing swaps for personal circumstances also go a long way toward keeping on-call sustainable rather than dreaded.
hint: Spread primary/secondary roles and tune alert noise so no single person carries the whole burden.

question: Your manager asks you to set an SLA for a new internal tool — what do you consider first?
answer:
Before setting a Service-Level Agreement (SLA) for a new internal tool, the first question is who actually depends on it and how their work is affected if it is slow or unavailable, because an SLA promising five nines of uptime for a tool three people use occasionally is wasted effort, while an SLA that is too loose for something the whole engineering org depends on invites frustration.

It also matters to distinguish an SLA, which is a commitment with consequences, from an SLO (Service-Level Objective), which is an internal target used to guide engineering decisions; for most internal tools, starting with a modest SLO and observing real usage patterns for a few weeks before committing to anything formal tends to produce a more realistic number than guessing upfront. Finally, the target should be something the team can actually staff and support, since promising a response time or uptime figure with no on-call coverage behind it just sets everyone up to break the promise.
hint: Start from who depends on the tool and how they're affected, not from an arbitrary uptime number.

question: Someone on your team caused an incident and feels awful about it — how do you handle that without it turning into a blame thing?
answer:
The most important first move is to separate the person from the outcome out loud, making clear that the goal of any review is to understand the system and process gaps that allowed the mistake to happen, not to establish who is at fault. Most incidents caused by "human error" turn out to have several contributing factors, like a confusing interface, missing safeguards, or unclear documentation, and looking for those factors is both more useful and fairer than looking for someone to blame.

On a personal level, it helps to check in with the person directly and normalize that this happens to everyone eventually; a team where nobody has ever caused an incident is usually a team that is not shipping much.

If people are afraid to admit mistakes, they start hiding them instead, and a hidden mistake is far more dangerous than one that gets reported.

Reinforcing that blameless culture in the actual postmortem meeting, and giving credit for how quickly the issue was caught or reported, does more to prevent repeat incidents than any amount of finger-pointing.
hint: Focus the review on system gaps, not the person, and say so explicitly.

question: How would you architect a system so one failure doesn't take everything else down with it?
answer:
The core idea is to design for failure isolation, so that a problem in one component degrades a small, well-defined part of the system instead of cascading everywhere. Common techniques include bulkheads, which partition resources like connection pools or thread pools per dependency so one slow dependency cannot starve everything else; circuit breakers, which stop calling a failing dependency after it crosses an error threshold instead of piling up retries against it; and timeouts set aggressively enough that a single slow call cannot tie up resources indefinitely.

At a system level, this also means thinking about blast radius when deciding how to deploy and route traffic: splitting a monolith's most fragile dependencies into isolated services, using cell-based or shard-based architectures so a bad shard only affects the customers on it, and avoiding shared infrastructure, like one shared database or one shared queue, for otherwise unrelated features. Graceful degradation is the natural complement to this: even when isolation works, the affected part should fail in a way that keeps the rest of the product usable.
hint: Use isolation techniques like bulkheads, circuit breakers, and timeouts to contain blast radius.

question: How do you actually test multi-region failover, and how often should you do it?
answer:
Testing multi-region failover for real means actually shifting production traffic to the secondary region on a schedule, not just verifying that the secondary environment exists and looks healthy in isolation, because the failure modes that matter, like DNS propagation delays, stale data replication, or capacity shortfalls in the secondary region, only show up under real traffic and real data volume.

A reasonable cadence is to run a planned, announced failover drill quarterly at minimum, treating it like a fire drill with a rollback plan and clear communication to stakeholders beforehand, and to complement that with smaller automated checks, such as verifying replication lag and health-check readiness, more frequently, perhaps weekly. Game days, where the team deliberately fails a region during business hours with everyone watching, tend to surface far more gaps than a middle-of-the-night automated test that nobody is paying close attention to.
hint: Actually shift real production traffic to the secondary region on a recurring schedule.

question: How do you balance reliability investment against feature velocity when leadership wants both?
answer:
Framing reliability work as being in competition with feature work is usually the wrong lens, since a certain baseline of reliability is what makes feature velocity sustainable in the first place; an unreliable system slows every future feature down because engineers spend their time firefighting instead of building. A practical way to make this concrete for leadership is to set an explicit error budget tied to an agreed SLO (Service-Level Objective): as long as the team is within budget, feature work proceeds freely, and once the budget is spent, reliability work gets priority until it recovers.

This turns an abstract values debate into a shared, numeric agreement that both engineering and leadership can point to, rather than relitigating the tradeoff every sprint. It also helps to track and share the cost of unreliability in terms leadership already cares about, such as incident hours, customer churn linked to outages, or support ticket volume, so reliability investment reads as risk management rather than as engineering preference.
hint: An error budget turns the reliability-vs-features tradeoff into a shared, numeric agreement.

question: What's a "pre-mortem," and how's it different from a postmortem?
answer:
A postmortem happens after something has already gone wrong and works backward from the actual failure to understand its causes; a pre-mortem happens before a project ships or a risky change goes live, and works forward by imagining that it has already failed and asking why. The team gathers, assumes the worst has happened, and brainstorms every plausible way that could have occurred, which surfaces risks that normal planning discussions tend to skip over because nobody wants to be the person raising doubts about a plan everyone is excited about.

The value of a pre-mortem is that it gives permission to voice concerns without seeming negative, since the exercise is explicitly about imagining failure, not criticizing the plan directly. Findings from a pre-mortem typically turn into concrete mitigations added before launch, like extra monitoring, a staged rollout, or a rollback plan, whereas a postmortem's output is usually corrective actions after the fact; used together, they form a loop where lessons from past postmortems directly inform what a team looks for in future pre-mortems.
hint: A pre-mortem imagines failure before launch; a postmortem examines it after the fact.

question: How do you run an incident when it spans multiple teams that all do things differently?
answer:
The first priority in a multi-team incident is establishing a single incident commander role who coordinates across teams, even if that person does not have deep expertise in every system involved, because without one clear owner of the overall response, each team ends up running its own parallel investigation and communication, which wastes time and confuses stakeholders about what is actually happening.

Since different teams often use different tools, terminology, and severity definitions, it helps to standardize a minimal shared vocabulary just for the duration of the incident, such as a single shared channel, a single timeline document, and a single severity scale that everyone agrees to use regardless of their own team's normal process. The incident commander's job is largely translation and sequencing: making sure each team's specialist knowledge gets applied at the right time, that findings get shared across team boundaries instead of staying siloed, and that a single, consistent story of impact and status goes out to leadership and customers rather than several conflicting ones.
hint: Appoint a single incident commander and a shared vocabulary across teams.

question: How do you know if your incident response is actually getting better over time?
answer:
Improvement in incident response shows up in a handful of measurable trends rather than in any single metric: time to detect an issue, time to acknowledge it once paged, time to mitigate customer impact, and time to full resolution should all trend downward over a period of months if the response process is genuinely getting better, not just the occasional lucky quarter.

Beyond speed, it is worth tracking whether the same root cause or the same class of failure keeps recurring, since a team that resolves incidents quickly but never fixes underlying causes is not actually improving, just getting efficient at repeating the same fire drill. Softer signals matter too: whether postmortem action items actually get completed instead of piling up untouched, and whether engineers report feeling supported rather than dreading their on-call rotation, both of which tend to predict future incident trends before the hard metrics catch up.
hint: Track detection, mitigation, and resolution time trends, plus whether the same causes keep recurring.

question: How would you design a system to degrade gracefully instead of failing completely?
answer:
Designing for graceful degradation starts with identifying which parts of a product are essential and which are enhancements, so that when something breaks, the system can consciously shed the non-essential parts while keeping the core function alive; an e-commerce site, for instance, can disable personalized recommendations or reviews under load while still letting people search, browse, and check out.

Technically, this often relies on setting sensible defaults and fallbacks: serving slightly stale cached data instead of failing when a dependency is slow, returning a generic response instead of an error when a non-critical service is down, and using feature flags that can be flipped quickly to turn off expensive features under load. It also requires the system to know when it is struggling in the first place, through load shedding and health signals, so that degradation is a deliberate, controlled response rather than an accidental one discovered by users hitting errors.
hint: Identify what's essential, then build fallbacks so only non-essential parts get shed under stress.

question: What is a JavaScript engine, and how does it work?
answer:
A JavaScript engine is the program that actually runs our code — V8 in Chrome and Node.js, SpiderMonkey in Firefox, JavaScriptCore in Safari. It doesn't run our source text directly; it turns it into something the CPU can execute.

// what an engine does with this one line:
const total = price * quantity;

// 1. Parse    -> build a tree (an AST) out of the source text
// 2. Interpret -> turn the tree into bytecode, run it line by line
// 3. Profile   -> notice this line runs on every render
// 4. Compile   -> turn the "hot" bytecode into fast machine code

The engine also owns two jobs on the side: allocating memory for every object we create, and running a garbage collector that frees memory once nothing references it anymore. We never call either one directly — they just happen.
hint: Parse to an AST, interpret it as bytecode, profile hot code, then compile it to machine code.

question: What is Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation, and how does it optimize JavaScript performance?
answer:
Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation is how an engine gets speed without a slow startup. It doesn't compile everything up front — it interprets our code first so it starts running immediately, and watches which functions get called over and over.

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

for (let i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
  add(i, 1);   // called a million times -> gets "hot"
}              // the JIT compiles add() to machine code partway through

Once a function is "hot," the JIT compiler compiles just that function into optimized machine code while the program keeps running. Every call after that uses the fast version instead of going back through the interpreter.
hint: Interpret first for a fast start, then compile only the code that actually runs often.

question: How does the optimizing compiler improve JavaScript performance?
answer:
The optimizing compiler doesn't just compile a hot function — it compiles a specialized version of it, based on what it has actually seen at runtime.

function double(x) {
  return x * 2;
}

double(4);   // engine notices: always called with a number
double(9);   // ...and specializes double() for "number in, number out"

double("4"); // surprise -- a string.
             // the specialized version can't handle this, so the engine
             // "deoptimizes": throws away the fast version and falls
             // back to the slower interpreted path

This speculate-then-verify approach is why keeping a function's inputs consistent — always numbers, or always the same object shape — tends to make it noticeably faster. Mixing types forces the engine to keep re-deoptimizing instead of settling on one fast path.
hint: It speculates based on observed types, compiles a fast path, and deoptimizes if that guess turns out wrong.

question: What is hidden class optimization in V8, and why is it important?
answer:
V8 doesn't store an object's properties in a plain hash map — looking a property up by name on every access is too slow to do millions of times a second. Instead, every object gets a hidden class: an internal record of its shape, meaning which properties it has and in what order.

function Point(x, y) {
  this.x = x;
  this.y = y;
}

const a = new Point(1, 2);  // shape: {x, y} -> hidden class C0
const b = new Point(3, 4);  // same shape     -> also hidden class C0

b.z = 10;                   // b's shape changed -> new hidden class C1
                             // a and b no longer share a hidden class

Objects that share a hidden class let V8 use inline caching: the engine remembers exactly where a property lives in memory and jumps straight to it instead of looking it up again. Once b gets a different shape, code optimized for shape C0 can't reuse that fast path for b anymore.

Practical takeaway: initialize every property in the constructor, in the same order, instead of adding properties conditionally afterward.
hint: Objects with the same shape share a hidden class, which lets inline caching skip property lookup.

question: What is an Execution Context, and how is it created in JavaScript?
answer:
An Execution Context is the environment the engine builds to run a piece of code. One gets created for the whole script, and a new one gets created every time we call a function.

function greet(name) {
  console.log("Hi, " + name);
}

greet("Maya");
// 1. creation phase: sets up a Variable Environment for greet(),
//    hoists "name" as a parameter, links to the outer (global) scope
// 2. execution phase: runs console.log(...) line by line

Function declarations and var are ready to use as soon as the creation phase finishes — that's hoisting. let and const are recognized too, but stay unusable until the execution phase actually reaches their line.
hint: Creation phase sets up the scope and hoists declarations; execution phase runs the code line by line.

question: What is the Execution Stack (Call Stack), and how does JavaScript manage function calls?
answer:
The Call Stack is how the engine tracks which function is running and what called it. Every call pushes a new Execution Context on top; every return pops one off.

function third()  { console.log("third"); }
function second() { third(); }
function first()  { second(); }

first();
// stack grows:   first -> second -> third
// stack shrinks: third returns, then second, then first

Because it's a stack, the engine only ever runs whatever is on top. A function that keeps calling itself with no exit eventually fills the stack and throws "Maximum call stack size exceeded".
hint: Every call pushes a new context on top; every return pops it off -- last in, first out.

question: What is the Scope Chain, and how does it help resolve variables?
answer:
The Scope Chain is the path the engine follows to look up a variable it can't find in the current context. Every context keeps a reference to the scope it was written inside of — not the scope of whoever called it.

const city = "Pune";

function outer() {
  const team = "Engineering";
  function inner() {
    console.log(team, city);  // not defined here -- walk outward
  }
  inner();
}
outer();
// inner  -> checks its own scope: no team, no city
// outer  -> finds team here
// global -> finds city here

Because this chain is fixed by where a function is written, not by who calls it, the same function always resolves an outer variable the same way. That's also the exact mechanism that makes closures work.
hint: Each context links to the scope it was defined in -- look up fails locally, walk outward until found or you hit global.

question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) in JavaScript?
answer:
The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) is the stretch of code between the start of a block and the line where a let or const variable is actually declared — accessing it in that stretch throws.

console.log(a);   // undefined -- var is hoisted AND initialized
var a = 1;

console.log(b);   // ReferenceError -- b is hoisted but not initialized
let b = 2;

var is hoisted and set to undefined right away, so reading it early just gives us undefined. let and const are hoisted too, but stay uninitialized until their own line runs — which turns a quiet bug into an error we notice immediately.
hint: let/const are hoisted but left uninitialized until their declaration line runs.

question: What is Closure, and how does it work internally?
answer:
A closure is a function that keeps access to variables from the scope it was created in, even after that outer function has already returned.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return function () {
    count += 1;
    return count;
  };
}

const counter = makeCounter();
counter();  // 1
counter();  // 2 -- count survived, private to this counter

Normally, once makeCounter returns, its Variable Environment would be garbage collected — nothing needs it anymore. But the inner function keeps a live reference to it, so count stays reachable for as long as the returned function exists.
hint: The inner function keeps a live reference to the outer function's scope, which is why that scope survives.

question: What is the this keyword, and how does it behave in different contexts?
answer:
The this keyword refers to whatever object a function is running on behalf of — and that's decided by how the function is called, not where it's written.

const user = {
  name: "Maya",
  greet() { console.log(this.name); }
};

user.greet();          // "Maya" -- called as user.greet()

const fn = user.greet;
fn();                   // undefined -- called with no object

user.greetArrow = () => console.log(this.name);
user.greetArrow();     // still whatever "this" was outside --
                        // arrow functions don't get their own this

When we need this pinned to a specific object no matter how a function gets called, call, apply, or bind let us set it explicitly. Arrow functions skip all of this by design — they capture this from their surrounding scope, which is exactly why they're the safe default for callbacks.
hint: this is set by how a function is called, not where it's defined -- except arrow functions.

question: How does JavaScript handle memory allocation and garbage collection?
answer:
Every value we create — an object, array, or function — gets space allocated on the heap. We never free that memory ourselves; the engine's garbage collector does it for us.

function loadUser() {
  let user = { name: "Maya" };  // allocated on the heap
  return user.name;
}

loadUser();
// after loadUser() returns, nothing references that {name: "Maya"}
// object anymore -> it's unreachable -> the garbage collector reclaims it

The collector starts from a set of roots — global variables, whatever is currently on the call stack — and walks every reference it can follow from there. Anything it can't reach gets reclaimed. Anything we accidentally keep a reference to, on purpose or not, doesn't. That's what a memory leak actually is.
hint: Values get allocated on the heap; the collector reclaims anything it can no longer reach from a root.

question: What is a memory leak in JavaScript, and how can you prevent it?
answer:
A memory leak is a reference we forgot to let go of — the object is done being useful, but something still points to it, so the collector can never reclaim it.

function setupWidget(el) {
  const bigData = new Array(1000000).fill("x");

  el.addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log(bigData.length);  // closure keeps bigData alive
  });
  // if the widget is removed but this listener is never removed,
  // bigData stays in memory for as long as el does
}

The usual suspects: an event listener that's never removed, a setInterval that keeps running after its component is gone, a global that keeps accumulating data, or a detached DOM node we still hold a reference to. The fix is almost always the same shape — match every listener or timer with a matching cleanup, and reach for a WeakMap when we want to attach data to an object without being the reason it stays alive.
hint: A leak is a reference we forgot to let go of -- match every listener or timer with a matching cleanup.

question: What are the different types of Garbage Collection algorithms? (Mark and Sweep, Reference Counting)
answer:
Two classic approaches: reference counting and mark-and-sweep. The difference between them explains a real limitation, not just a historical curiosity.

let objA = { name: "A" };
let objB = { name: "B" };
objA.ref = objB;   // A points to B
objB.ref = objA;   // B points to A

objA = null;
objB = null;
// nothing outside can reach A or B anymore, but they still point
// at each other -- a reference-counting collector never sees
// either count reach zero, so neither one gets freed

Reference counting frees an object the moment nothing points to it — simple, but it can't collect two objects that only reference each other, like objA and objB above. Mark-and-sweep sidesteps this: it starts at the roots, marks everything it can actually reach, then sweeps away anything left unmarked, including that circular pair.

This is why V8 and every modern engine use mark-and-sweep, with a generational strategy on top, as the real algorithm -- reference counting only shows up in narrow, supporting roles.
hint: Reference counting can't collect two objects that only reference each other; mark-and-sweep can.

question: How do WeakMap and WeakSet help with memory management?
answer:
WeakMap and WeakSet hold their entries weakly — the garbage collector can reclaim a key even while it's still sitting inside one, as long as nothing else references it.

const cache = new Map();
let el = document.getElementById("save-btn");
cache.set(el, { clicks: 0 });  // Map holds a strong reference to el
el = null;                      // we're done with el...
// ...but the Map still references it, so el can never be collected

const weakCache = new WeakMap();
let el2 = document.getElementById("save-btn");
weakCache.set(el2, { clicks: 0 });
el2 = null;
// once nothing else references el2, both el2 and its entry
// in weakCache become collectible together

A regular Map keeps every key alive for as long as the map exists — using an object as a key can quietly become the leak. A WeakMap is built for exactly this case. The trade-off is that neither structure is iterable or exposes a size, because its contents can disappear at any moment.
hint: A WeakMap doesn't keep its keys alive -- once nothing else references a key, both can be collected together.

question: How can you monitor and optimize JavaScript memory usage?
answer:
The fastest way to actually find a leak is a heap snapshot, not a guess. In Chrome DevTools' Memory panel, we take a snapshot, repeat some action a few times, take another snapshot, and compare — whatever object count keeps climbing is usually the leak.

// Node.js -- check memory programmatically
console.log(process.memoryUsage());
// { rss: 45MB, heapTotal: 20MB, heapUsed: 15MB, external: 1MB }

setInterval(() => {
  console.log(process.memoryUsage().heapUsed);
  // healthy: rises, then drops back down after GC runs
  // leaking: keeps climbing and never comes back down
}, 5000);

The Performance panel's memory timeline shows the same idea visually — a sawtooth that rises as we allocate and drops when the collector runs. A healthy page returns to roughly the same baseline every time; a leaking one keeps creeping up. Once we know where memory is going, optimizing usually means allocating less in hot paths — no new objects or closures inside a function that fires on every scroll or animation frame — and reaching for a WeakMap wherever we're attaching data to objects we don't want to keep alive ourselves.
hint: Heap snapshots to find what's growing, the memory timeline to check it returns to baseline after GC runs.

question: A job posting asks for 'strong ES6 knowledge' and a teammate assumes ES6 is a separate language from JavaScript. What is ES6, and how does it relate to the JavaScript that runs in a browser?
answer:
ES6, more formally ECMAScript 2015, is not a separate language — it is a specific version of the ECMAScript specification that JavaScript implements.

Each yearly release of that specification (ES2015, ES2016, and so on) adds new syntax and features. let/const, arrow functions, classes, and template literals were all introduced specifically by ES6.

Browsers and Node.js implement these specification versions through their JavaScript engines, so writing "ES6 code" just means writing JavaScript using the syntax that version introduced — not switching to a different language.
hint: ES6/ECMAScript is a specification version JavaScript implements, not a separate language.

question: Two developers on the same project run npm install on the same package.json, but one ends up with a subtly different (and buggy) version of a dependency than the other. Both package.json files are identical. What's the likely cause, and what file prevents this?
answer:
package.json usually pins dependency versions with a caret (^) or tilde (~) range rather than an exact version, so npm install is free to pull the newest version matching that range at whatever moment it runs — which can differ between two installs done on different days.

"dependencies": {
  "some-lib": "^2.1.0"
}

The package-lock.json file records the exact resolved version, and the full dependency tree, that was actually installed. As long as it is committed to the repository, npm install uses those exact pinned versions instead of re-resolving the range, so every developer — and the deployment server — ends up with an identical dependency tree.
hint: package.json often allows a version range; package-lock.json pins the exact resolved versions.

question: A conditional if (count == '0') skips a block when count is the number 0, but a teammate insists it should only match the string '0', not the number. console.log(0 == '0') confirms it's true. What's causing this, and how would switching to === change the behavior?
answer:
The == operator performs type coercion before comparing. Since one operand here is a number, JavaScript converts the string '0' to the number 0, and 0 == 0 is true.

This coercion is convenient in some cases, but it produces surprising results, like '' == 0 or null == undefined also being true, when the intent was a stricter check.

console.log(0 == '0');  // true
console.log(0 === '0'); // false

The === operator compares both type and value without coercing anything first, so 0 === '0' is false because a number is never equal to a string. Using === by default, and reserving == for the rare cases where automatic coercion is genuinely wanted, avoids these accidental matches.
hint: == coerces types before comparing; === checks both type and value.

question: A function sets a default with const quantity = input || 1;, intended so quantity falls back to 1 when input isn't provided. But when a user explicitly enters 0, quantity still becomes 1 instead of staying 0. What's causing this, and what operator fixes it?
answer:
The || operator falls back to the right-hand value whenever the left-hand value is falsy, and 0 is falsy in JavaScript — just like '', null, undefined, and NaN — so || cannot distinguish "nothing was provided" from "a legitimate falsy value was provided."

const quantity = input || 1;  // 0 becomes 1 - wrong
const quantity2 = input ?? 1; // 0 stays 0 - correct

The ?? (nullish coalescing) operator only falls back when the left-hand value is exactly null or undefined, leaving 0, '', and false untouched. Rewriting the line as const quantity = input ?? 1; keeps an explicitly entered 0 as 0, while still defaulting when input is genuinely missing.
hint: || falls back on any falsy value; ?? only falls back on null or undefined.

document.createElement('li') only builds a detached element in memory — it exists as a JavaScript object but is not connected to the page's DOM (Document Object Model) tree yet, so nothing renders.

items.forEach(item => {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = item;
  list.appendChild(li); // the missing step
});

The missing step is actually inserting the element into an existing parent, for example list.appendChild(li) or the newer list.append(li), right after setting its content. Without that insertion step, any number of elements can be created and none of them will show up anywhere on the page.
hint: createElement only builds the element in memory — it still needs to be attached to an existing parent.

question: An event handler is attached to a
answer:
event.target is whichever exact element the click actually landed on, and since a click inside the button can land on the img or the span before it bubbles up, target changes depending on where the pointer was.

event.currentTarget is always the element the listener was actually attached to, regardless of where inside it the click landed, so referring to event.currentTarget instead of event.target inside this handler reliably returns the button every time.
hint: target is where the click actually landed; currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to.

The spread operator only performs a shallow copy — it copies the object's top-level properties, but any property whose value is itself an object or array is copied by reference, not by value.

const copy = { ...settings };
copy.theme.colorMode = 'dark'; // also changes settings.theme.colorMode

settings.theme and copy.theme still point to the exact same nested object after the spread, so mutating one mutates the other.

Avoiding this means either deep-cloning the whole structure, for example with structuredClone(settings), or spreading each nested level individually, like { ...settings, theme: { ...settings.theme } }.
hint: Spread only copies one level deep — nested objects are still shared by reference.

var is function-scoped, not loop-scoped, so there is really only one shared i variable across the entire loop. By the time any of the setTimeout callbacks actually run 100ms later, the loop has already finished and i has already reached 3, so all three callbacks read that same final value.

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100);
}
// logs 0, 1, 2

let is block-scoped, so each iteration of the loop gets its own fresh binding of i, and each callback captures the value i held during its own specific iteration — which is why switching to let prints 0, 1, 2 as intended.
hint: var shares one variable across the whole loop; let creates a fresh binding for every iteration.

question: A data layer throws a plain Error for both a failed validation and a failed network request. Calling code tries to tell them apart by checking whether err.message contains the word "network", and the check breaks the first time someone rewords a message. What is a more robust way to distinguish error types, and how is it typically implemented?
answer:
String-matching on err.message is fragile because the message text is meant for humans and can change wording at any time without warning the code that depends on it.

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
  }
}
class NetworkError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'NetworkError';
  }
}

A more robust approach gives each failure its own error class that extends the built-in Error, each calling super(message) in its constructor and setting this.name to match the class name.

Calling code can then branch on err instanceof ValidationError or err.name instead of scanning the message text, and that check keeps working even if the wording of the message changes later.

This is the same type-based thinking behind inspecting an error's type inside a generic catch block — a dedicated error class just makes that type explicit and checkable instead of implicit in a string.
hint: String-matching on err.message breaks when wording changes — what makes an error's type checkable instead of just readable?

question: A form submission sends data with fetch(url, { method: 'POST', body: formValues }), where formValues is a plain JavaScript object. Server logs show the request body arriving as the literal text [object Object], and none of the expected fields are readable. What is wrong, and how is this usually fixed?
answer:
fetch does not know how to turn a plain JavaScript object into a request body on its own. When something that is not already a string, FormData, or similar is passed as body, it gets coerced to a string using its default toString() behaviour, and for a plain object that produces the literal text "[object Object]" instead of the object's actual fields.

fetch(url, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify(formValues)
});

The usual fix is to serialize the object explicitly with JSON.stringify(formValues) and add a Content-Type: application/json header so the server knows how to interpret the body.

Both pieces matter together — stringifying without the matching header can lead the server to misinterpret a correctly-serialized body as the wrong content type.
hint: A plain object passed as a fetch body gets coerced with toString() — what does that produce, and what actually serializes it correctly?

question: A project's package.json doesn't set "type": "module", but a developer's script uses import fs from 'fs' at the top of a plain .js file, and Node.js throws "SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module". What's going on, and what are two ways to fix it?
answer:
Node.js treats a .js file as CommonJS by default, and CommonJS does not understand import/export syntax at all — it expects require() and module.exports instead. That mismatch is exactly what produces the SyntaxError.

There are two common fixes.

  • Adding "type": "module" to package.json makes Node.js treat every .js file in the project as an ES module.
  • Renaming just that one file to .mjs, which Node.js always treats as an ES module regardless of the package.json setting.

The reverse situation, forcing a single file to stay CommonJS inside an otherwise ESM project, uses the .cjs extension instead.
hint: Node treats .js as CommonJS unless package.json sets "type": "module", or the file uses .mjs.

question: A developer's app calls localStorage.setItem() to cache a growing dataset. It works fine in testing, but in production some users hit an uncaught exception the moment the cache is written, and the app crashes. What's the likely cause, and how should it be handled?
answer:
localStorage has a per-origin storage limit, commonly somewhere around 5-10MB depending on the browser, and calling setItem() past that limit throws a QuotaExceededError instead of silently failing or evicting old data on its own.

try {
  localStorage.setItem('cache', JSON.stringify(data));
} catch (err) {
  // clear old entries, store less, or skip caching
}

Production users tend to accumulate far more cached data over time than a freshly cleared test environment ever does, so they are far more likely to hit that ceiling. The fix is to wrap setItem() calls in a try/catch block and handle the error gracefully, for example by clearing older cached entries, storing a smaller subset of the data, or falling back to not caching at all, rather than letting the exception propagate and crash the app.
hint: localStorage has a per-origin size limit — setItem() throws QuotaExceededError past it, so writes need a try/catch.

question: A generator function opens a resource and wraps its yield loop in a try/finally block to close it: `function* readLines(file) { const handle = open(file); try { for (const line of handle) yield line; } finally { handle.close(); } }`. A consumer uses `for (const line of readLines(f)) { if (line === 'STOP') break; }` and the handle is closed correctly. A second consumer instead calls `.next()` manually in a while loop and uses `break` to stop early, and the handle stays open. Why does the first case clean up correctly but the second does not?
answer:
for...of calls the iterator's return() method automatically whenever the loop exits early, whether that is through a break, a thrown error, or a return statement inside the loop body. Calling return() on a generator forces it to resume at its currently suspended yield and immediately run any pending finally block.

function* readLines(file) {
  const handle = open(file);
  try {
    for (const line of handle) yield line;
  } finally {
    handle.close();
  }
}

for (const line of readLines(f)) {
  if (line === 'STOP') break; // triggers iterator.return() -> finally runs
}

This is why the try/finally in readLines closes the handle in the first case. A manual while loop that calls .next() directly and then simply breaks out of the loop never calls return() on the iterator — the generator is left suspended mid-execution, and its finally block, along with the cleanup inside it, never runs.

const it = readLines(f);
let result = it.next();
while (!result.done) {
  if (result.value === 'STOP') break; // handle.close() never runs
  result = it.next();
}

To get the same guarantee outside for...of, the consumer needs to call iterator.return() explicitly when stopping early, or use a helper that does so on its behalf.
hint: for...of calls the iterator's return() on early exit, which runs pending finally blocks — a manual .next() loop with break skips that call.

question: A page has a touchstart listener attached to the body that calls event.preventDefault() conditionally to block pull-to-refresh in one specific area. After adding it, scrolling and touch interactions across the whole page feel noticeably laggy, even in places that never call preventDefault(). A teammate says the listener itself is the problem, not what it does inside. What's happening and what's the fix?
answer:
By default, the browser cannot start scrolling in response to a touch or wheel gesture until every registered touchstart, touchmove, or wheel listener on the event path has finished running, because any one of them might call event.preventDefault() and cancel the scroll.

document.body.addEventListener('touchstart', (e) => {
  if (inRestrictedArea(e)) e.preventDefault();
});

This forces scrolling to wait on the main thread for the listener to finish running, which is why the lag shows up everywhere the listener is attached, not only in the specific area where preventDefault() actually runs.

el.addEventListener('touchstart', handler, { passive: true });

The fix is marking a listener as passive via the options object, as shown above. This tells the browser upfront that the listener will never call preventDefault(), so scrolling can begin immediately on the compositor thread without waiting for the handler to finish.

Since this specific case needs to call preventDefault() conditionally in one area, the passive flag can be applied to whichever listeners never cancel the gesture, while the one that does call preventDefault() stays non-passive but is attached to a narrower target than the entire body.
hint: Non-passive touch/wheel listeners block scrolling until they finish running — { passive: true } lets the browser scroll immediately.

question: A test suite has 40 tests. Each one passes when run individually with `--testPathPattern`, but running the whole suite together produces 3 random failures, and which 3 fail changes between runs. What class of bug does this point to and how should the tests be restructured?
answer:
Tests that pass in isolation but fail unpredictably when run together are almost always sharing mutable state — a module-level variable, a database row, a file on disk, or a cached singleton that one test modifies while a later test unknowingly depends on it being in its original state.

Because test execution order is not guaranteed to be identical across runs, and some runners parallelise tests, the particular combination of tests that collides changes from run to run, which produces the random, shifting pattern of failures.

The fix is isolating each test's setup and teardown:

  • State that a test creates or mutates is reset in a beforeEach, or recreated fresh for each test.
  • Anything left behind is torn down in an afterEach instead of being left for the next test to inherit.
  • For a shared resource like a database, each test typically runs inside its own transaction that gets rolled back afterward, or against data seeded fresh for that test rather than leftovers from another one.
hint: Random failures only when tests run together, not alone, points to shared mutable state — fix with proper per-test setup/teardown isolation.

question: A third-party analytics widget injects a `<div>` into the page after an unpredictable delay, and a developer needs to run code as soon as that div appears, without knowing exactly when. They currently poll with setInterval(checkForDiv, 100). A teammate suggests MutationObserver instead. Why is it a better fit and how would it be set up here?
answer:
Polling with setInterval(checkForDiv, 100) checks the DOM (Document Object Model) on a fixed schedule whether or not anything has actually changed, wasting work most of the time and adding up to 100ms of avoidable delay before the div is noticed.

MutationObserver subscribes directly to DOM mutations instead, so its callback only runs when a relevant change actually happens — no polling interval, and typically far lower latency:

const observer = new MutationObserver((mutations) => {
  const found = document.querySelector(".analytics-widget");
  if (found) {
    observer.disconnect();
    handleWidget(found);
  }
});

observer.observe(document.body, {
  childList: true,
  subtree: true
});

It is set up by creating the observer with a callback, then calling observe() on a stable ancestor, often document.body, together with the mutation types to watch.

  • childList watches for child nodes being added or removed.
  • subtree extends that watch to all descendants, not just direct children.

Calling observer.disconnect() as soon as the div is found stops the observer from continuing to run on every subsequent mutation.
hint: MutationObserver reacts to real DOM changes as they happen instead of polling on a fixed interval — observe() with childList + subtree covers descendants.

question: A team's counter utility exposes a `count` variable directly on the module object, and various parts of the codebase end up setting `count` directly instead of calling `increment()`, causing the tracked value to drift from reality. A senior developer suggests wrapping the internal state in a closure so only specific functions can touch it. What pattern is this and how does it fix the bug?
answer:
This is the Module pattern: a function, often an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression), creates a private scope through closures and returns only the methods meant to be public.

const counter = (function () {
  let count = 0; // private — lives only in this closure

  return {
    increment() { count += 1; },
    getCount() { return count; }
  };
})();

counter.increment();
counter.getCount(); // 1
counter.count;      // undefined — not reachable

Internally, count lives inside the closure and is never attached to the returned object, so it cannot be reached or reassigned from outside. Callers can only interact with it through the exposed functions, such as increment() and getCount(), which keep the internal state consistent instead of letting it drift.

Because plain object literals have no native private keyword, the Module pattern is the classic way to hide implementation details behind a small public interface.
hint: Module pattern: closures hide internal state — only the returned functions can touch it.

question: A notification service starts by sending emails. Requirements grow: some notifications should also log to a file, some should retry on failure, and the combinations vary per call site. A developer wants to avoid a combinatorial explosion of subclasses like `EmailWithLoggingAndRetryNotifier`. A colleague suggests wrapping the base notifier in small objects that each add one behaviour and share the same interface. What pattern is this and why does it avoid the subclass explosion?
answer:
This is the Decorator pattern. Each decorator — a logging wrapper, a retry wrapper — implements the same interface as the object it wraps, for example a send() method, and forwards the call to the wrapped object while adding its own behaviour before or after.

function withLogging(notifier) {
  return {
    send(msg) {
      console.log("sending:", msg);
      return notifier.send(msg);
    }
  };
}

function withRetry(notifier, attempts = 3) {
  return {
    send(msg) {
      // retries notifier.send(msg) up to the given number of attempts
    }
  };
}

const resilientNotifier = withRetry(withLogging(emailNotifier));

Because every decorator shares the notifier's interface, they can be composed in any combination and order without a new class being written for each combination. Subclassing would need a separate class for every combination of behaviours — EmailWithLoggingAndRetryNotifier and so on — growing combinatorially as more cross-cutting concerns are added.

Decorators instead compose linearly: one small wrapper per behaviour, mixed and matched as needed.
hint: Decorator pattern: wrap a shared-interface object to add one behaviour at a time, composable in any combination.

question: A codebase has near-identical retry loops copy-pasted around several API calls: each one retries up to 3 times with a delay before giving up. A teammate suggests extracting a single higher-order function that takes any async function and returns a retrying version of it. What makes this a higher-order function, and why is it a better fix than adjusting each copy-pasted loop individually?
answer:
A higher-order function is a function that takes another function as an argument, returns a function, or both. withRetry(fn, attempts) qualifies on both counts: it takes the async function fn and returns a new function that wraps it in retry logic.

function withRetry(fn, attempts = 3) {
  return async (...args) => {
    for (let i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) {
      try {
        return await fn(...args);
      } catch (err) {
        if (i === attempts) throw err;
      }
    }
  };
}

const safeFetch = withRetry(fetchUser, 3);

Any call site can be upgraded by wrapping it once, as with safeFetch above, instead of duplicating the same loop at every call site. Fixing a bug in the retry logic, or adding something like exponential backoff, means changing the one higher-order function — every wrapped call site picks up the fix automatically, since they all delegate to the same implementation rather than carrying their own copy of the loop.
hint: A higher-order function takes and/or returns a function — one retry implementation wraps any call instead of copy-pasted loops.

question: A code reviewer flags a line — `const getActiveNames = users => users.filter(u => u.active).map(u => u.name)` — and suggests rewriting it in a point-free style using existing curried `filter` and `map` helpers, without naming the `users` parameter at all. What does point-free mean here, and what is a real downside to be aware of before adopting it everywhere?
answer:
Point-free style, also called tacit programming, writes a function without naming its main argument.

// Not point-free — users is named and threaded through
const getActiveNames = users => users.filter(u => u.active).map(u => u.name);

// Point-free — composed from curried helpers, users is never mentioned
const getActiveNames = pipe(filter(isActive), map(getName));

The point-free version reads as a description of the transformation steps themselves, rather than as a manipulation of a named variable, which can make a simple pipeline easier to scan at a glance.

The downside is that heavily point-free code can become harder to debug and read once the pipeline grows longer or the helper functions are unfamiliar, since there is no intermediate variable to inspect in a debugger or to name meaningfully at each step.

Point-free style tends to be most useful for short, well-named transformations rather than as a rule applied everywhere.
hint: Point-free (tacit) style omits the named argument in favour of composed functions — readable for short pipelines, harder to debug for long ones.

question: Which of the following is the correct way to write a comment in HTML so the browser ignores it when rendering the page?
answer: HTML comments start with <!-- and end with -->. Everything between those markers is parsed but never rendered or executed, which makes it useful for leaving notes in markup without affecting the page.

options.option: <!-- This is a comment -->
// This is a comment
/* This is a comment */
# This is a comment

question: What's the real difference between an HTML "tag" and an HTML "element"?
answer:
A tag is just the bracketed notation, such as

or

. An element is the whole unit: the opening tag, everything nested inside it, and the closing tag together. People often use the words loosely as synonyms, but that's the technical distinction.

options.option:
A tag is the markup notation itself (like

or

); an element is the opening tag, its content, and its closing tag together
A tag only exists in the browser's memory; an element only exists in the source file
There is no difference — the two words are strictly interchangeable in the HTML spec
A tag can have attributes but an element cannot

question: Why is HTML called a "markup language" rather than a "programming language"?
answer: Markup languages annotate content to describe its structure and meaning — headings, paragraphs, links, and so on — rather than expressing computational logic such as loops, conditionals, or functions. That lack of program logic is exactly what separates HTML from a language like JavaScript.

options.option: It describes the structure and meaning of content instead of expressing logic like loops and conditionals
It cannot contain any attributes or values
It only runs on the server and never reaches the browser
It has no formal specification, unlike programming languages

question: An <img> tag's alt attribute value itself needs to contain a double quote character, like a photo caption reading a "great" view, and the attribute is wrapped in double quotes. What actually happens?
answer: The parser treats the first unescaped double quote it meets as closing the attribute value, so an embedded double quote ends the value early and turns the rest of the intended text into stray, invalid markup. The fix is to either use the " entity inside the value, or wrap the attribute in single quotes instead.

options.option: The markup breaks — the embedded quote ends the attribute value early, and the rest is parsed as separate, invalid markup
The browser automatically escapes the inner quote for you
Nothing breaks — HTML5 allows nested double quotes inside a double-quoted attribute
It only breaks in XHTML, not in regular HTML5

question: Which organization currently maintains HTML as a continuously updated "living standard" rather than issuing versioned releases like HTML4 or XHTML1?
answer: The WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) maintains the HTML Living Standard, which is updated continuously instead of being released as numbered versions. The W3C, which previously published the versioned HTML4/HTML5 specs, now aligns its own HTML spec with WHATWG's living standard.

options.option: WHATWG
ECMA International
IETF
ISO

question: A developer writes <DIV CLASS="Header"> in all caps instead of <div class="Header">. What actually happens when the browser parses it?
answer: HTML tag and attribute names are case-insensitive, so <DIV> and <div> are parsed identically. Lowercase is still the strongly preferred convention for readability and consistency, and it's actually required if the document is served as strict XHTML, but plain HTML5 itself doesn't enforce it.

options.option: It still works — HTML tag and attribute names are case-insensitive to the parser, though lowercase is the near-universal convention
It silently fails and the element is dropped from the page
It works only because the browser is running in quirks mode
It works for the tag name but breaks the attribute name

question: Which meta tag configures how a page scales and lays out on mobile device screens?
answer: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers how to size the page's layout viewport, typically matching it to the device's width and setting an initial zoom level. Without it, mobile browsers default to rendering the page as if on a wide desktop screen and then shrinking it down, which makes text unreadably small.

options.option: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<meta name="description" content="...">
<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="30">

question: A page needs every relative link and image path to resolve against a completely different folder than the page's own URL, without editing every individual link. Which single element inside <head> does that?
answer: <base href="...">, placed once in <head>, sets the base URL that every relative link, image, and script path on the page resolves against, instead of the page's own URL. It affects the whole document at once, which is exactly why it's useful when content is served from a different location than usual.

question: A document accidentally includes two <meta charset> declarations with different values. What does a browser actually do with them?
answer: A browser applies the first charset declaration it encounters while parsing and simply ignores any later ones, since encoding has to be locked in early to interpret the rest of the bytes correctly. This is also why <meta charset> should be the very first thing inside <head> — declaring it late, or having conflicting ones, risks the browser having already guessed wrong and needing to reparse.

question: Which attribute, added to a link pointing at a file, suggests a filename and triggers a save-to-disk instead of navigating to the file?

question: A link is written as <a href="#pricing">, but clicking it does nothing. What's the most likely reason?

answer: Once a <base href> is set, every relative URL on the page, including link href values, resolves against that base instead of the page's own URL. So contact.html resolves to https://cdn.example.com/assets/contact.html, not to a path relative to wherever the page itself is hosted.

question: Which tag renders text below the normal baseline, the way the 2 in a chemical formula like H2O is typically displayed?

question: Which element is intended to reference the title of a creative work, such as a book or movie, rather than to quote its text?

question: What is the purpose of the title attribute when used on an <abbr> element?
answer: The title attribute on <abbr> supplies the expanded, full-text version of an abbreviation or acronym, which browsers commonly show as a tooltip on hover and which assistive technology can announce.

question: You want to display a multi-line code snippet exactly as written, preserving line breaks and spacing, with monospace styling. Which combination of elements is the standard approach?

question: A document needs to show that a price was changed, with the old price struck through and the new price shown alongside it, in a way that's semantically meaningful rather than just styled. Which pair of elements fits this?
answer: <del> marks content that has been removed or is no longer accurate, typically shown with a strikethrough, while <ins> marks content that has been newly inserted, typically shown underlined, which together semantically represent an edit rather than just visual styling.

question: What is the correct way to nest a sub-list inside an existing list item?

question: What's the key difference between a disabled input and a readonly one?
answer: A disabled input is excluded entirely from form submission and can't receive focus, while a readonly input still gets submitted with whatever value it holds and can still be focused and selected, the user just can't edit it. That distinction matters whenever a field's value needs to reach the server even though the user shouldn't be able to change it.
