splice mutates the original array in place, removing however many elements we ask for starting at the given index, and hands back exactly those removed elements as its own new array. This is different from slice, which copies a range out without ever touching the original.

This logs false, false, then true.

Every array or object literal creates a brand new value in memory, so two separately written literals are never === equal, even with identical contents. === only returns true when both sides point to the exact same object, which is why comparing x to itself works.

This logs object, then true.

Arrays are a specialized kind of object under the hood, so typeof reports them the same as any other object — it can't tell an array apart from a plain object. Array.isArray exists specifically to answer that question correctly.

This logs -1, then true.

indexOf compares values with strict equality, and NaN === NaN is famously false, so it can never find a match and gives up. includes uses a slightly different comparison internally that treats NaN as equal to itself, so it correctly reports that the array contains one.

This logs [1, 10, 2, 21], not the numeric order we'd expect.

Without a comparator function, sort() converts every element to a string and compares them alphabetically, and "10" sorts before "2" as text. Sorting numbers correctly needs an explicit comparator, like nums.sort((a, b) => a - b).

This logs [1, 2, 3].

A Set only ever stores unique values — adding a duplicate is silently ignored. Spreading it back into an array is a common one-line way to deduplicate a list.

This logs 4, then [1, 2, 3, 4].

Adding 2 again does nothing, since it's already in the set. Adding 4 does grow it, bringing the total unique count to four values, in the order they were first inserted.

This logs value1, then 2.

A Map can use an actual object as a key, not just a string, and that object key is a completely separate identity from the string 'keyObj'. So this map really does hold two distinct entries, and looking it up by the object reference returns the value stored against that exact object.

This logs b 2, then a 1.

A Map always iterates in the exact order entries were inserted, regardless of what the keys look like. That's a real, guaranteed advantage over a plain object, whose key ordering has historically been less predictable, especially with numeric-looking keys.

This logs Alice 18.

Destructuring can happen directly in a function's parameter list, pulling name and age straight out of whatever object gets passed in. Since age isn't present on the argument, it falls back to its default value of 18.

This logs [0, 1, 4, 9, 16].

Array.from with an object that just has a length property is a common way to generate a sequence without a real array to start from. The mapping function runs once per index, here squaring each position to build the list.

Both lines log undefined.

Optional chaining works on function calls too, not just property access. If user.greet or user.sayHi is missing or null, ?.() simply short-circuits to undefined instead of throwing "is not a function", which is exactly what would happen with a plain () call here.

This logs 50, then 0.

0 is falsy, so || treats it the same as if volume were missing and falls back to 50. ?? only falls back when the value is actually null or undefined, so a deliberately set 0 passes straight through untouched.

This logs 0, then 1, then 10.

A default parameter expression is evaluated fresh on every call where the argument is omitted, not just once. The first two calls each run count++ and get the next value, while the third call passes an explicit argument, which always skips the default entirely.

This logs 1.

An arrow function assigned as a class field captures this from the surrounding context once, at the moment the instance is created, rather than depending on how it's later called. That's why detaching it into a plain variable and calling it standalone still correctly updates the original instance.

This logs ['fulfilled', 'rejected'].

Unlike Promise.all, allSettled never short-circuits on a rejection. It waits for every promise to finish one way or another and reports each individual outcome, which makes it useful when we genuinely want to know the result of every operation, successes and failures alike.

Promise.any resolves as soon as the first promise fulfills, ignoring any rejections along the way entirely. It only rejects itself if every single promise in the list rejects.

Throwing inside an async function doesn't behave like a normal synchronous throw that needs a try/catch right there. It's automatically converted into a rejected promise, which is exactly what .catch() on the returned promise is built to handle.

Even though the second promise actually finishes first, in 50ms versus 100ms, Promise.all always returns results in the same order as the input array, not completion order. It just waits until every promise has settled before resolving with that ordered list.

An async function always returns a real promise, even when the value it returns is a plain number with no promise in sight. Calling it never gives back the raw value directly — we'd still need to await it or chain .then() to actually get 42 out.

await doesn't require its operand to actually be a promise. Awaiting a plain value just resolves to that same value immediately, on the next microtask tick, which is why non-promise values can be freely awaited without causing an error.

A regex with the g flag is stateful — it remembers where it left off in lastIndex between calls on the same regex object. The first test() finds "123" and moves lastIndex to 6, right after the match. The second call starts searching from index 6, finds nothing left, and returns false, even though the string clearly contains digits.

This is a classic gotcha: reusing the same global regex across calls, or in a loop, can silently skip matches unless lastIndex is reset first.

question:
console.log('2024-01-15'.match(/(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})/));

What does this log?
answer:
This logs an array: ['2024-01-15', '2024', '01', '15', index: 0, input: '2024-01-15', groups: undefined].

Without the g flag, match() returns rich detail about a single match: index 0 is the full matched string, and each following index is one parenthesized capture group in order. It also attaches index (where the match starts) and input (the original string) as extra properties.

groups is undefined here because none of the capture groups were named — that property only gets populated by (?<name>...) named groups.

This logs ['c', 'b', 'r'].

matchAll() returns an iterator, not an array, so it has to be spread (or looped) to actually collect the results. Each item it yields is a full match object, just like a single match() result — so m[0] is the whole match (e.g. 'cat') and m[1] is the first capture group (e.g. 'c'), which is exactly what's being pulled out here.

matchAll requires the g flag; calling it without one throws a TypeError.

question:
console.log('John Smith'.replace(/(\w+) (\w+)/, '$2 $1'));

What does this log?
answer:
This logs 'Smith John'.

Inside the replacement string, $1 and $2 refer back to whatever the first and second parenthesized groups captured — here, 'John' and 'Smith' respectively. Writing them in reverse order in the replacement string swaps the two words in the output.

This pattern — capture groups plus $1/$2 references — is a common way to reformat text without manually splitting and rejoining it.

This logs 2024 01.

(?<year>...) and (?<month>...) are named capture groups — they capture the same way regular parentheses do, but the matched text also gets attached by name on the result's .groups object.

This reads more clearly than indexing into result[1] and result[2], especially once a pattern has several groups and it's easy to lose track of which number is which.

question:
console.log('price: 10, 20, 30'.replace(/\d+/g, n => Number(n) * 2));

What does this log?
answer:
This logs 'price: 20, 40, 60'.

replace() accepts a function instead of a plain replacement string, and calls it once per match, using whatever it returns as that match's replacement. Combined with the g flag, every number in the string gets passed through the callback, doubled, and swapped back in.

This is the go-to pattern whenever a replacement needs to be computed from the matched text rather than being a fixed string.

This logs ['a', 'b', 'c', ''], then ['a', '1', 'b', '2', 'c', '3', ''].

split() normally throws away whatever it split on, keeping just the pieces in between — that's the first line. But if the regex has a capturing group, split() also includes what that group matched, right in the returned array, interleaved with the regular pieces.

The trailing empty string in both cases is because the string ends right after a digit, leaving nothing after the last split point.

^ and $ anchor a pattern to the very start and end of the string, so /^\d+$/ only matches when the entire string is digits — "123abc" fails because of the trailing letters. Drop the anchors, as in the third line, and the regex is happy to match digits anywhere inside the string, so it succeeds even though the string as a whole isn't purely numeric.

Forgetting anchors is a common source of validation bugs that let obviously-invalid input slip through.

structuredClone performs a deep copy: nested values like the tags array get their own independent copy rather than a shared reference, so mutating copy.tags leaves original.tags at its original length. The clone and the original are also two separate top-level objects, hence copy === original is false.

Unlike JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)), structuredClone also preserves real types through the copy — the cloned joined field is still a genuine Date instance, not a string.

structuredClone implements the structured clone algorithm, which can copy plain data — objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer — but has no way to serialize a function, since a function closes over live, unclonable execution state. Any object containing a function (or a DOM node, or most class instances with non-plain internals) throws a DataCloneError when passed to it.

This is why structuredClone is suited to copying data payloads, not arbitrary objects with attached behavior.

A BroadcastChannel delivers a posted message to every other channel object subscribed to the same channel name — it never delivers the message back to the instance that sent it. a and b share the name 'sync', so b receives what a posted, but a itself is excluded, the same way a broadcaster doesn't hear its own transmission echoed back.

In a real app a and b would typically live in separate browser tabs (each holding one channel connected to the same name) — the self-exclusion rule is exactly what makes it safe to have every tab both send and listen on the same channel without an infinite ping-pong.

AbortSignal.timeout(ms) returns a signal that starts out not aborted and needs no manual AbortController or setTimeout wiring — it aborts itself automatically once the given number of milliseconds passes. When that happens, the abort event fires, signal.aborted flips to true, and signal.reason is set to a DOMException named TimeoutError.

It's typically passed straight into fetch(url, { signal }) to auto-cancel a request that's taking too long, without hand-rolling a timer-plus-controller pair.

question: A component schedules a visual update with requestAnimationFrame(paintUpdate) and schedules a background analytics call with requestIdleCallback(logAnalytics). Which callback is timed to run right before the next screen repaint, and why would swapping the two be a mistake?
answer:
requestAnimationFrame(paintUpdate) is the one timed to run right before the browser's next repaint, once per frame — that's exactly the slot a visual change like a transform update needs, so it lands in sync with what the screen actually draws.

requestIdleCallback(logAnalytics) runs only when the browser has spare idle time between frames, with no repaint-timing guarantee at all; under a busy main thread it can be delayed well past the next several frames.

Swapping them would be a mistake: deferring the transform to idle time would make the animation stutter and lag behind user input, while running low-priority analytics logging on requestAnimationFrame would burn frame budget on work nobody is watching.

question: A page calls navigator.sendBeacon('/api/analytics', ...) inside a pagehide listener to report that the user is leaving, instead of using a normal fetch() call to send the same analytics payload. Why is sendBeacon used here instead of fetch()?
answer:
sendBeacon hands the request off to the browser itself, which queues and delivers it reliably in the background — even as the page is actively being torn down. A fetch() or XHR call started during pagehide is frequently cut short before the request completes, because navigation can dismantle the page's execution context before the response (or even the request) finishes.

It's also fire-and-forget by design: it returns synchronously with a true/false queued-or-not result and gives no way to read a response body, which fits an exit-time ping that nothing needs to react to.

That combination — delivery survives unload, no response handling needed — is why sendBeacon is the standard tool for last-moment analytics and logging calls.

The console shows only after pushState. The popstate listener never fires from this code.

history.pushState() only updates the URL and adds a new entry to session history — it does not dispatch a popstate event itself. popstate fires exclusively when the active history entry changes because of navigation: the user clicking Back/Forward, or a script calling history.back(), forward(), or go().

This is why an SPA router that calls pushState on every route change has to run its own render logic right after the pushState call, and separately listen for popstate to handle the user navigating with the browser's Back/Forward buttons.

The first line logs red. The second logs ['red', 'blue'].

form.get('color') returns only the first value ever appended under that key, silently discarding the rest. form.getAll('color') returns every value appended under that key, in order, as an array.

This matters because a FormData object — just like an HTML form — allows the same field name to be appended more than once, as happens with checkbox groups or multi-selects. Reaching for get() on a repeatable field quietly drops everything but the first entry; getAll() is the one that surfaces all of them.

Only run: c logs, once, after the 50ms delay. 'a' and 'b' never log at all.

Every call to the debounced function runs clearTimeout(timer) first, cancelling whatever timer the previous call scheduled, before starting a brand-new one. Since log('a'), log('b'), and log('c') all run synchronously with no gap between them, each call cancels the last one's pending timer — only the final call's timer ever survives long enough to fire.

This trailing-edge debounce is the shape used for something like a search box that should only fire a request once the user pauses typing, not on every keystroke.

fired: 1 logs immediately, then fired: 4 logs about 150ms later. log(2) and log(3) never produce output.

The first call runs fn right away (leading-edge) and sets blocked to true for 100ms; log(2) and log(3) arrive while still blocked, so they're dropped entirely. By the time log(4) runs at 150ms, the window has reopened and blocked is back to false, so it fires.

Unlike debounce, throttle guarantees at most one call per fixed window rather than waiting for calls to stop — the pattern fits things like a scroll handler, where you want a steady capped rate of updates rather than one deferred final update.

callCount ends up at 2, not 3.

The memoized wrapper keeps a Map keyed by argument. The first fastSquare(5) misses the cache, runs slowSquare, and stores the result under key 5. The second fastSquare(5) finds 5 already cached and returns that stored value directly — slowSquare is never called again for it. fastSquare(6) is a new argument, so it's a genuine second call to slowSquare.

Memoization only pays off when the same input recurs; each distinct argument still costs one real underlying call the first time it's seen.

The last assignment throws a TypeError, which gets caught and logged as caught: age must be a number.

The Proxy's set trap intercepts every property assignment on the object before it actually happens. Here it specifically checks writes to age and rejects any non-number value by throwing; every other property, like name, passes straight through and is written normally via target[prop] = value.

This is the standard way to bolt validation or side-effects onto plain object writes without changing how calling code interacts with the object — it still looks and behaves like an ordinary property assignment from the outside.

They print Cat makes a sound, then true, then false.

Putting speak on Animal.prototype — instead of assigning this.speak = ... inside the constructor — means every instance shares the exact same function reference. That's why cat.speak === dog.speak is true, and why cat.hasOwnProperty('speak') is false: speak isn't cat's own property, it's inherited through the prototype chain from Animal.prototype.

This is exactly what the class keyword does under the hood too — class Animal { speak() {...} } also places speak on Animal.prototype, not on each instance. The pre-ES6 constructor-function pattern and a modern class are two syntaxes producing the same shared-method-on-prototype structure.

a === b logs true — both calls to getInstance() return the same cached instance from the private static #instance field. a === c logs false.

That second result exposes a real gap: the constructor itself was never guarded, so new Logger() still works from outside the class and happily builds a second, fully independent instance that getInstance() knows nothing about.

A properly enforced Singleton needs to block direct construction too — for example by throwing from the constructor when #instance is already set, or by hiding construction behind a closure or module entirely. Exposing a getInstance() method alone doesn't stop anyone from calling new directly.

heard: first logs exactly once. The second emit produces no output at all.

on(fn) pushes the listener into the closured listeners array and returns a fresh closure that remembers that specific fn and knows how to find and splice it out. Calling unsubscribe() runs that closure, removing the listener from listeners before bus.emit('second') ever runs — so by the time the second emit iterates the array, it's empty.

This is why having on() return its own unsubscribe closure is the cleaner ergonomic choice over requiring callers to hold onto the original function and pass it back into a separate off() method.

initializing app logs exactly once, from the very first call. config.name ends up being app, not ignored.

once is a decorator: it wraps fn in a closure holding a called flag and a cached result. Every call after the first sees called is already true and just returns the previously cached result without ever touching fn again — so the third call, init('ignored'), doesn't re-run the wrapped function at all; it hands back the object built during the very first call.

This is the pattern behind one-time setup/initialization guards. It differs from memoization in that it ignores its arguments entirely and caches a single result forever, rather than caching one result per unique input.

This logs string 51. localStorage can only store strings, so setItem silently coerces the number 5 to the string '5' before saving it.

getItem then hands that string back, so typeof count is 'string', not 'number'. The + operator sees a string on the left, so count + 1 triggers string concatenation instead of addition, producing '51' rather than 6.

To get a real number back out, it has to be converted explicitly, e.g. Number(localStorage.getItem('count')).

localStorage.length logs 2, and Object.keys(localStorage) logs ['a', 'b'] in insertion order. Modern browsers expose each stored key as an enumerable own property on the localStorage object, which is why Object.keys and even for...in happen to pick them up.

The documented way to iterate, though, is key(i) combined with length: for (let i = 0; i < localStorage.length; i++) { console.log(localStorage.key(i)); }. It's the API the spec actually defines for iteration, rather than relying on the object incidentally behaving like a plain object with enumerable keys.

This is by design: the event exists to let other tabs react to a change they didn't cause, not to notify the tab that already knows what it just did. If a second tab on the same origin had this exact listener attached, it would log 'storage event fired' the moment the first tab's setItem call ran.

It logs theme light dark. The StorageEvent passed to the listener carries the key that changed along with its oldValue before the write and its newValue after it, all as strings.

This is what makes the storage event useful for syncing state across tabs: a listener can inspect exactly which key changed and diff the before/after values without re-reading the whole of localStorage.

The event also carries storageArea (the affected Storage object) and url (the document that made the change), though key/oldValue/newValue are the ones used most often.

The cookie is sent automatically — every request to the same domain includes the full Cookie header, so sessionId=abc123; theme=dark travels with every page load, image request, and API call. localStorage data is never transmitted on its own; it only leaves the browser if code explicitly reads it and includes it in a request.

This is why cookies should stay small: a bloated cookie adds overhead to every single request, even ones that never need that data. localStorage is the better fit for bulkier, client-only data like recentSearches that the server doesn't need on every round trip.

The cookie is gone — max-age=60 tells the browser to expire and delete it 60 seconds after it was set, and this happens automatically, with no page reload required. The localStorage value is untouched; localStorage has no built-in expiration mechanism at all.

Anything written with setItem stays until code explicitly calls removeItem/clear, the user clears site data, or the browser evicts it under storage pressure. If an app needs a value to expire, it has to store its own timestamp alongside the data and check it manually on read.

cartCount goes back to 0 — it's just a JavaScript variable, and the whole script re-runs from scratch on refresh, wiping out any in-memory state. sessionStorage.getItem('cartCount') still returns '3' after the refresh.

sessionStorage survives page reloads and same-tab navigations; it's only cleared when that specific tab or window is closed. That's the real meaning of "session" here — it's the tab's lifetime, not a single page load.

The order is outer capture, inner bubble, outer bubble. The click first travels down from the document through outer in the capturing phase — since that listener was registered with true, it fires here, before the event ever reaches inner.

The event then reaches its target, inner, and its listener runs. From there it bubbles back up through the ancestor chain, so outer's bubble-phase listener (registered without the capture flag) fires last.

Passing true (or { capture: true }) as the third argument to addEventListener is what puts a listener in the capturing phase instead of the default bubbling phase.

No — only 'first' is logged. stopImmediatePropagation() stops not just propagation to ancestor elements, but also any remaining listeners registered on this exact same element, so the second click handler on btn never runs.

If stopPropagation() were used instead, 'second' would still log — stopPropagation() only prevents the event from continuing on to ancestor (or descendant, in the capture phase) elements; it has no effect on other listeners already registered on the same element.

It logs false, and preventDefault() does nothing. The load event is not cancelable — there is no default action to cancel — so calling preventDefault() on it is silently ignored.

Whether preventDefault() has any effect is governed by the event's own cancelable property. Events like a form's submit or a link's click are cancelable, so calling it actually blocks their default behavior; lifecycle events like load are not, so calling it there is always a no-op, no matter where in the handler it's called.

This logs 3. CustomEvent lets code create its own named event and attach arbitrary data to it via the detail option in its constructor.

dispatchEvent(evt) fires that event on document just like a native event, and any listener for 'cart:updated' receives the same event object, reading the payload back off event.detail. This is the standard way unrelated parts of an app can communicate through the DOM instead of calling each other's functions directly.

No, it's still attached — clicking btn still logs 'clicked'. Each arrow function expression creates a brand-new function object, so the function passed to removeEventListener is a completely different reference from the one passed to addEventListener, even though the code inside them is identical.

removeEventListener only removes a listener when given the exact same function reference that was originally registered. To make a listener removable, it has to be stored and reused, e.g. const onClick = () => console.log('clicked'); btn.addEventListener('click', onClick); btn.removeEventListener('click', onClick);.

No — scrolling still happens normally. Setting passive: true is a promise to the browser that the listener will never call preventDefault(), which lets the browser start scrolling immediately without waiting for the handler to finish running.

Because of that promise, the engine ignores preventDefault() even if it's called anyway — it has no effect, and most browsers log a console warning about it. A listener that genuinely needs to block default touch behavior must be registered without passive: true (or with passive: false explicitly), accepting the scroll-jank cost that comes with it.

This logs LI UL. event.target is the actual element the user interacted with — the <li> that was clicked — and it stays the same as the event travels through the DOM.

event.currentTarget is whichever element the listener is currently attached to and executing on — here, the <ul>. In a handler attached directly to the clicked element the two are identical; they diverge exactly in cases like this one, where the listener sits on a parent and the click originates from a descendant — which is also the basis for event delegation.

When increment() mutates count inside counter.js, every module that imported it sees the updated value immediately, without re-importing anything. This differs from CommonJS, where require() returns a snapshot of module.exports at call time, so a later internal reassignment inside the required module wouldn't be visible to the caller.

This logs string then true. import.meta.url is a property available inside any ES module that holds the module's own URL — in Node it's a file:// URL pointing at the module's file on disk; in a browser it's the URL the script was loaded from.

It's commonly used to build paths relative to the current module, e.g. new URL('./data.json', import.meta.url), which works no matter where the module is imported from — unlike __dirname, which isn't available in ES modules at all.

The order is start import, before, after, got ready: true. ES modules can use await at the top level, outside any function — when config.js hits its await, evaluation of that module pauses right there.

Because main.js imports it with a dynamic import(), which itself returns a promise, main.js waits too: the await import(...) line doesn't resolve until config.js finishes running top to bottom, including its own await. Top-level await effectively lets anything importing a module wait for that module's async setup to finish before continuing.

Yes, this works and logs Hello, Sam 1.0. A single module can freely mix one export default with any number of named exports — they're independent export mechanisms.

On the import side, the default export is captured with a plain identifier (greet, no braces) and the named exports go in { } alongside it, in either order: import greet, { version } from './greet.js'. This pattern suits a module with one obvious "main" export plus a few smaller related values.

Yes — this works fine and logs button-element. A default export isn't tied to any particular name; export default exports a single unnamed value, so whoever imports it is free to bind it to any local identifier they like.

This is the opposite situation from a named import, which must match the exported name exactly — import { Button } from './Button.js' would fail here, since there is no named export called Button, only a default one. Naming freedom is one of the main practical differences between default and named exports.

'store.cjs running' logs only once, then [ 'apple' ] and true. Node caches modules by resolved file path — the first require('./store.cjs') runs the file and caches its module.exports; the second call returns that same cached object instead of re-executing the file.

Since storeA and storeB are literally the same object reference, mutating storeA.items is visible through storeB too, and storeA === storeB is true. ES modules share this same caching guarantee — a module's top-level code runs exactly once no matter how many places import it — but this demonstrates it with CommonJS's synchronous require.

Groups nest, so city: Pune sits two levels deep between the two open groups, and active: true drops back to one level once groupEnd() closes the "Address" group.

login: 1

login: 1

console.count(label) keeps a counter per unique label — independent of the arguments passed to login — and logs label: N, incrementing by one on every call. console.countReset('login') resets that label's counter back to 0, so the following login('c') call starts counting again from 1.

console.assert(condition, message) only logs when the condition is falsy, prefixing the message with Assertion failed:. The second call's condition (15 >= 10) is true, so nothing is logged for it at all.

Unlike Node's assert module, console.assert() never throws — it's purely a conditional log, so execution always falls through to the next line whether the assertion passed or failed.

{ tag: 'div', attrs: { id: 'app', data: { level: [Object] } } }

{
  tag: 'div',
  attrs: {
    id: 'app',
    data: { level: { deep: { value: 42 } } }
  }
}

This is exactly why console.dir() with an explicit depth option is the better tool for inspecting deeply nested structures like a DOM node or a large config object, where console.log()'s default would hide most of the detail.

user Alice scored 91.7 points extra

%s substitutes a string and %o substitutes a generic object inspection. %d converts its argument with Number() rather than truncating — despite the letter suggesting "integer", 91.7 prints as-is, not rounded or floored.

Any argument left over once all format specifiers are filled — here, 'extra' — is simply appended to the end of the line, space-separated, exactly like an ordinary multi-argument console.log() call.

items: 3 [ 1, 2, 3 ]

The + version forces string concatenation instead: count becomes '3', and the array is coerced through its default toString() into '1,2,3' — a comma-joined string with no brackets or spaces — so the whole line collapses into one string with no separators between the original pieces.

console.log() writes to stdout, while console.warn() and console.error() both write to stderr. Redirecting 2> /dev/null only silences stderr, so the warning and error lines never reach the terminal.

This is why piping or grepping a script's stdout won't capture its warnings and errors unless you explicitly merge the streams (2>&1) — they're separate output channels by design, not just a color or styling difference in DevTools.

assert.deepStrictEqual() compares structure: same keys, same values, recursively — so two different objects with identical contents pass. assert.strictEqual() uses ===, which compares object references — a and b are two distinct objects in memory, so it throws an AssertionError even though their contents are identical.

This is the core distinction to remember: reach for deepStrictEqual when comparing data like objects or arrays, and keep strictEqual for primitives or for the rare case where you specifically need two variables to point at the exact same object.

test 1 passed is printed, then the script crashes before test 2 passed ever logs.

The second call also throws a RangeError — the function itself behaves correctly — but the validation object expects name: 'TypeError'. Since the thrown error's name doesn't match, assert.throws() itself throws an AssertionError.

The useful distinction: assert.throws() doesn't just check that something was thrown — when given a validation object as the second argument, it also checks the thrown error matches those specific properties.

Indexing further — calls[1][0] — reaches into the second call's first argument, the string 'final'. No test framework is required to get this behavior; it's ordinary closures and array pushes.

It prints Hello, Test User. realDb is never called at all — greet() only calls whatever db object it's handed, and this call passes stubDb instead.

This is stubbing: stubDb.getUser is a fake implementation that always returns a fixed, predictable object rather than doing whatever the real dependency does (here, throwing, since there's no real database available in a test run). Because greet depends on an injected db parameter instead of importing a fixed dependency, swapping in the stub needs no mocking framework — just a different object.

The test can now exercise greet's own logic — the template string — without needing a real, slow, or unreliable database connection.

test one calls: 1
test two calls: 2

testTwo reports 2 calls, not 1, because track is a single spy shared across both "tests" and its calls array is never cleared between them — the count from testOne leaks straight into testTwo.

This is exactly why real test runners reset mocks between tests, such as Jest's beforeEach(() => jest.clearAllMocks()) — or here, simply reassigning track.calls = [] before each test. Without that reset, tests aren't actually isolated: a call-count assertion in one test silently depends on execution order and on whatever prior tests already ran.

scoreTest: marked done prints first. The failing assertion inside the async test function only runs about 10ms later, after runTest has already logged that the test is done — it then crashes the process as an unhandled rejection instead of failing the test cleanly.

runTest calls testFn() without awaiting it. An async function returns a promise immediately, before its internal await fetchScore() line has resolved, so the synchronous call to testFn() returns right away and runTest moves straight on to the "marked done" log.

This mirrors a real, well-known test-writing bug: if a test runner doesn't wait for the promise an async test returns, it can consider that test finished — and even record it as passing — before the assertions inside it have actually run.

It prints true then false.

calledWith reimplements what Jest's toHaveBeenCalledWith() matcher does under the hood: it scans every recorded call in spy.calls and checks whether any of them structurally matches the expected arguments, using assert.deepStrictEqual inside a try/catch to turn a thrown mismatch into a plain boolean.

The first check finds an exact match against the recorded first call, so it's true. The second check looks for a call with status: 'cancelled', which was never made — the actual second call had status: 'pending' — so no recorded call matches and it returns false.

It prints failed — passed never logs.

Even though [1, 2, 3] and [1, '2', 3] look almost identical, assert.deepStrictEqual() checks types as well as values at every position. The second element is the number 2 in one array and the string '2' in the other, and since 2 !== '2' under strict equality, the whole comparison fails.

That's the "strict" in deepStrictEqual: it never coerces types the way == or the older, non-strict assert.deepEqual() would (which treats 2 and '2' as equal). For data coming from places like JSON parsing or form inputs — where numbers can accidentally end up as strings — that strictness is exactly what catches real bugs instead of masking them.

It prints [ '1', '2', 'b', 'a' ] — not the insertion order b, 2, a, 1 you might expect from watching the assignments happen.

Ordinary objects follow a specific enumeration rule (spec'd since ES2015): keys that look like array indices — non-negative integers in their canonical string form — are always listed first, sorted in ascending numeric order, no matter when they were added. Every other key, like 'b' and 'a', comes after, in the order it was actually inserted.

This is why numeric-looking keys seem to "jump to the front" in Object.keys(), for...in, and JSON.stringify() output, while string keys keep behaving like a normal insertion-ordered list.

It prints [ '1', '2', '01', 'a' ]. '01' does not jump to the front with '1' and 2 — it stays with the string keys, in the order it was inserted.

The integer-index fast path only applies to keys whose string form is the exact canonical decimal representation of a non-negative integer, meaning no leading zeros. String(1) is '1', not '01', so '01' fails that round-trip check and is treated as an ordinary string key rather than an array-like index.

This is a real trap with zero-padded ids or codes used as object keys — they look numeric but sort and enumerate like plain text.

It prints [ '1', '2', '-1', '1.5' ]. Only 1 and 2 get the numeric-first treatment; -1 and 1.5 are pushed to the end, in insertion order.

The spec's integer-index rule only covers non-negative integers written in canonical form — that excludes negative numbers and anything with a fractional part. -1 and 1.5 both get stringified to a key that doesn't qualify, so they fall back to being ordinary string keys and keep their insertion position.

The practical takeaway: "looks like a number" isn't the rule engines use for key reordering — only "is a non-negative integer index" is.

It logs:

forEach: [ 1, 3 ]
map: [ 10, <1 empty item>, 30 ]
for-of: [ 1, undefined, 3 ]
JSON: [1,null,3]

forEach and map both skip holes entirely — the callback is never invoked for index 1, so seen only has two entries and mapped keeps the hole in place instead of computing undefined * 10. for...of behaves completely differently: it iterates every index up to length via the array's iterator protocol, so the hole reads back as an actual undefined value. JSON.stringify takes a third approach and converts holes to null.

There's no single rule for "what a hole does" — each API defines its own hole-handling, which is exactly why relying on sparse arrays is risky.

Both typeof checks print 'function' — classes really are functions under the hood, engine-wise. But calling Widget() without new throws, logging caught: TypeError, while OldStyle() runs with no error at all, then logs OldStyle() called fine.

Every class declaration carries an internal flag marking it as "only constructible," which is exactly what a plain function declaration lacks. The spec has the engine check that flag on every call and throw a TypeError ("Class constructor Widget cannot be invoked without 'new'") if the class was called instead of constructed.

So typeof can't tell you whether something is class syntax or a plain function — both report the same type — but their calling conventions are enforced very differently at the engine level.

No. Object.keys(obj) logs [ '1', '2', '3' ] — reordered numerically — while [...map.keys()] logs [ 2, 1, 3 ], preserving the exact order the entries were set.

Plain objects apply the integer-index enumeration rule described in the spec: numeric-looking keys always sort ascending ahead of everything else, regardless of insertion order. Map has no such special case — by design it's a pure insertion-ordered structure for every key type, numbers included, which is one of the concrete reasons Map exists as a separate structure rather than everyone just using objects as key-value stores.

Note also that Map keeps 2 as a real number, not the string '2' objects would coerce it to — another difference in how the two structures actually store keys.

It logs get: ok, then size: undefined, then caught: TypeError.

WeakMap deliberately has no .size property at all — there's no way to ask how many entries it holds, which is intentional: exposing a count would let code detect that an entry disappeared, indirectly revealing garbage-collection timing that the spec refuses to make observable. The thrown error comes from a separate rule: a WeakMap key must be an object (or, as of newer JS, certain Symbols) — passing a string like 'stringKey' is rejected outright with TypeError: Invalid value used as weak map key.

Both restrictions exist for the same reason: WeakMap only makes sense as a GC-friendly structure when its keys are objects the engine can track weakly, and when nothing about the structure lets you observe collection happening.

It logs map size: 2, lookup with new object: undefined, via userA: stored for A, and via userB: undefined.

Map and WeakMap both key by object identity, never by shape or value equality. The two { id: 1 } literals passed to map.set are two distinct objects that happen to look alike, so they become two separate entries — and a third, freshly-created { id: 1 } passed into get matches neither of them. Same story with userA and userB: they're separate object references with identical contents, so storing data under userA tells you nothing about userB.

This is exactly why WeakMap works well for "private data per instance" — each live object reference is its own unique key, with no risk of accidental collisions between look-alike objects.

It logs has: true, forEach: undefined, size: undefined, then caught: TypeError - ws is not iterable.

WeakSet only exposes add, has, and delete — there is no forEach, no size, and critically it does not implement the iterable protocol at all, so spreading it with [...ws] fails the same way spreading any non-iterable value would.

This isn't a missing feature, it's the whole point: if you could enumerate a WeakSet's contents, you could observe exactly which of its members are still alive versus collected, which would make garbage collection observable and pin the engine to specific timing guarantees it doesn't make. You can only ever check membership for an object reference you already hold.

It prints A: 2 and B: 1.

Each call to createCounter() creates its own private count variable, and the two methods returned alongside it — increment and read — form a closure over that exact variable. Even though createCounter has long since returned and its execution context is gone, count is still reachable and mutable through those closures, which is why calling increment can keep changing a value that a completely separate call's closure never sees.

This is the mechanism behind both a useful pattern (private state without a class) and a real leak risk: as long as any function retains a reference to a closure, every variable that closure can reach stays alive in memory, even variables the outer function itself no longer has any way to touch.

Yes. It logs session variable: null, then cache size: 1, then still cached -> { userId: 42 } : session-data — the entry is fully intact and iterable even though the only other variable pointing at that object was just cleared.

A Map keeps its own independent, strong reference to every key it's given; setting session to null only removes that one variable's reference, and the Map's internal reference is completely unaffected. This is precisely why a growing Map used as a cache is a classic memory-leak shape: the objects you store as keys stay reachable — and therefore ineligible for garbage collection — for as long as the Map itself exists, no matter what happens to the variables you originally used to build it.

WeakMap exists specifically to avoid this: it doesn't hold that extra strong reference, and not coincidentally, it also gives you no way to iterate or count its entries.

It logs [ 10, 20 ] and length: 2. Assigning to .length doesn't just change a number the array reports — when the new value is smaller than the current length, every element from that index onward is actually deleted.

length on an array isn't a stored count, it's a live property with its own setter defined by the spec: setting it to a smaller value truncates the array in place, and setting it to a larger value pads it with holes (not zeros or undefined values — genuine empty slots).

This makes arr.length = n a fast, allocation-free way to shrink an array in place, which is exactly why it shows up in performance-sensitive code that wants to reuse an existing array rather than build a new one.

No. Raw, they print differently already — sparse is [ <3 empty items> ] while dense is [ undefined, undefined, undefined ]. The gap matters once you call .map(): sparse.map(...) still logs [ <3 empty items> ] — the callback never runs, because map skips holes — while dense.map(...) logs [ 0, 2, 4 ], because every index genuinely holds a value the callback gets called on.

new Array(3) only sets the length property; it never actually assigns any of the three indices, so they're holes. Array.from({ length: 3 }) reads that length and then explicitly writes undefined into each index one at a time, producing a fully dense array.

If the goal is a real array you intend to .map() or .fill() over, Array.from({ length: n }) (or new Array(n).fill(undefined)) is the safe choice — new Array(n) alone silently produces something most array methods will skip right over.

Neither does. It logs { maxRetries: 3 } — the original value, no new timeout property — and isFrozen: true.

Object.freeze() marks every existing property non-writable and non-configurable, and blocks adding new properties entirely. In an ordinary (non-strict) script, both kinds of rejected write just fail silently: no error, no effect, execution continues as if nothing happened. That silence is exactly what makes accidental frozen-object mutation easy to miss during debugging.

The same code inside a module, a class body, or anything else that runs in strict mode behaves differently: the identical assignments would throw a TypeError instead of failing quietly. Whether a rejected write throws or just does nothing depends entirely on strict mode, not on freeze itself.

No. It logs { name: 'app', limits: { maxRetries: 99 } } — the nested maxRetries really did change to 99 — and nested isFrozen: false.

Object.freeze() is shallow: it locks down the property slots directly on the object you called it on, but it has no effect on whatever those properties point to. settings.limits is just a reference to a separate, completely unfrozen object, so reassigning its properties works exactly as normal — only the top-level assignment settings.name = 'changed' was actually blocked.

Freezing nested data for real means walking the object graph and freezing each nested object individually (a "deep freeze"), not just calling freeze once on the outer object and assuming everything under it is protected too.

No, very different results. The first logs alias after length=0: [] — alias got emptied too. The second logs originalB after reassign: [ 1, 2, 3 ] — originalB is completely untouched.

original.length = 0 mutates the actual array object in place, and since alias points to that same object, it sees the change immediately — there was only ever one array. aliasB = [] does something entirely different: it makes the variable aliasB point at a brand-new, separate array, leaving the original array — still referenced by originalB — completely unchanged.

This distinction matters anywhere an array is shared by reference (a module-level cache, a value closed over by a callback): truncating with .length = 0 is a mutation every holder of that reference observes, while reassigning a variable to [] only ever affects that one variable's binding.

It logs "number", "string", then "boolean" — one line per reassignment.

JavaScript is dynamically typed: a variable itself has no fixed type, only the value currently sitting in it does. value is just a label pointed at a number, then a string, then a boolean, and typeof reports whatever it happens to be pointing at right now.

This differs from statically typed languages, where a variable's type is locked in at declaration. In JS, the same variable can legally hold any type across its lifetime — there is no compiler stopping you.

Both lines print 100. Assigning to a bare identifier that was never declared doesn't throw — in non-strict ("sloppy") mode it silently creates a new property on the global object instead of a local variable.

That is why y is readable outside test() at all: it was never local to begin with. The second log, globalThis.y, proves it landed directly on the global object (window in a browser, globalThis everywhere).

This is one of the classic reasons "use strict" exists — in strict mode this same code throws a ReferenceError instead of leaking a global.

The first three lines print undefined, "undefined", and "undefined". The fourth line doesn't log anything — it throws an uncaught ReferenceError: z is not defined and stops the script.

a is declared but unassigned, so it holds the value undefined — a real, readable value meaning "no value yet". z was never declared at all, which is a different problem: typeof is specifically forgiving about undeclared identifiers and reports "undefined" instead of throwing, but actually reading z's value (not just asking its type) throws.

So "undeclared", "undefined", and "null" are three distinct ideas: undeclared means the name doesn't exist at all, undefined is the default value of a variable that exists but wasn't assigned, and null is a value a developer assigns on purpose to mean "intentionally empty".

It prints undefined — not the object.

JavaScript's Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI) inserts a semicolon right after return because a line break immediately follows it, turning the code into return; { value: 42 };. The function returns immediately with no value, and the object literal on the next lines becomes a dangling, unreachable block.

The fix is to keep the opening brace on the same line as return: return { value: 42 };. This is one of the few places ASI actively breaks code instead of quietly helping it.

It logs "truthy", "truthy", "falsy", "truthy".

Only the number 0 is falsy here. The string "0" is a non-empty string, and every non-empty string is truthy regardless of what characters it contains. Likewise [] and {} are truthy — an empty array or object is still an object, and every object is truthy no matter how "empty" it looks.

JavaScript only has a short, fixed list of falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, and NaN. Everything else — including empty arrays, empty objects, and the string "0" — is truthy.

It logs true, false, true, false, true, false — in every pair, == says yes and === says no.

== ("loose equality") converts the two operands to a common type before comparing: "5" becomes the number 5, and true becomes the number 1. null == undefined is a special case baked into the spec — they are loosely equal to each other and to nothing else. === ("strict equality") never converts types: if the types differ, it's false immediately, no matter what the values look like.

This is why most style guides push === as the default — it avoids these type-coercion surprises entirely.

It logs A, B, C — the message inside later never appears.

A script executes as a single pass, top to bottom, running each statement as it's reached. console.log("A") runs immediately, then the engine reaches the function later() {...} statement — but defining a function only creates it in memory, it doesn't execute the code inside. The function's body only runs when something actually calls later(), which never happens here.

This trips up beginners coming from a "run the whole file" mental model: writing a function is not the same as running it, and everything outside a function body fires exactly once, in file order, on that first pass.

The final order is A, C, B.

appendChild(b) puts B in as the only child: [B]. prepend(a) inserts A before everything currently inside the element, giving [A, B]. insertBefore(c, b) then inserts C immediately before its second argument, the existing node b, landing it between A and B: [A, C, B].

The key difference: appendChild always adds at the end, prepend always adds at the start, and insertBefore(newNode, referenceNode) is the only one of the three that lets you target a specific position relative to an existing child.

The first log prints an empty string, the second prints "Hello".

textContent = 'Hello' works by creating a text node inside original and setting that as its child. cloneNode(false) is a shallow clone — it copies the element itself (tag, attributes) but none of its children, so the text node never gets copied and shallow.textContent comes back empty. cloneNode(true) is a deep clone — it copies the element and its entire subtree, including that text node, so deep.textContent matches the original.

The argument matters because omitting it defaults to false (shallow) per spec — a common source of "my clone lost all its content" bugs.

The first log prints true; the second prints null.

parentNode returns the parent exactly as it is in the tree, whatever kind of node it happens to be — here that's the DocumentFragment, so div.parentNode === frag is true. parentElement is narrower: it only returns the parent if that parent is specifically an Element. A DocumentFragment is a node but not an element, so parentElement falls back to null instead.

The two usually agree because most parents in a real page are elements, but they diverge for the handful of non-element parents: fragments, and the document node itself — document.documentElement.parentElement is also null.

live.length is 2; snapshot.length is still 1.

getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection — it isn't a fixed list, it's a query that re-evaluates against the DOM every time you read it, so the newly appended .tag element is picked up automatically. querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList — a frozen snapshot taken at the moment it was called, which doesn't change even though the DOM does afterward.

This is a common source of bugs when code caches a getElementsByClassName result and assumes its length is fixed, or conversely expects a querySelectorAll result to pick up elements added later.

It prints true false.

classList.toggle(token, force) takes an optional second argument that turns "flip it" into "force it to a specific state." Passing true means "make sure this class is present" — add it if missing, leave it if already there, never remove it. Passing false means "make sure this class is absent" — remove it if present, leave it if already missing, never add it.

Here 'active' was already present, so toggle('active', true) is a no-op and it stays. 'hidden' was never added, so toggle('hidden', false) is also a no-op and it stays absent. Without the second argument, toggle() simply flips whatever state a class is currently in.

The first line logs {"name":"Ana"}; the second logs [1,null,null,"x"].

Inside a plain object, JSON.stringify silently drops any property whose value is undefined or a function — those keys don't exist in JSON at all, so they're simply omitted from the output. Inside an array, position matters: dropping an element would shift every index after it, so instead of omitting undefined or function values, JSON.stringify replaces each of them with null to preserve the array's length and order.

This asymmetry is easy to get bitten by — the exact same value, undefined, produces two different results depending purely on whether it sits in an object property or an array slot.

It prints {"name":"Kim","role":"admin"} — the password key is gone entirely.

The second argument to JSON.stringify can be a replacer function, which gets called once for every key/value pair being serialized (including the root object itself). Whatever the function returns is used in the output in place of that value. Returning undefined for the "password" key tells JSON.stringify to treat that property as if it were undefined, which — same as the plain-object case — gets omitted from the serialized result.

This is a common, deliberate pattern for redacting sensitive fields like passwords or tokens right at serialization time, instead of copying the object and manually deleting keys first.

It logs {"name":"Widget","price":25} — only those two keys survive.

When the second argument to JSON.stringify is an array of strings, it's treated as an allow-list: only properties whose keys appear in that array get included in the output. Everything else — id and internalCode here — is skipped entirely, even though they exist on the object.

This is the simpler alternative to a replacer function when all you need is to keep a fixed set of top-level keys, with no extra transformation logic involved.

It produces a multi-line, indented string instead of one compact line — each key ends up on its own line with 2 spaces of indentation, rather than the default single unbroken line like {"a":1,"b":2}.

The third argument to JSON.stringify controls pretty-printing. A number tells it how many spaces to use per indentation level; you can pass a string instead, like '\t', to use that string as the indent unit. Passing nothing, or 0, gives the compact single-line form.

This argument only affects whitespace, purely for human readability — it has zero effect on how JSON.parse reads the string back.

Both catch blocks log SyntaxError — neither string is valid JSON, even though both look like reasonable JavaScript object literals.

The first fails because of the trailing comma after 2 — JSON's grammar doesn't allow a comma after the last property, unlike modern JavaScript object literals, which tolerate it. The second fails because JSON requires property names and all strings to be wrapped in double quotes specifically; single quotes are never valid JSON syntax, only a valid JavaScript one.

This trips people up because both strings would be perfectly legal if typed as a JavaScript object in source code — JSON's grammar is a stricter subset of JS syntax, not the same thing.

It logs {"title":"Launch","date":"2026-01-15"}.

JSON.stringify has a rule baked in: before serializing any value, it checks whether that value has a toJSON() method, and if so, calls it and serializes that return value instead of the object's own properties. Here event.toJSON() returns a plain object with a trimmed, date-only string, so that's what ends up in the JSON — the original Date object and its full ISO timestamp are never directly serialized.

This is exactly how Date objects normally serialize too — Date.prototype defines its own toJSON() that calls toISOString(), which is why JSON.stringify(new Date()) gives a timestamp string instead of {}. Defining your own toJSON on any object lets you override how it appears in serialized output.

The first log prints 'inside'. The second line throws ReferenceError: blockScoped is not defined and the script stops there.

var is function-scoped (or global-scoped), not block-scoped — an if block does nothing to contain it, so hoisted is really attached to the surrounding function or global scope and stays readable after the block ends.

let is genuinely block-scoped: blockScoped only exists between the if's { and }. Once the block ends, the binding is gone entirely — this isn't the Temporal Dead Zone (which is about reading a binding before its declaration line, within a scope where it does exist); here the variable is simply out of scope, which is why the error message says "not defined" rather than "before initialization".

The first line logs 'hello from declaration'. The second line throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'greetExpression' before initialization.

A function declaration is hoisted completely — both its name and its entire body are set up during the creation phase, so it is fully callable from anywhere in its scope, even above its textual position.

greetExpression is different: only the const binding name is hoisted, not the function value assigned to it. The assignment happens when that line actually runs, so calling it earlier hits the Temporal Dead Zone instead of getting a usable function.

It logs ['c', 'b', 'a'].

Every function call pushes a new execution context onto the call stack, and each context stays on the stack until its function returns. By the time c() creates the Error, three contexts are stacked up: c on top (most recently entered), then b below it, then a at the bottom.

Error().stack captures those frames from the top down, which is exactly why they print in call order rather than definition order — it's a direct, inspectable snapshot of the call stack, not just a mental model.

It logs true, then 'Maximum call stack size exceeded'.

recurse has no base case, so every call immediately makes another call before returning. Each of those calls pushes a fresh execution context onto the call stack, and none of them ever get popped off.

The call stack has a fixed size limit in every JS engine. Once that limit is hit, the engine throws a RangeError instead of letting the stack grow forever — and like any other runtime error, it's a normal, catchable exception rather than a hard crash.

typeof secret logs 'undefined'. getSecret() logs 'hidden'.

secret is declared with let inside a plain { } block, so it exists only for that block — once the block ends, the name is simply out of scope outside it, not even reachable to check. typeof on a name with no visible binding just reports 'undefined' rather than throwing.

The arrow function assigned to getSecret was created inside the block, so it closed over secret at that moment. That closure keeps the variable alive and reachable through getSecret long after the block's own scope is gone from the outside world.

It logs 1, 2, 3.

level3 is defined two functions deep inside level1, but the scope chain still lets it reach all the way up to count — level2 doesn't need to reference count itself for that link to work.

level1() only runs once, creating a single count variable shared by run going forward. Each call to run() re-enters level2/level3 fresh, but they all close over that same count, so the increments accumulate across calls instead of resetting.

It logs 1, 2, 1.

Every call to makeCounter() runs the function body again, creating a brand-new count variable and a brand-new closure around it. counterA and counterB are backed by two completely separate count bindings, not one shared value.

That's why counterB() starts back at 1 instead of continuing on from counterA's 2 — closures are created per call to the outer function, not per function definition.

admin('admin') logs 'admin'. checkRole() logs 'guest'.

admin's parameter is also named role, so it shadows the outer let role for the entire body of admin — including inside the nested log function. log resolves role by walking its scope chain outward, and the nearest match it finds is the parameter, not the module-level variable.

checkRole was never nested inside admin, so its scope chain skips straight past that shadowed role to the real outer variable, which admin never touched in the first place.

Both lines log 'total: 6' — identical results.

call() and apply() both explicitly set this to whatever object you pass as the first argument, here ctx. The only real difference between them is how the remaining function arguments are supplied.

call() takes them as a plain, comma-separated argument list: sum.call(ctx, 1, 2, 3). apply() takes them bundled into a single array: sum.apply(ctx, [1, 2, 3]). Reach for apply() whenever your arguments already exist as an array and you don't want to spread them out first.

It logs 'Priya', not 'Tom'.

bind() permanently locks this to whatever object you pass it at bind time — here, userA. That lock cannot be undone or overridden later, no matter what object the bound function ends up attached to or how it's called.

Even though whoAmI is sitting on userB and gets called with normal method syntax (userB.whoAmI()), which would ordinarily bind this to userB, the hard binding from bind() takes priority over that call-site binding.

It logs true, then 'object'.

standalone() is a regular function called with no receiver at all — there's no object before the dot, so this is the classic "default binding" case. In a plain Node CommonJS file with no 'use strict' pragma, the module wrapper Node generates does not make your code strict, so ordinary sloppy-mode rules apply: an unbound this falls back to the global object, which in Node is globalThis.

This result is specific to plain CommonJS scripts. The exact same function would log undefined instead if the file started with 'use strict', or if it were loaded as an ES module (a .mjs file, or under "type": "module") — ES modules are always implicitly strict, so the global-object fallback never applies there.

It logs 'Zoe', then true.

bind() usually locks this permanently, but new is the one exception. Calling a bound function with new ignores the bound this entirely: JavaScript still constructs a brand-new object and runs the original target function against that new object, exactly like a normal constructor call.

BoundPerson still points back to the original Person function, so p comes out as a normal Person instance with its name set by the constructor call itself — the { name: 'ignored' } object passed to bind() never gets used.

It logs true, false, then 'hi'.

Object.create(proto) builds a brand-new object whose prototype is exactly the object you passed in — not a copy, the same object — which is exactly what Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) === proto confirms.

greet lives only on proto, never on obj itself, so obj.hasOwnProperty('greet') is false. That doesn't stop obj.greet() from working: property lookup walks up the prototype chain and finds it there.

It logs 'a square', then 'a shape'.

Square defines its own describe, so it shadows — completely overrides, for normal lookups — the same-named method on Shape.prototype. sq.describe() finds Square.prototype.describe first and never even reaches Shape's version.

But overriding only hides the parent's method from normal lookup, it doesn't delete it. Shape.prototype.describe still exists untouched, and nothing stops you from grabbing it directly and running it with sq as this via .call().

It logs true, true, true, true, false.

instanceof walks the entire prototype chain, checking each link against the target's .prototype, so it correctly reports true for every ancestor — Dog, Animal, and Living — no matter how many extends hops away it is.

Object.getPrototypeOf() works differently: it only ever returns the single immediate parent. For a Dog instance that's Dog.prototype, not Animal.prototype. To reach Animal.prototype or beyond, you'd have to call Object.getPrototypeOf() again on each result, one step at a time.

It logs 'shape', 4, then ['sides'].

Object.create() takes a rarely-used second argument that defines own properties directly on the new object using property-descriptor syntax, the same shape Object.defineProperty uses. That's how obj ends up with its own sides property set to 4.

kind is never an own property of obj — it's only inherited from proto — but that doesn't stop obj.kind from resolving through the prototype chain. Object.keys() only lists own enumerable properties, so it prints ['sides'] and leaves the inherited kind out entirely.

Array.from(pair()) and [...pair()] both log [ 1, 2 ] — the string 'ignored' from the return never appears in either array.

Both Array.from and the spread operator drive the generator's iterator protocol by calling .next() repeatedly and collecting values only while done is false. The final call, where done becomes true and value is 'ignored', is where collection stops — that last value is discarded by both consumers.

This is why a generator's return value is really a signal for manual .next() consumers (or delegation via yield*), not a way to append a final item to a spread or array conversion.

It logs generating 1, generating 2, generating 3, then [ 1, 2, 3 ] — even though naturals() loops forever, it only ever runs three iterations.

take pulls the generator's iterator directly and calls .next() exactly n times. Each call resumes the paused while (true) loop just long enough to run one more console.log and hit the next yield, then execution suspends again until the next call.

That's the practical payoff of generator laziness: an infinite sequence stays safe to use as long as something like take(n) controls how many values get pulled, instead of trying to materialize the whole sequence at once.

It logs b c, not a b.

Array destructuring on an iterable works by calling its Symbol.iterator method and then pulling values with .next(). A generator object is its own iterator, so gen()[Symbol.iterator]() returns the same it — there's no separate fresh iterator to restart from the top.

Because it.next() already consumed 'a' before the destructuring line ran, the destructuring picks up wherever it currently is: x gets 'b' and y gets 'c'.

The first spread logs [ 1, 2, 3 ]. The second logs [] — an empty array, not a fresh [1, 2, 3].

counter makes itself both the iterable and the iterator: [Symbol.iterator]() returns this instead of building a new iterator object each time. So both spreads call .next() on the exact same object, and current only ever counts up — after the first spread it's already sitting at 4.

Contrast this with a generator function like function* counter() {...}: calling counter() a second time creates a brand-new generator object with its own fresh state. An object that hands out this as its own iterator is single-use across independent iterations unless it explicitly resets its state.

It logs Ada Lovelace, then Grace Lovelace.

fullName is an accessor property defined with get syntax right inside the object literal — it isn't a stored value, it's a function that runs fresh every time person.fullName is read. There's nothing cached from the first read.

That's the difference from a plain data property computed once and assigned: changing firstName automatically changes what the next read of fullName returns, with no extra code needed to keep the two in sync.

normal's descriptor is { value: 1, writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true }. special's is { value: 2, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false } — every flag defaults to false.

A property created with ordinary object-literal syntax gets writable, enumerable, and configurable all set to true automatically. Object.defineProperty works differently: any flag you don't explicitly list is filled in as false, not copied from that same default.

This is a common trap — defining a property with only value silently produces a locked-down, hidden, unconfigurable property unless you deliberately pass writable: true, enumerable: true, and so on.

config.env stays 'prod', but config.retries becomes 5 — the log reads prod 5.

Unlike Object.freeze, which locks down every property on an object at once, Object.defineProperty lets you target a single property. Redefining just env with writable: false makes that one assignment silently fail (this runs in non-strict mode, so no error is thrown), while retries — untouched — remains a perfectly ordinary writable property.

This selective locking is useful when only specific fields, like an ID or a fixed config key, need to be immutable while the rest of the object stays editable.

It logs setter ran, v = 5, then after assign: 50, then after spread: 0 — the setter only fires once, for the Object.assign call.

Object.assign(target, source) copies properties using real property assignment onto the existing target, so it triggers whatever setter target already has for that key — here count's setter runs and multiplies the value by 10 into _count.

Object spread instead builds a brand-new object literal from scratch, and object-literal properties are always defined directly rather than assigned through a setter. It reads count off the source (getting undefined, since makeState() only defines a setter, no getter), and the trailing count: 5 in the literal simply defines a plain data property — no setter anywhere is ever invoked, so _count is left at its untouched default of 0.

It logs 32.

compose uses reduceRight, which walks the fns array from the last element to the first. So transform(3) applies addOne first (3 → 4), then square (4 → 16), then double (16 → 32) — the rightmost function in the argument list runs first.

That right-to-left order is the whole point of the name compose: compose(double, square, addOne)(x) reads like the nested calls double(square(addOne(x))), mirroring mathematical function composition.

It logs [ 2, 4, 6 ].

reduce walks the array once, carrying an accumulator that starts as []. For each item, the predicate decides whether to fold it into a new array with [...acc, item] or leave the accumulator unchanged — that's a complete reimplementation of filter's behavior using only reduce.

This works because reduce is the more fundamental operation: map, filter, and plenty of other array methods can all be expressed as a fold over the array with the right accumulator logic, even though each has its own dedicated, more readable method in everyday code.

It logs [undefined] (auth) token expired — not the presumably intended [WARN] (auth) token expired.

bind only pre-fills arguments from the left. The goal here was to fix module to 'auth' while leaving level to be supplied later, but bind has no way to skip over an earlier parameter — the only way to reach the second argument is to also supply something for the first, and undefined was used as a placeholder, which then prints literally.

This is the real limitation of positional partial application with bind: it can only pre-fill a contiguous run of arguments starting at position zero. Fixing a later argument while leaving an earlier one open needs a small wrapper function instead of bind.

The first line logs [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] — both variables show the mutated array, because push changes original in place and result1 is just a reference to that same array. The second line logs [ 1, 2, 3 ] [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] — original2 is untouched, and result2 is a distinct new array.

addImpure has a side effect: anything else holding a reference to original sees the change too, even though it never called addImpure itself. addPure instead builds a new array with the spread operator and leaves its input alone, so the only way to get the updated list is through its return value.

Same inputs, same apparent job, observably different effects on shared state — that's exactly why pure functions are easier to reason about in a codebase where the same data gets passed around to multiple places.

question: Your app uses NgModules everywhere, and a teammate wants to move to standalone components. What's one real benefit, and one migration cost we'd need to plan for?
answer:
The main benefit is less indirection. A standalone component lists its own dependencies in its imports array, so there's no wrapper module to keep in sync, and a single component can be lazy-loaded with loadComponent without building a feature module just to hold it.

{
  path: 'settings',
  loadComponent: () => import('./settings.component').then(m => m.SettingsComponent)
}

The main cost is the bridge work. Libraries built around forRoot() and forChild() still expect modules, so their providers have to come in through importProvidersFrom(). Per-component imports arrays can also get long without the shared module that used to bundle common imports.

Because the two models work together, the migration is usually done file by file rather than as one big rewrite.
hint: Weigh boilerplate removal against what existing code and libraries assume about modules.

question: A new engineer puts a stateful service in a feature module's providers array instead of using providedIn: 'root'. When does that actually make a difference, and when doesn't it?
answer:
It makes a difference when the feature module is lazy-loaded. Every lazy module gets its own child injector, so a service listed in its providers array becomes a separate instance scoped to that module. It won't share state with the instance the rest of the app gets from providedIn: 'root'.

When the module is eagerly imported (for example by AppModule), its providers are merged into the root injector. Only one injector is involved, so the result is a single app-wide instance, exactly like providedIn: 'root'.

One difference remains even then: providedIn: 'root' is tree-shakable, so an unused service is dropped from the bundle, while a service listed in a providers array always ships.
hint: The deciding factor is whether the module ever gets its own separate child injector.

question: A common rule says SharedModule should only declare and export components, pipes and directives, and never provide services. What goes wrong if we break that rule?
answer:
SharedModule is usually imported by several feature modules, and some of them are lazy-loaded. Each lazy module has its own child injector, so a service listed in SharedModule's providers array gets a new instance for every lazy module that imports it.

@NgModule({
  declarations: [PriceDisplayComponent],
  exports: [PriceDisplayComponent],
  providers: [CartService] // one CartService per lazy module that imports this
})
export class SharedModule {}

Nothing throws an error, so the bug is quiet: two features that both "use the same service" end up with separate state that doesn't sync. App-wide services belong in providedIn: 'root' instead.
hint: Trace what happens to a provider the moment more than one lazy module imports the module that declares it.

question: What's the difference between listing a service in a standalone component's providers and using providedIn: 'root'? How many instances do we get when the component appears in several places?
answer:
With providedIn: 'root', there's exactly one app-wide instance, however many times the component appears on screen.

With the component's own providers array, every instance of the component gets a new instance of the service, created and destroyed along with it.

@Component({
  selector: 'app-counter',
  standalone: true,
  providers: [CounterService], // a new CounterService per <app-counter>
  template: '{{ counter.value() }}'
})
export class CounterComponent {
  counter = inject(CounterService);
}

If <app-counter> is rendered five times, there are five separate CounterService instances, each with its own state. That's useful for per-widget state, and a bug when the state was meant to be shared.
